1813200: On Date at ZZZ airport, I fueled the airplane, conducted a preflight (includes checking oil quantity and taking a sample of all three fuel sumps), reviewed my direct course back home and updated my weather (VMC) for the short flight to ZZZ1. During the pre-takeoff checklist (engine run up), I notice a slight roughness in the engine. I leaned out the mixture control which cleared out the roughness. I set the mixture control for my takeoff, but not to full rich. I left it leaned out a little for the departure and climb. During my climbout, I always look for off airport landing spots (should I need one). I did not see any good locations and I told myself that I want 4,500 feet once clear of the Class B airspace altitudes. It was shortly after my desire to get to 4,500 feet MSL ASAP that the engine was not performing as it should in cruise climb. I applied full power and checked the engine instruments (all green, but RPM was towards the low end). I was getting a shallow climb at an airspeed of about 90. I then immediately performed the initial emergency procedure, carb heat on, mixture full (then adjust if needed) and check fuel selector on both. That seemed to bring the performance back, but not immediately. Shortly after that the engine then started to run rough. My thought was spark plug fouling or magneto (I know it was not a cylinder failure, because I have experienced that in a twin engine airplane). I adjusted the mixture control first. This is logical, because if you check the mags before the mixture control you could increase spark plug fowling. At some point through all this my mind went into altitude, altitude, altitude. Unfortunately, I had that 4,500 feet MSL in my mind. While dealing with the engine situation, I continued my climb to that altitude. I got the rough running engine cleared out. Once I was done keeping the airplane in the air (dealing with low performance and then the rough running engine during the cruise climb phase), I checked my position and noticed that I was in ZZZ3 Class B airspace (west end of and close to the 6,000 feet MSL corridor, but I was in the 4,000 feet MSL corridor). I immediately descended below 4,000 feet MSL (3,800 feet MSL). Once clear of the Class B airspace/Mode C veil, I climbed back to 4,500 feet MSL. No airplane conflicts were noted. Once on the ground at the ZZZ1, I performed an engine runup and checked the mags full and leaned mixture settings. Both checked out okay. My plan is to check the oil, fuel and talk with a mechanic. I am confident that the fuel is okay since I checked it after fueling at the ZZZ (but I will check it again). I have cancelled my planned flying for the next week and no flying the Skyhawk until the items are checked out. Once I got home, I chair flew the scenario that I just experienced and realized that all my training and personal home chair flying has been geared to multi-engine, on an IFR flight plan and in radio communications. My scenario was single engine, VFR and not in communication. Do not get me wrong, I always review the emergency procedures before a flight for the airplane that I am flying. Also, the poor engine performance that I experienced did not seem to be carb icing. Since the air filter and bracket were replaced at the annual inspection, the carb air intake system will be looked at. What I learned and what I will do going forward so that this does not happen again:I learned that in my continued personal chair flying training that I need to go over single engine emergency, VFR and not in communications scenarios. This situation reinforced with me that single engine performance (VFR, non-communications) incidents come with a high workload especially when dealing with keeping the airplane in the air. It showed me that I became focused on keeping the plane in the air (altitude and rectifying the engine situation) and that navigating and communicating was lacking with this incident. Going forward, in addition to reading theemergency procedures that I currently do for every plane that I fly and chair flying multi-engine scenarios, I will chair fly single engine (SE) scenarios. I need to emphasize aviate, navigate, and communicate in any SE situation. When flying under Class B airspace and within a Mode C veil do the following:1. Obtain flight following when flying VFR, especially when flying in a Mode C veil. I would already be in communications should I need to report a problem. 2. Mark along the course line a line with an arrow from the departure airport to the point when the plane will be cleared of the Mode C veil. Also, put a B next to this manually drawn line.3. Apply a post-it-note on the instrument panel that I am in a Mode C veil airspace.I will talk to my Flight Instructor and review this flight to obtain feedback and discuss my ideas and additional ways to prevent this from happening again.
1813228: The WEAZL4 departure off Runway 36C calls for heading 003 to 1260 ft. then 330 heading. We had just rolled out on the 330 heading when we hit the wake causing a significant roll rate to the left. The left bank angle reached approximately 45 degrees. The aircraft would not respond to full right aileron input. I made certain the yoke was full right, and the Captain joined me on the controls so I know we definitely had full right aileron in. I gently toed the right rudder and that was enough to bring the aircraft out of the roll. We had taken off immediately behind an Airbus (I do not remember the specific type). We estimate we were approx 1,800 ft. AGL.
1813254: I was working a sector with weather building. The warning areas were hot with numerous aircraft deviating into active military airspace. I was unaware at the time that the only plan was to depend on the military to take point-outs to work aircraft through that area. With no notice the adjacent sector said I can't take anymore northbound aircraft because the controlling facility will not take point-outs. At the time I had several aircraft within minutes of their airspace that required 90 degree turns to miss the sectors airspace. I had to reroute almost every aircraft on my frequency. This reroute put aircraft into weather and overloaded the next receiving sector. This last-minute major increase in workload resulting in Aircraft X not being issued weather. The aircraft flew through moderate to heavy precipitation and encountered severe turbulence which resulted in two passenger injuries.I have NO recommendations this will absolutely happen again. For the years I have been at ZJX, aircraft deviating into active military airspace is normal operations. Look at my previous reports and my co-workers in other areas. Numerous conditions happen in ZJX south area to overload the sectors that cause weather not to be called. After this incident I returned to the south area to see this exact scenario unfolding again. An air carrier flight was in active military airspace [requesting priority]. The only reason this is even being discussed is because a passenger was injured on Aircraft X. If an injury would not have occurred nobody would have investigated what was going on in the ZJX south area. This has been going on for years in the south area with numerous reports. Nothing will change and this will happen again.
1813268: Descending into ZZZ at the ZZZZZ Arrival at the ZZZZZ way point, the FMC AP/RST (Flight Management Computer Auto Pilot Reset) light Illuminated at the ZZZZZ turn point, disengaging the LNAV, VNAV, and the autopilot. ATC communication was congested, and as we were troubleshooting, and attempting to communicate with ATC, the PF who was hand flying, allowed the aircraft to get high on path and deviate laterally from the course. It took several attempts to communicate with ATC and re-establish the lateral and vertical course. Doing so caused our speed to be above the charted speed at ZZZZZ1, and ATC cleared us on a heading and descent below the ZZZZZ1 fix restriction. The Pilot Flying hand flew until on the base turn, the autopilot was re-engaged in the Heading Select and Vertical Speed mode.Landed safely, and the malfunction was reported to Maintenance Control and documented in the logbook. This was my second leg in a MAX 8 aircraft in more than two years, and the aircraft differences, although not great, were distracting and likely aggravated the situation.As always, when automation fails or malfunctions, select another mode or turn it off, and revert to basic airmanship and fly the aircraft. Do not get buried in troubleshooting. Lost LNAV over ZZZZZ2 fix got a AP RST yellow light. Couldn't reset anything. Hand flew, we were high and fast over ZZZZZ1.
1813302: I was the pilot monitoring and my captain was the pilot flying. The aircraft in front of us reported a drone at about 4,200 ft on final landing on into ZZZ. ATC told us about the possible drone on final. At about 3,500 ft at almost the final approach fix we see a drone pass off the right side maybe within 50 ft of us. 1813322: Event occurred during descent phase. Captain was the pilot monitoring, First Officer (F/O) was the pilot flying. Aircraft had sat for several days down for maintenance. [The maintenance airport] experienced heavy rainfall for an extended period prior to flight. Flight was uneventful until the descent phase of flight. At approximately FL220, the radar showed 'Weather (WX) FAIL' accompanied by a grinding noise, as if the radar was stuck on one side of the sweep. Radar was secured. At approximately 15,000 MSL and 325 knots in the descent, an additional loud bang and excessive airflow noise occurred, accompanied by multiple EICAS messages, including 'IAS DISAGREE.' Captain's side display was showing approximately 250 knots. F/O's side display was showing approximately 330 knots, which agreed with standby instrumentation. F/O called for 'AIRSPEED UNRELIABLE' checklist. The autopilot and autothrottles (A/T) were disengaged, and the A/T ARM switch was turned off. F/O continued flying manually throughout the remainder of the flight. Captain elected to leave the Flight Directors on, as the lateral guidance was still valid, we were VMC, and at that range we already had the field in sight. It was agreed that the F/O would disregard the pitch guidance until the instrumentation issue could be corrected. Captain continued running through the checklist from the QRH, it was determined that the F/O's instrumentation was valid, and the Captain selected the right side Air Data Compute (ADC). From that point forward, as we slowed to 250 knots, the airplane essentially flew normally. F/O continued to manually hand fly the descent and approach to an uneventful landing. After inspection, the aircraft was taxied back normally. On post-flight inspection, the radome had a large structural failure, which likely caused an asymmetric airflow disruption which affected the Captain's instrumentation.
1813324: Taxi clearance: taxi from ramp position XX, right turn onto W3, left turn EW, right turn S7A, then S7, hold short S7C. As a crew, we were a little bit tired from our 1st leg in the middle of the night, our scheduled ground stop time plus the delay as maintenance took care of a Pressure Regulating Valve issue. In any case, if you take a look at the VVNB Airport Moving Map (AMM) taxi chart, it appears as though EW is a separate taxiway. The color differentiation of light gray versus the ramp coloration of dark gray gives the impression we would be taxiing from the ramp onto a separate, defined taxiway, not onto a yellow line that is at the outer edge of a parking ramp. In addition, S1 (the taxiway that is adjacent and parallel to EW) had green lights illuminated, again giving the impression S1 was the active taxiway EW. So as we taxied via W3, EW looks like it's part of the ramp. In other words it does not appear to be EW taxiway. S1 appears to be EW. The poor signage does not help as well. Clearly the main issue here is that we had never been to Hanoi and never experienced this. That said, as we taxied out and entered S6A, the intersection between EW and S1, my copilot notified me we had passed EW. We stopped there. We advise ground we missed EW and needed to take S1. Ground control gave us S1, routed us back onto EW, then S7A, S7 and then our takeoff. That said, no conflict with any traffic, only one maybe two other aircraft moving on the airport at that time. Ultimately it was a non critical event. To help prevent this from happening in the future, a caution note regarding taxiing at any time (i.e. taxing in or taxing out) when given EW would be helpful. After setting up the cockpit for the ZZZZ1-ZZZZ leg, we sat in the back to rest while Maintenance was working with an MEL item. The aircraft was one hour later than schedule to allow extra time for maintenance. Fatigue was now starting to show after two 18-24hr overnights in lockdown. After final setup and brief, we received our taxi clearance, from spot XX, E3.EW.S7A.S7.S7C hold short [Runway] 11L. We discussed the route that appeared clearly marked on the Airport Moving Map (AMM) page and began taxiing. We realized we had crossed beyond the centerline of EW and were unable to make the turn and stopped. After calling the controller of our position, he gave us S1.S6A.EW....the rest was normal. Looking back, the green taxi lights were lit on S1.S6A.EW and FD Pro AMM page in dark mode makes EW look very different from the ramp area. Expectation bias may have played a role in how controllers have started using follow the greens (used in SIN but not in HAN) and what we interpret as a clearance. I will personally pay closer attention to where we are in the future.
1813350: An initial takeoff roll, my copilot said airspeed alive and I said checked, then my copilot said 80 knots and I said checked and then immediately got a indicated airspeed disagreement on the Captains airspeed indicator the copilot had the same thing and I rejected the takeoff. We notified Tower and returned back to the gate.IAS DISAGREE on both the Captain and Copilot IAS.I return to the gate and turn the aircraft over to Maintenance. I also took the passengers off the airplane and put them into the terminal building where it was much cooler. On initial takeoff roll I called out airspeed alive then 80 knots. The 'IAS DISAGREE' indicator cam on and I announced 'airspeed disagree'. The Captain rejected the takeoff. We notified the Control Tower and exited the runway, back to the terminal.Visual detection 'IAS DISAGREE' in yellow letters.IAS DISAGREE indications on both displays.Performed rejected takeoff, and returned to the gate where maintenance was performed.
1813366: The crew flew the RNAV X RWY to 34R at RNO in day clear weather with winds reported at 260/26G31. During the flare, the crew executed a go around due to a strong gust destabilizing the approach. During climb out, the Tower Controller called the winds stronger out of the West and suggested a visual approach to Runway 25. Although having reviewed the 10-7 Special Considerations page earlier in the flight, the crew did not recall the takeoff and landing restriction on Runway 25.The crew configured for a 5 mile visual approach to Runway 25, then briefed and commenced the approached. Descending on the approach with the terrain visible and safely below the aircraft, it became apparent that the terrain east of the airport would not allow a safe approach. At approximately the same time, our descent rate in combination with the terrain resulted in a brief 'Terrain' warning, the pilot flying adjusted the aircraft flight path and then executed a go-around. The crew then flew and landed from the RNAV X to RWY 34R. I believe rushing and a false sense of familiarity with the airport led to an incomplete recognition of all the information in the 10-7 pages. I have operated into RNO regularly but not often and always to light winds down the primary runway. Arrivals and approaches are briefed extensively and flown according to standards. The day of the event, we conducted a thorough briefing for the approach, to include reviewing the operating manual about the exact procedures for executing the EO (Engine out) SIDs at RNO and which RNAV approaches we were authorized to fly.Despite my review, to include Special Considerations/Restrictions, I did not refresh the [Runway] 7/25 restriction in my mind and in the moment I did not recall the critical restriction. Additionally at the time, I did not feel like we rushed the visual approach. However, I now realize that I was focused too much on flying a stable visual approach and landing into the wind and not taking the time to truly review the approach and missed approach. Take the time to thoroughly familiarize yourself with all the applicable notes during your airport review and briefings. RNAV X 34R to RNO in day VMC, reported winds were very close to limits (260/26 G31). Due to an extremely strong gust which destabilized our approach we executed a go around. After max effort go around and stabilized climbing clean, Tower suggested we use Runway 25. Even though we had both reviewed the 10-7 pages earlier in the flight, at that particular moment we did not recall the prohibition to landing on that Runway. After agreeing that we would look at it, I as Pilot Monitoring set up the box for a visual by extending a 3 degree GS to an extended 5 mile Center Line to give us VTI.The Pilot Flying double checked the 10-9A page and the landing app. While still considering this option, we maneuvered towards the extended Center Line and set and then descended to an altitude above the depicted altitude in that area. Our rate of descent combined with rising terrain triggered the EPGWS (Ground Proximity Warning System) to a 'TERRAIN' call. The Pilot Flying immediately altered his flight path and the terrain remained visible and well below us. It became abundantly clear that a stable approach would not be possible and we abandoned this option. We opted for another attempt at the RNAV 34R, and despite strong gusty crosswinds were able to maintain a stable condition to touchdown and landing.Things I have taken away from this event: The winds Tower reports may not be the winds you experience at the Runway. By sticking to a ridged stable approach and associated Standard Operating Procedure's mantra we kept from bending metal, violating a FAR, exceeding a limit or attempting something really stupid. And although RNO is a complex city and we review the notes every time we go there, the [Runway] 25 note was momentarily forgotten. We reviewed the 10-9a pages but somehow forgot to review the 10-7 pages in that situation. A mistake I (or my First Officer) will never make again.I firmly believe that this is a onetime incident. A few moments either way and we would have missed the gust and landed uneventfully. And I have a hard time imagining that another crew, or me again, would ever forget the 10-7 notes in a complex city. But again thanks to our training department's dogma regarding stable approaches, we are self-reporting not something far worse.
1813371: Departed [Runway] 26R ONT on the RAJEE3. Controller was extremely busy. Leveled at 7,000 [feet]. Approaching ELLBO wondering if we were going to get 8,000 [feet] or the restriction. Made several radio calls but were ignored. Finally got cleared to 8,000 [feet]. I don't remember the exact distance past ELLBO, but we were left at 8,000 [feet] until what appeared to be within 30 to 40 KM of significantly rising terrain based on GPWS display. The Controller kept telling everyone to not call. We finally tried to call a few times to no avail. I was seriously considering my options if I couldn't get a hold of the Controller regarding terrain clearance. We finally got a hurried call to expedite to 13,000 [feet] call, which we did. I don't want to make a huge deal about this but it felt like we were on the edge of things getting very interesting regarding terrain clearance. Controller busy with planes on approaches and putting off other traffic. I certainly don't know but I might have heard a voice change so possibly training in progress. I know it gets hectic but ATC should at least acknowledge you're there when leaving you low or at an abnormal altitude.
1813388: I was the Relief First Officer sitting in the right aft seat with a very limited view of the PFD;s and MFD;s of the aircraft. Shanghai Approach Control issued us a different arrival than what the company had filed and what we already had planned. The communications were ambiguous at best and we all agreed to get a clarification on which arrival was being issued. There were four arrivals that had the suffix '81A'. The pronunciation was tough to understand. It took some clarification but we all confirmed the new arrival as the 'DUM 81A' arrival. At some point after DUMET there was a transmission from Shanghai Approach to 'comply with all restrictions' At the same time the PF was slowing down and trying to get down with deploying the speed brakes to meet the restrictions of PD230. Shanghai approach made the same transmission again. I unbuckled my seat belt to stand up see what the displays were showing and wanted to confirm the altitude in the alt window was correct. It was set correctly to 6,980 feet which was equivalent to 2,100 meters issued to us. The aircraft showed a little high on the path but was correcting and it showed very close to the speed restriction of 230 kts. I sat back down and verified the restrictions on my tablet. There was a lot of foreign language chatter on the radio. Upon crossing the fix, Shanghai issued a clearance direct to MPI which was the IAF for the approach to [Runway] 16L. It wasn't until after we landed that the PF and PM were talking about being high over the PD230 fix however they agreed they were on speed.Understanding which arrival they were trying to issue took more time than necessary. The pronunciation of the arrival was very hard to understand. This complicated things more than usual and it cost time. The frequency congestion in a foreign language complicated things when trying to get them to repeat the clearance. On a side note this was the first time I've ever heard an approach clearance to a runway with a Left designator as 'Cleared for 16 Lima' ...the PM was corrected to say 16 Lima after she responded with 16 Left. it didn't make sense. When passed on to the Tower Controller, they correctly said 16 Left.My only suggestion is if you look high on a path, Flight Level Change works pretty good to hustle down to the altitude. I can't say for sure if this descent was done in PATH or FLC. The language barrier is what it is and probably won't change much. I was the pilot monitoring. On 123.8, China approach cleared us for Dum81A, Comply with restrictions. FO crossed PD230 on speed at 230 KT. And high. I could not ask for altitude relief due to frequency congestion. We were filed for Dum92A. There was confusion among the crew about the assigned arrival. We queried Approach again. The verification of the clearance and the CDU, contributed to our delayed descent.Ask China control (previous frequency) which arrival is planned. So we definitely would know earlier.
1813397: Equipment overheat EICAS msg. Followed checklist. Checklist said land at nearest suitable airport.
1813401: On descent, we received a L hydraulic system pressure message The First Officer continued to fly and i worked through the QRH. After running the QRH we decided to [advise] with ZZZ Approach. We also had a jumpseater in the back who had just transitioned from the B757 to the [aircraft] so I asked if he would join us in the cockpit as an extra set of eyes. At this time the left hydraulic fluid was so low that alternate means had to be used to extend LE and TE flaps and the landing gear. After an extended down wind to configure we advised the Tower that we would need [to be] towed off of the runway and would be making a full stop on Runway XXL. Captain's landing was smooth and light braking was used and the airplane was brought to a stop at [taxiway] 1X and shut down. After arriving at the gate, the First Officer, jumpseater and I went inside to go over it as I was curious to see what things i could have done better. I had full intention of immediately calling the [Chief Pilot] right after this, but in the mix, I forgot and didn't speak to him for almost an hour and a half. I also did not put that [we advised ATC] in the write up. Being my first [priority event] with the maintenance software I selected the '[advised ATC]' switch to yes and made the wrong assumption that this would suffice. Lesson learned. On descent into ZZZ, a Left Hydraulic System Pressure malfunction illuminated. I was Flying Pilot and continued to fly while the Captain commenced QRH procedures for the associated malfunction. Once the QRH procedures were completed, we [advised] ZZZ Approach. We elected to get our one jumpseater who is typed in the B757 and [aircraft] to assist as needed in the cockpit. With loss of left hydraulic fluid, we needed to lower flaps/slats and landing gear via alternate means. Both procedures were properly completed as per the QRH. We notified ATC that we would need assistance upon landing and that we would be a full stop on the runway. Landing was uneventful and shutdown was per QRH and normal procedures while on Runway XXL. Normal communications were established with ZZZ rescue. Company maintenance personnel arrived to the aircraft and towed the jet to Gate XX without incident. Fire/Rescue escorted jet to gate, no services required. Suspected hydraulic system pressure/fluid loss on left hydraulic system.
1813403: Received ACARS from an A-300 that stated 'emergency loss yellow hyd'. Acknowledged message and replied to let me know if they needed any additional help on my end. Notified Dispatch Manager and freight recovery accordingly. Station [personnel] observed crew talking with Maintenance at ZZZ via ground radio before landing. In addition they did not observe emergency equipment being deployed on field. Flight landed safely without incident.

During boarding the number 2 flight attendant report to the cockpit, there was an odd smell entering the aircraft when they boarded. And then the number 1 repeated the claim, also to the cockpit. And spent X days there in the hotel. I was grounded for additional time, because I had fluid in my lungs. I went to the ER [at domicile]. I found out I still had carbon monoxide poising still in my blood, X days later. After a couple days. I went to the Company clinic in the airport at ZZZ2. I was told by the doctor he would not release me to come back to work, he felt I was unsafe to fly. He wanted me to see a neurology doctor. Also I know the aircraft in question was grounded in ZZZ1 for at least X days, waiting on a part. This whole incident could have been avoided, if the Captain investigated before we closed the door and went to ZZZ1.
1813458: I mentioned to the Captain the fume in the cabin. Our Number 1 asked everyone to open the air vents and I asked the Captain if he wanted me to crack a door. He informed me that we never 'crack a door' because of the odor in the cabin. I was told to ask, previous to this flight a few years ago. And reassure us we can go to professional standards if someone is requesting something out of normal procedure.
1813504: Landing at ZZZ on Runway XX in Cessna Skylane, a strong gust of wind in excess of 20 knots crosswind component almost flipped the airplane. Full left aileron and right rudder kept the airplane from running off the runway or flipping. But there was a propeller strike as the plane came down on the right main then hard on the nose gear. The nose tire developed a leak and went flat over 15 minutes. The plane taxied back to the FBO without much vibration from the propeller and no abnormal engine sounds. [Current weather] information reported 11 knots from 060 and the Tower reported winds had started gusting and were erratic. I had 20 degrees of flaps in and manifold pressure of 12 inches on touchdown. On approach, the plane tracked the centerline of the runway with left aileron and rudder. The crab component was corrected at touch down before crossing Runway XY. With only a light touch the plane went airborne again a few feet only as it crossed [Runway] XY. Then bounced, started to flip with a large gust of wind. There was just enough control authority to prevent the wing from touching the runway but not enough to prevent the propeller strike. No damage was done to the air-frame and the engine continued to run smoothly. No injuries occurred.
1813505: When operating single pilot, pilot's used to crew operations should consider risks of reliance on other pilots as they would in a crew operation. Even experienced and competent pilots in the same manner as fully trained crew members specific to make and model. They may or may not have correct knowledge of procedures - they have not been tested.I preflighted the aircraft from the outside the other pilot preflighted from the inside - just like crew flying. Possibly the exit handle was not fully engaged due to maintenance action at pre-buy inspection. The aircraft had been flying for 2+45 through some notable turbulence, on descent in smooth air and passing through a wind shift (355/12-250/12), the emergency exit hatch departed the aircraft.ATC was [advised] and a safe landing ensued at ZZZ. Reports were made to Center, the FAA office, and the NTSB.
1813519: I was on a longish downwind to Runway XX at ZZZ. A local flight school was doing pattern work in a C172 using Runway XX. AWOS 070v080 degrees at 7 to 9 knots. Then another aircraft called on CTAF to announce they were going to land Runway XY. I believe the flight school C172 pilot or instructor advised Runway XX was in use at ZZZ. C33 pilot grumbled winds were calm and we should use Runway XY, acknowledging not knowing the local weather as had just departed a different airport a few miles southeast.Then C33 pilot, who at times identified a Debonair and other calls as a Bonanza, called for entering a downwind for Runway XX and I had expected them to follow me as I was established and had made calls for being in downwind for [Runway] XX. However, they turned in front of me, perhaps they had a good visual, but never called out having traffic in sight, until I identify them in my 2 o'clock. Perhaps were not as close as it seemed. I turn a little west and decide after turning base to do a go around as the C33 landed long and was still on the runway. I then executed a standard pattern and uneventful landing. Again the C172 was not a factor.
1813521: Left and nose gear lights failed to illuminate. First action was to toggle nav light switch and test the bulbs, since in this aircraft the gear lights dim when the nav light is on. Once it was confirmed that the bulbs were fine, landing gear handle was toggled. When it was returned to the DOWN position, the left and right main lights illuminated, but the nose gear light remained unlit. We reported to the ZZZ1 CTAF we would extend our downwind.I asked my passenger, a low-time private pilot, to read the checklist for a gear light failure. This included toggling the gear handle again, which we did to no avail, and utilizing the emergency gear release lever, which had no discernible effect. During this time, we noticed the ammeter showing a very high charge.A pilot on the CTAF asked if we intended to stay in the pattern and I reported our problem. They offered assistance, so I turned back to the airport and asked if anyone could visually check our nose gear. A pilot on the ground at midfield confirmed our nose gear was down during a low approach. With this information, I decided to return to ZZZ, where the aircraft is based, about 30 miles away.I initially planned to [advise ATC] at ZZZ.I called ZZZ Tower 20 miles out and explained the situation, and my concern that the nose gear was not locked, even though it was down. The Tower asked if we would like to do a flyby of the Tower for them to check the gear, which I accepted. The Tower asked for fuel amount and time, and passengers, to which I replied we had 60 gallons and plenty of time, 2 souls.We did a low approach over [Runway] XXR, and the Tower confirmed that the gear was down and locked. They asked if we would prefer to land on the north runway, which was the active runway. I said yes and planned a soft field landing to [Runway] XXL. Since the gear was locked and I was being given priority and any resources I needed, I amended my decision to [advise ATC], as I felt it would not get me anything else I might need to land safely that I wasn't already being provided.My passenger pointed out that the gear pump circuit breaker was popped. She tried pushing it in, which caused the ammeter to spike, so we pulled it out and left it out.The Tower asked if I wanted additional resources waiting on the ground. I decided no additional resources were needed, and proceeded to land using soft field technique, holding the nose gear off for most of the ground roll. Tower again confirmed nose gear was locked and I made a sharp turn to exit the runway once I confirmed steering was good.I was cleared to taxi to the plane's flight school where an airport ground personnel met me to get a report. He then asked us to call the Tower, which also asked for a report detailing my route of flight.After the plane was repaired, Maintenance reported that the gear switch actuator was replaced, but I never got an explanation for the gear pump electrical problem.
1813523: Aircraft and Drone in-flight near miss. Drone appeared off my left wing moving behind aircraft heading south east Drone heading north west
