1813610: While approaching Runway XXL in ZZZ we were given takeoff clearance while simultaneously being given the Runway Awareness Announcement that is installed in the MAX. This prevented us from fully hearing our clearance.After flying the MAX since its return, I have experienced the installed awareness functions interrupt communication approaching the runway 50% of the time. Predictably, in each instance, we have had to stop and ask ATC to repeat these clearances.I see real communication risks and hazards with this system as it currently functions in the MAX.1) When rolling out on shorter runways, it will call out runway remaining at 1000, 500 and 100 feet. A certain risk that these calls could prevent the hearing of ATC taxi instructions likely to happen at this time.2) All calls from the system (runway awareness, altitude chimes) are wired into the headsets which completely obliterates any communication that happens simultaneously. While not on this particular flight, we were listening to an important ride report from another aircraft when the altitude chime went off in our earpiece. We initially missed the information because of it.
1813633: TCAS RA. On departure from ZZZ on Runway XX, we were given left turn to 149, climb 6,000 feet. In the turn, ATC said maintain 4,000 feet for traffic at 10 o'clock at 4,500 feet. As I went wings level, I could see the helicopter at 10 o'clock within a half mile of our current position. About 3,500 feet, we got a TA. I slowed my vertical speed as I approached 4,000 feet but upon capture, we got a RA telling us to 'monitor vertical speed.' The red line for the RA was on the horizon so I pitched just below the horizon. The First Officer informed ATC of the RA and that we were in a descent. ATC responded saying we were below the MVA (Minimum Vectoring Altitude) and to get back to 4,000 feet when able. At 3,600 feet, we were clear of conflict and climbed back to 4,000 feet. We continued the departure as normal. There wasn't much room for vectoring because of the mountains surrounding the valley. I believe the helicopter was VFR because of their altitude. ATC could have possibly kept us on the ground longer or given a delayed turn until helicopter was no longer a conflict. TCAS RA on departure from ZZZ. Initially received climb via the ZZZZZ4 SID except maintain 5,000 feet. Prior to takeoff received amended clearance of left turn 149 climb 4,000 feet. ATC called traffic in the turn and we were looking. Nearing completion of turn and climb received TA followed by RA target 700 feet to 500 feet above and got the 'monitor vertical speed' we descended and made the standard callouts to ATC. At 3,700 feet ATC warned of low altitude and below MVA (Minimum Vectoring Altitude). We were VMC and received the 'clear conflict' and climbed back to 4000 feet and continued the flight uneventfully.I think ATC knew about this target prior to takeoff and that's why they amended the clearance. I believe their hands were tied with a vector because of rising terrain and altitude separation due to Minimum Vectoring Altitude. We followed our training and everything worked out, would have been worse in IMC. Captain (Pilot Flying) says he saw helicopter but I couldn't see from First Officer seat in left turn.
1813646: Responded to an RA on TCAS at 4,600 MSL. Advised ATC, ZZZ Approach Control. No response, 3 times we told Approach responding to RA. No response. Executed GA climbed out on LOC to 6,000 feet then they gave us Fly LOC to 6,000 feet. They did not respond to our 'Responding to RA' calls. I (Pilot Flying) was not actively monitoring guard 121.5, by my mistake I did not have it selected. Our radios did appear there was some static, but not a factor. We heard all other aircraft, I'm guessing ATC was shift change? Or ATC was saturated. ZZZ is a saturated airport. They normally stagger [Runway] XXR aircraft on approach with those on [Runway] XXC. Our RA was virtually next to us and within 400 feet of our altitude.
1813664: We were climbing out on the SID when we realized that our onboard weather (WX) Radar might be inoperative (INOP). Just then, ATC asked us if we would like to deviate left or right around WX. We asked if we could stay on our present heading (HDG) 325, which was a left deviation, and that our radar might be INOP. He cleared us to continue, and advise. Unbeknownst to us are present HDG would take us direct to ZZZ. The importance of that will be apparent, shortly.I transferred control to the First Officer (FO) and began to troubleshoot the problem. Finding no approved procedure I contacted Dispatch. They advised that if we cannot continue to ZZZ1, we should consider a divert to ZZZ. I determined distance, checked WX, and did a non-standard landing assessment. All were satisfactory, we would be under maximum landing weight (MAX LDG WGT) and outside visual reference showed no convective activity ahead, to the horizon. I notified dispatch that we agreed. Dispatch amended our release for diversion to ZZZ and we informed ATC. At this point we were approximately 94 nautical miles from ZZZ. I asked the FO to handle the radio while I briefed the Flight attendants (FA's) and the passengers (PAX). I briefed the FA's that we were diverting for INOP WX radar and that it would be a 'Precautionary landing'. The FO was already given a routing to ZZZ so I had an accurate arrival time. Next, I briefed the PAX and I sent the diversion report to dispatch.After, completing my briefings I rejoined the FO and he briefed me, that we were cleared direct to STAR and descending to 24000. We were told to contact ZZZ approach. I informed them of our situation and notified ATC. We completed the arrival briefing and accomplished the Descent Checklist. I called ZZZ operations to verify that they had been informed of our arrival and reconfirm our gate assignment. I asked them to send a Customer Service Manager to help with the PAX. We landed and taxied to the gate without further incident. Roughly two hours later we departed for ZZZ1 and landed there, also without further incident.The reasons for submitting this report are as follows. 1. To voluntarily share the details of our event so that the program can glean important data, and use it to remedy any deficiencies or discrepancies discovered.2. To afford me the protections guaranteed by the program, should, during the course of it's review, company discover that any actions or omissions on my part, though inadvertent and unintentional be determined to be in violation of applicable FARs or company policies. During climbout, we realized weather (WX) radar was not working. Captain (CA) transferred controls to FIRST Officer (FO) and began to troubleshoot. No approved procedure was found in QRH. CA coordinated with dispatch, who recommended ZZZ as a divert. We [notified ATC] and requested divert to ZZZ. Cleared STAR. Landed without incident. Once at gate, we coordinated with dispatch and maintenance. Once WX radar system was reset, we continued to original destination ZZZ1.System failure: Consider adding circuit breaker reset for this system in QRH. This ended up being the corrective action taken by maintenance and could have avoided diversion and lengthy delay.
1813667: Aircraft had been written up by the previous crew as having a potable water leak of unknown origin. Maintenance Techs did their inspection and could find no leaks or indication of water damage. They filled the water tank and signed the aircraft off for flight. Within 10 minutes of departure flight attendants report water tank was down to 70% and lavatory sinks had no water coming out. Within 25 minutes of departure tank was empty. We called Dispatch and Maintenance. Decision was made to return to ZZZ. Overweight landing was made because we had no idea where the water was leaking to and we did not want to expose ourselves to compounding failures. Advised ATC due to overweight landing. Landing was uneventful. ARFF followed us to the gate as we monitored brake temperatures.We suggest Maintenance review their task card for potable water leak of unknown origin and possibly make revisions.
1813681: I was conducting an SIC (Second in Command) checkride. We had just executed a missed approach out of ZZZ off the VOR-A. As we were climbing northwesterly on the missed, we got a TA for traffic at about our 2 to 3 o'clock. They were slightly above our altitude and began turning to the north as we leveled off and began heading more westerly. As we were visually searching for that traffic, we got another TA for traffic slightly below us and at 12 o'clock. We began to climb in order to climb above their altitude and continued our turn towards the west/south. I was unsure of their direction of flight and it ended up being southwesterly. We got to within 300 feet of vertical separation at the closest. Between the missed approach and the initial traffic, we were caught off guard by the second traffic alert. My suggestions is once traffic is in sight, ensure one pilot is monitoring that traffic, while the other monitors the instruments (and other traffic displays).
1813720: Crew was waiting to board. On jet bridge when chemical smell very strong came upon us. We felt like we were ingesting it. Eyes teared throat burned. Looked at the plane and first class Galley was being boarded door was opened. That's why the smell came into the jet bridge. I immediately got my eucalyptus spray and tried to breathe it in. I have asked for over a year for the actual ingredients and again no reply. After being masked during boarding on the way to ZZZ. No APU. Sweltering in back of plane. Captain said was trying to get outside air. It is absolutely horrible that we have to deal with this and feel like there is a diaper on our faces. Absolutely disgusting! Can't breathe properly, can't hear my own flying partner yesterday at all. It creates a frustration and headache asking pax and [flight attendants] to repeat themselves over and over. This is the continuous of over a year and I wrote at that time that I do not consent to this experimental tyranny. I can't see faces, can't describe anyone and it brings on anxiety when I can't even breathe. Being masked as a healthy person is the worst thing to do. It destroys our immune system.
1813732: At approximately XA:30 hours, just moments prior to boarding, I smelled a very strong, musty, wet dog like odor inside the cabin. As I walked back towards the AFT galley (at approximately mid-cabin), the odor became much stronger. I immediately called out to the lead F/A and asked her to come back to observe what I was smelling. [Lead F/A] stated she could also smell the odor. Accordingly, I immediately made my way to the cockpit. The odor became so strong that my throat started to burn, and I began coughing. I told the Captain that we were being fumed and that I was going to notify the boarding agent to immediately stop boarding in order to prevent further issues (i.e. passenger exposure.) The Captain stated that he was notifying maintenance and agreed to hold boarding. I left the aircraft (no passengers were onboard). While making my way up the jet bridge to notify the agent, customers were beginning to walk down the jet bridge since boarding had commenced. I was able to stop the passengers and advised them to stop, turn around and go back into the terminal since we were having maintenance come to the aircraft. I did not advise them why. I entered into the terminal and advised the agent in a discreet manner to stop boarding as we were experiencing an aircraft fume event. I then returned to the aircraft briefly to advise the Captain that the agent was notified. The crew exited the aircraft and we remained in the jet bridge area for a few moments until maintenance arrived. We collected our belongings and exited the jet bridge into the terminal to gain better air quality. I continued to experience a burning throat and my cough continued. At that time, it was prudent to seek medical attention, therefore, I contacted Medical to seek advisement. I was given a clinic appointment at [medical name] and was seen by a doctor accordingly.Improper aircraft maintenance was the cause.Recommendations - Contacting numerous departments, is too much following an incident like this. One call should automatically provide the needed support, guidance and direction that we require during events like this. Because this is my 3rd fume event, I was able to more quickly identify the inherent risks, take appropriate action to limit passenger exposure, and limit extended exposure, however, it was still medically concerning and we should have less calls to make following these dangerous occurrences. During the preflight the ground air was not sufficient to cool the aircraft. I had the ground crew turn off the ground air and the CA started the APU. After APU start, the CA started the APU BLEED. Almost immediately the CA and I smelled something strange. It did not smell terrible right away but it was cause for investigation. No passengers were on board yet. A FA came up to the flight deck saying he noticed a smell. At the point I radioed maintenance about the problem and we all exited the aircraft. A few minutes later the maintenance staff said they could smell the problem in the jetway. The whole crew then started the Fume Event process. We were all checked out at the on airport [company name] clinic. Reporter stated the cause was Aircraft XXX [which] is a known Fume Event multiple offender. I remember from my walk around that the belly of the aircraft had a high amount of oil streaks. When was this last belly washed? Airbus knows this is a problem and does not take it seriously. Reporter suggested company take known Fume Event aircraft out of service. Use them for parts, excluding the APU. Put filters like [other air carriers] has to protect crews and passengers. Implement bad air detection systems.
1813764: After T/O (takeoff) from ZZZ on Runway XX, I accidentally climbed into class C airspace. Initially the plan was to T/O on Rwy XY. The wind was almost a direct crosswind. while taxing to XY from the GA ramp, a small jet taxied out from someones residence coming the opposite direction. I asked if he was taxiing for T/O. He said yes, on Rwy XX. He said he had already advised ZZZ he was using that runway on an IFR clearance. I advised him I would change runways and follow him to RWY XX. That was mistake number one. I then moved the scale of the display window down to the lowest scale for taxi information. I had never been to this airport. I forgot to expand the scale before T/O which did not allow me to see clearly where Class C space was located after T/O. Mistake number two. After T/O I began an immediate left turn to avoid ZZZ Class C airspace and prepared to call to pick up my IFR clearance. It was bumpy due to afternoon surface heating. I reached for my pen to copy my clearance from ZZZ. I knocked my pen in the floor. Mistake number three. I thought first I will establish a heading on course away from ZZZ. I looked at the flight display screen for my initial fix only to realize my flight plan had dropped out. Before departure I was showing a friend how to load a flight plan from my mobile device. I shut the display down to start the engines and forgot the flight plan would drop out and need to be reloaded. Mistake number four. So, no initial heading information was available. at that point I tried to retrieve my pen to get the clearance. while my head was down in the floor I climbed to around 1,500 feet. 300 feet inside class C airspace. Mistake number five. I called ZZZ for clearance and was instructed to remain clear of Class C. Due to the partial disorientation of not having a route, I wasn't sure whether I was in it or not. to be safe I descended to 1000 feet and reloaded the flight plan. The point here is after a series of mistakes I ended up with an airspace deviation. How could it have turned out differently? I could have used the autopilot. I could have used my spare pen. I still could have departed [Runway] XY after the jet departed [Runway] XX. I should have checked that my flight plan was still in the aircraft's computer.
1813786: We were enroute back to home base in early evening on after dropping passengers. Two Crew were onboard. First indication of any concern was a 'Chip Detect' annunciation. Following the checklist all oil temps and pressures were noted and observed normal. While in cruise we began noting very small needle deflections in the oil pressure and the real likelihood that the left engine was in distress. Following the checklist we began a decent to single engine altitude and prepared for an engine shut down. Within short time of this action the engine began to loose power and fail. Engine securing procedures were followed using the checklist ATC was advised. We were still at higher altitude over and passing ZZZ [Airport] so several options were available as far as final landing destination. Given the current state of runways at home (Only +/-3900ft available per NOTAM) and lack of any onsite support service that might be needed we decided to reverse course and divert to ZZZ, without further incident we landed safely.
1813810: On final approach for landing on Runway 18 at TME, aircraft switched to Tower frequency. Tower advised crew to call a five mile final to Runway 18. Approaching the five mile call, crew noticed Aircraft Y coming from the right to left directly in front of crewed aircraft. Crew was getting ready to call the five mile distance, but instead crew executed an immediate left turn to avoid a collision and notified the tower of the situation. Crew continued left turn per tower instructions and climbed to 2,000 feet. Crew was advised to fly back towards the runway at 2,000 feet and contact Departure Control. Departure Control gave crewed aircraft vectors for right downwind and crew conducted an uneventful landing at TME. Crew was advised by tower personnel on the ground that there is no radar at the field and they depend on position reports. Crew was approaching the five mile call when they noticed Aircraft Y cut in front of the crewed aircraft. Crew asked the tower personnel if the Tower knew the aircraft was inbound then why did they not inquire the position of our aircraft before they turned Aircraft Y.
1813818: I, RPIC, was tasked with conducting cell tower inspections in the greater pacific northwest area for the drone company. I was using a drone that had known issues with camera gimbal yet with no other options or support from the company, I had to continue to fly with this drone. This drone was known for its gimbal locking and or becoming unresponsive to the drone's heading when flown. Problems with this drone were brought to my attention by my flight trainer prior to me taking over the drone, and I had also informed my mission coordinator of the problems with the gimbal after I had taken over the drone to continue the operation. Upon take off, I encountered the gimbal lock again. Before I could land and calibrate the gimbal, a substantial gust overcame my area of operation from the West/Southwest. As a reactionary response, I pushed the right stick forward (into the Southern Direction) to send the drone away from the traffic behind me, to the North. The gusts appeared to be above the operational limits of the drone and I adjusted the right and left stick to aim into the wind. I looked back up in the air to find the drone to evaluate if it was safe to do an emergency landing into the grand land, or to find a safe descend path. With the gimbal unresponsive to the drone's heading, I was unable to correctly judge the drone's flight path which was directly into an oncoming tree. This tree was outside my operational area, and therefore was above my MOCA (Minimum Obstacle Clearance Avoidance). It was not my intent to fly beyond my operational area, but as an inadvertent contingency for safety of those on the road, the safest area for an emergency landing was beyond the grounds of the tower. My thought was that the grass seed would have been a suitable/softer area to land, versus the hard gravel of the maintenance road, or induce the hazardous possibility of a highway incursion with highway traffic. The justification for my flight response is that by flying towards the grass seed land, I would have absolutely mitigated the risk of causing serious injury or death, and or substantial damage by causing an aviation accident with the highway or any case that could have been defined by the 49 CFR 830. By the time I reacted to the tree being in frame of my camera, my counter maneuvers did not prevent the drone from colliding with the tree. The anti-collision sensors of the drone also did not prevent the drone from colliding with the tree. The drone has and always was in Position Hold mode and was not deviated from. Even with the wind gusts pushing the drone to its limit, the anti-collision sensors should have detected the tree and stopped the aircraft from colliding with the tree or at least assisted my counter maneuvers in preventing the accident. In response to the weather, my anemometer was reading 2-9 mph on the ground. This wave of gusts was unexpected and arbitrary to the regular wind speeds I had been enduring for the entire site audit. To the Southwest, I did notice very dark cumulonimbus clouds which may have been a severe thunderstorm forming, which may have caused instability upwind. I was able to find the drone near the tree in the grass seed bush. The camera has completely broken off, the landing gear had sustained fractures, the main profile has been disconnected, and one propeller was broken. This drone is not safe to fly in its current state and will need repair from manufacturer. In this flyaway accident, there was no serious injury, death, or substantial damage that occurred beyond the aircraft and the surrounding environment. I wanted to bring this accident to light because of the post crash situation. The drone was lost in grass seed bushes that were at least 4-5ft tall. I had to walk through the bush with my best guesses to where the drone was actually at. Since the drone battery had disconnected with the drone, I was not able to use the GPS homing software on the tablet to find where the drone was. After some timesearching, I eventually found the drone and the camera. But I have yet to find the battery. From my understanding of the DJI drones, if the battery is disconnected while it is in the 'on' mode, the battery will continue to discharge. After some time, the LiPO battery will eventual become depleted and not pose as a threat to the grass seed bushes. However, in any case that the battery should still pose a threat to the grass seed bushes, I think a contingency should be put in place with modern commercial drones that would benefit and promote safety in post crash events. My thought is that audible micro speakers could be places with the intelligent flight batteries that will sound an alarm if the battery is armed and not in a fixed / connected position with the aircraft. It is the same principles as black boxes for manned aviation. In this scenario, this battery is lost in some field of very high and very dense bush that does not allow me to find the battery without extra aid from more people, metal detectors, or other mechanical means of detection. But, that some chime or sound be presented by an improperly disengaged 'on' battery, I would have been able to find and locate nearly all components of the air craft swiftly and with haste. The fact that even with me scanning a 50ft radius of the crash site and I could not find the most critical and unsafe component to the drone raises the question of 'how can we improve post commercial drone crashes.' I think by having some alarm attached to the battery would aid in the post crash finding time and recovery. Even with the battery discharged, it may still pose a threat to the field, making it unsafe for its presence to be there. In theory, by attaching a speaker to the battery, you would add a safety system is another line of defense in protecting the crash scene environment from future substantial damages. Contributing factors are company's lack of critical response for repairs or replacements of a commercial aircraft, extreme weather phenomena changes, hardware failure in the anti collision sensors, and hardware failure in the main visual optical sensor.
1813826: ZZZ Tower called for a release on Aircraft X, with visual separation with previous arrival. The [agreement] with ZZZ requires they climb the Departures to 14,000 feet. The field elevation at ZZZ is XXXX feet. I missed the aircraft checking at [923 feet above field elevation], because that is so far out of the expected. Our MIA (Minimum IFR Altitude) at the field is 6,000 feet. I assume this was a readback error between Tower and the pilot. Tower was hustling to get the departure off before the arrival landed. It was starting to raise an alarm in my mind right before the pilot requested higher. I should of caught it when the pilot checked on. The Mode C hit of 4,100 feet reinforced my expectations that they would be climbing to 14,000 feet.
1813859: After arrival landing Runway 19L we were given instructions to proceed eventually Taxiway C enroute to Gate X. After switching to Ramp Control, we were given instructions to enter Spot X to Gate X. However, there was an aircraft outbound toward Spot Y. Taxi light on, still moving, and uncertain clearance in my opinion between two large transport category aircraft if I continued. Ramp came up again to state go to Spot X and enter and 'You can't stop there.' Before I could speak to ramp on be radio suggestion allowing the outbound aircraft to taxi out our outbound Company aircraft just went for it, scooted over to Spot X and went left on C toward [Runway] 26R and begged forgiveness with Ground Control. This never should have been an issue. In every other city we would have been held short of the alley a minute or two, wait for outbound aircraft to clear the alley, then taxi to the gate. And there is even a parallel Taxiway B available if jamming up C at that point is so critical. We try to embrace Ramp Resource Management (RRM) as Pilots. Maybe LAS Ramp Control needs a tutorial on this. And perhaps include LAS ATC if the Ramp Controller is not authorized to hold an inbound aircraft on Taxiway C to allow an outbound to clear. Looks like barrier to Safety for the back C alley in LAS needs some fixing. LAS Ground and Ramp Control should be advised that holding an inbound aircraft for the back alley to allow for outbound aircraft to clear is by far the safer and most stress-free option and will only delay their taxi plan less than a minute.
1813866: As this report is not timely, it is to the best of my recollection. Approach phase of the flight to DEN. Briefed and installed the SSKII 2 RNAV/ILS 16R. On arrival we a received multiple speed and heading changes but we were back on course and LNAV/VNAV path were engaged. At some point prior to CLIFF, for whatever reason ATC changed clearance to RNAV 16R for us and the Aircraft (AC) behind us. I was Pilot Not Flying (PNF) so I installed the approach/transition. The AC ahead of us was in sight and was on the arrival but still assigned the ILS 16R. The approach was verified by both the First Officer (FO) and myself. LNAV/VNAV were still engaged and the speed window was open as ATC had already been assigning speed changes. The FO located the Approach briefing guide for the RNAV/RNP approach and RNP values for the approach were line selected and installed. All altitudes for the approach were verified. I made the comment that 'Since ATC has been messing with our speed so much, the speed window is already open'. So far the approach was flawless and the aircraft (AC) was on the vertical and lateral profile.Upon reaching CLIFF the AC began a descent as it should have. TDZ had been set and VNAV Path was engaged. As we approached CEPEE the MCP/FMA's had not changed SPD/LNAV/VNAV path were engaged. The magenta track depicted CLIFF;CEPEE;AAGEE;JABRO;JETSN, RW 16R, as it should. It was upon arrival at CEPEE that the event occurred. The AC continued to descend and VNAV path remained engaged. But, the AC continued to track straight ahead. CEPEE had not become active and the vector leg out of CLIFF was still engaged. I had been so concerned with the vertical profile that I failed to notice CEPEE was not active. Realizing what had happened I went to the FMC to LS AAGEE, but ATC noticed at the same time and assigned us either a 080 or 090 heading. ATC also canceled the RNAV approach clearance for the AC behind us. We landed without further issue. Once inside the terminal, still pissed that I allowed this to happen, I located the Captain of the AC that landed behind us to apologize. He informed us that ATC had mistakenly given him the # to call. I took the number (#) and called immediately. After a conversation with the supervisor I was informed that there was no safety issue, no loss of separation, and no need to file a report.Looking back, how this could have been avoided... first of all, I could have just said 'unable' when ATC switched us to the RNAV RNP 16R. Although not a big deal at the time...after flying all night, briefing and installing one arrival and approach then, at the last minute being reassigned to a RNAV/ RNP approach which requires lots of briefing and changes, and programming, was probably not the thing to do. What else could I have done...I allowed myself to get distracted. I should have continually monitored the lateral path to insure the AC was doing what we thought it was going to do. It was very clear and it was easy to look outside to follow traffic. It was also the FO's first Pilot Flying leg so there was instruction taking place and attention was diverting to multiple places.The FO did a great job when we were reassigned to the RNAV RNP Z 16R. He did not miss a checklist, procedure, or setting.I'm disgusted that I allowed this to happen. I am unfortunately or fortunately very familiar with the airspace and lateral/ vertical deviation issues in the area. I'm not the first and sure won't be the last, but I know what I will and won't do next time. During the SSKII 2 RNAV Arrival phase, we were advised by ATC to expect the ILS 16R approach. A few minutes prior to CLFFF, the last point on the SSKII 2 arrival, we were assigned the RNAV (RNP) Z R16R approach. We were on a northerly heading in HDG mode at this time for vectors for the previously expected ILS. The Captain, as Pilot Monitoring (PM), selected the correct RNAV Z 16R approach as well as the correct transition (CLFFF transition) in the FMC. I verified the selected approach and transition after he did so. I then set up the approach per all steps of the Approach Briefing Guide and briefed the approach. We were then given direct CLFFF and selected LNAV. We were cleared for the RNAV RNP Z R16R approach shortly before arriving at CLFFF. Upon arriving at CLFFF, I verified that the CLFFF waypoint sequenced in the FMC to ensure we were now on a published segment of the approach. I selected LNAV, VNAV, opened the speed window for the appropriate speed, requested the PM set touchdown zone elevation (which he did), and verified that the ENGAGED FMA's were in green LNAV and VPATH. The aircraft began a descent per the VPATH glide slope. I ran through the items again to verify that the approach was proceeding correctly. I verified again that the FMA's showed an engaged green LNAV and engaged green VPATH. The approach was proceeding as expected. At the CEPEE waypoint, the aircraft should have begun a right turn towards the AAGEE as part of the track towards the final approach point and final approach course. The aircraft did not turn and continued in a straight course after passing CEPEE. I immediately checked the FMA's again to ensure it did not revert to HDG mode. The FMA's were still in green, engaged LNAV and VPATH. The aircraft was also still in an expected VPATH descent to the TDZE. Within a few seconds, and before we could figure out why the aircraft did not turn, ATC called to cancel the RNAV approach and gave us a right turn for a visual approach to runway 16R and gave clearance for the visual approach. We proceeded uneventfully for the visual approach and landing. After arriving at the gate and leaving the aircraft, a pilot from another aircraft that was behind us during the arrival and approach advised us that he was mistakenly given a phone number by ATC to call regarding the RNAV Z 16R turning issue that we actually experienced. We got the phone number from him and the Captain called. The ATC supervisor said that no report would be required, there was no loss of separation, there was no safety issue, and how just wanted to know what happened. The Captain and I reviewed everything we did in setting up, preparing, and executing that approach and could not figure any reason why the aircraft did not initiate a turn at CEPEE and continued straight while engaged in LNAV with the proper approach waypoints, altitudes, and sequencing verified in the FMC.
1813875: Requested the SAALR2 STAR with SJU Approach Control. They informed me that ALL the STARs were NOTAMed out in 2013. Which is interesting for three reasons, 1. All the STARs are dated NOV, 2018. 2. The ZZZ-SJU flight plan didn't contain any NOTAMs for the STARs. 3. Jeppesen Flitedeck Pro (FD PRO) also didn't show any NOTAMs for any STARs.
1813915: Flight was cleared for approach into Runway XX at ZZZ. After noticing the approach was too high, the flight crew executed a go-around and missed approach. The flight crew then tried to re-establish contact with ATC but was not successful. After reaching missed approach altitude the flight crew decided to turn and make left hand traffic for Runway XX, where we made a visual approach and landing while making position reports on the local CTAF frequency. After landing, it was realized that the flight crew could have potentially violated the proper missed approach procedure or additional approach clearances into ZZZ after not being able to contact ATC. After parking at gate, Captain called ATC via phone to cancel IFR.One possible cause could be the relatively rare experience of flying into an uncontrolled field at night and the procedures that are associated with that. There was also some confusion about the type of approach the flight was cleared to execute, in this case, RNAV or visual approach into Runway XX. We believed we were cleared for the visual approach. However, being unable to contact ATC added confusion and doubt to the situation after landing. Flight delays most likely added stress as well.The first suggestion for future experiences would be to be more mindful and diligent about confirming the type of approach we are cleared to execute. This would have clarified the proper procedure when executing a go-around. A second potential solution would have been to gain altitude in order to try and contact ATC. As for the approach, the flight crew could have requested vectors to leave and then rejoin the approach when the aircraft was at a more appropriate altitude before needing to execute the go-around. After executing the go around, [we] climbed to pattern altitude to make a left traffic pattern instead of executing the published missed approach. [We were] unable to re establish contact with ATC after the go around. [We] did a visual approach to a landing. Crew believed ATC cleared for visual approach, therefore not requiring the published missed approach. [We should] clarify approach clearance with ATC [next time].
1813934: Upon accepting Aircraft X, the inbound Captain, told me details about an MEL for Bulk Fuel Temp. He stated that there was an associated CAS MISCOMP" (Crew Alerting System Miscomparison) status message and that this was relayed to him by the previous Captain. They had no issues on their flight. We accept aircraft and depart ZZZ1. Not long after reaching cruise about 60 miles SE of ZZZ we lost our left fuel tank quantity indication along with our total fuel quantity indication. I had also recently updated the fuel in the FMS after reaching cruise altitude. Due to the MEL, we had been monitoring the fuel system for any possible errors and we had additional fuel after reaching altitude than planned. Right before we lost our left fuel indication both tanks were even. We did not receive any cautions, nor any indication on the fuel EICAS page of a "Fuel Channel Fail" status or caution like you are supposed to. After approximately 3 minutes of no left tank fuel quantity indication, we referred to the QRH for "Fuel CH 1/2 FAIL" for guidance and equalized our fuel flow between engines. In this circumstance, in addition to another aspect of already have a MEL on the "BULK FUEL TEMP", along with not receiving EICAS indications like the system is designed to, we decided to divert to ZZZ. At some point during the beginning half of our descent to ZZZ, our left fuel quantity indication came back but my decision to divert was already made. We didn't have any fuel indication for approximately 8-12 minutes. We followed all procedures as far as alerting Dispatch, Flight Attendant, ATC, made a PA to passengers, In range to the line, followed by below the line and ensured we would not be overweight. We did not declare an emergency at that time. Upon getting vectors to final approach for runway, we intercepted the localizer below the glide slope. Approx 7-8 mile final when I called for 'Gear Down, Flaps 30;' but the gear did not move. Shortly after we received a "GEAR DISAGREE" master warning. We were at approx 3,400 ft flying the glide slope and not yet past [the] FAF so instead of calling for a go around, I disconnected the autopilot and asked for delay vectors to troubleshoot. We received an altitude assignment of 3,000 ft, heading 190, which required a descent.We then ran the QRH for "GEAR DISAGREE", and after multiple attempts using the gear handle we used the alternate gear extension as called for in the QRH. All three gear came down and were indicating green. At this point I let ATC know we were ready to return for landing and we requested priority and to have trucks ready just in case. We also followed procedures to inform company of the [situation] and informed the flight attendants (FAs) of new situation. We also told the FAs to perform a "BRACE" command just in case due to the QRH stating directional control on the runway might be difficult. We ran through all the proper procedures except for the Go Around checklist. Looking back, we should have even though we did not miss any items. At the time, I did not consider the vectors as a go around due to being 6 miles out and having to descend to the assigned altitude. Upon touchdown, we received a "STEERING INOP" caution and I noticed directional control required more rudder than normal. Runway XXL does not have any high speed exits so we stopped on the runway, coordinated with airport command, and waited for buses to deplane the passengers.We did not use a tug to be pulled off the runway because I was unsure if the alternate gear extension was applying pressure to the nosewheel similar to nosewheel steering. I talked to Maintenance and they were also unsure. We did our best to keep the passengers up to date while waiting for the buses to deplane the passengers. We did not evacuate as there was no imminent danger after landing and the runway being closed. Unrelated to the gear, I should not have assumed and trusted another persons word that a CAS MISCOMP (Crew Alerting System Miscomparison) status message was in association to an MEL without verify the MEL procedure, and not just reviewing the MEL. We should have written that up at the gate in ZZZ1 although it may be completely unassociated to all our issues. I should have called for the go-around checklist to reconfirm we completed all the items even though we did not do a go-around maneuver."
1813938: I was given clearance to depart RWY XXL in ZZZ. Up through that point everything went okay. I had no issues with Preflight, Engine start, Taxi etc. After taking off, rotating, and pulling the gear handle up with a positive rate of climb, I was awaiting all the proper lights to extinguish. All lights did extinguish, except the NOSE gear light. I do not recall hearing or feeling the normal audible 'thump'. Although these things happened while I was communicating with Tower on Frequency 1, I was transferred over to Departure on Frequency 2 and waited until I was with Departure to state that I had an issue with the landing gear. I recognized the issue almost simultaneously with the transfer and instinctively pressed the annunciator light check button to see if all the proper lights came on, and they did. The first Departure Controller sounded female. She asked what I wanted to do, what I recall saying is that I thought I might have to return to the airport and requested extended vectors so I could run my checklists. She leveled me off at 2,000 MSL. I believe once leveled off she asked me if it were an emergency, and I said not yet, but not completely sure. I grabbed the company QRH while climbing and started reading the Abnormal Landing Gear Will Not Retract Hydraulically checklist. After level at 2,000 [feet] and configured for cruise, I read the note and checklist, then fully cycled the gear once. When I put the gear handle in the down position, I watched all the proper lights illuminate, until everything indicated fully down and locked. When I retracted the gear, I watched all the proper lights illuminate, but continued to receive the initial result. The NOSE light remained illuminated, while all the other lights were extinguished. At this point, I knew I could not proceed over water to another destination. I let Departure know I would definitely need to return to the airport. She asked if I was [advising], and initially I said no, because it was an abnormal checklist, but then said yes because it was the NOSE wheel and I was afraid of a possible tip over and prop strike. At this point I didn't know if I could trust the gear being up or down. Since the checklist flowchart answer was YES, I immediately moved to Abnormal Landing Gear Down and Locked Light Illuminated with the Gear Switch Up and HYD PRESS Light Out checklist as it instructed. I read the complete checklist and slowed down to 120 KIAS, to meet the 130 KIAS requirement, put the gear handle in the down position, and pulled the HYD circuit breaker. Departure checked on me to see how I was doing, and asked me to tell her when I wanted to turn back. I was still running checklist and said OK. Once I completed all steps, I read the Abnormal [checklist] Landing with Defective Nose Gear asked to return to the airport, as the checklist instructed. I let Departure know I was ready to return, she asked which way I wanted to turn. I requested turns to the right. She asked me which runway would I like to use and I said [Runway] XXR. She asked if I was sure, so I changed to [Runway] XXL since it was longer, but had already started vectoring right. She asked me what happened. I said the landing gear light remained illuminated after takeoff. I cycled the gear to see if it would go out and it didn't, I went through my checklists and now I was flying at 120 KIAS to keep from damaging the gear. She clarified by asking something like 'so one of the landing gears would not go up, right?' and I confirmed that and said I could no longer trust the lighted indication, so I pulled the emergency gear down. After a few moments of silence, a different Departure controller came on. This controller sounded male. The rest of them from now until I safely parked did. At this time, I was flying a downwind direction and I prepared for the approach to Runway XXL. Departure stated that he would have me turn base XX miles away. I set up the GPS and briefed the approach plate for RNAV XXL. Once done, I kept reading the checklist to ensure I was clear on what to do and when. All other aircraft landings and departures were continuing on XXR. I was vectored to final for XXL somewhere prior to the FAF approach, and asked to intercept the LOC for XXL, but since I'd selected the RNAV XXL and briefed that approach already, and it was VMC, I didn't change my configuration to the ILS to keep from becoming task saturated prior to an [urgent] landing. I was switched to Tower, who notified me of traffic landing on XXR and cleared me to land. I turned off all switches except mags, flared and landed with the nose wheel kept high, then turned off mixtures and mags. Everything seemed to be done safely with no issues. When the nose wheel came down, it was slowly, gently and the plane remained upright. On the rollout, at about taxi speed, I turned on the battery and avionics (only) to speak to ATC, and stated that I had left over momentum and was exiting left on Taxiway Q but the engines were off due to completion of the checklists. I tried to completely clear the runway. I noticed that a white pickup truck that had been holding short of XXL followed behind me on the runway and then drove around the plane to check it out and reported back to ATC that I was indeed past the hold short line and everything looked okay. I did not initiate a ground evacuation, because I had no passengers, I felt safe, and hoped to get normal operations back as soon as possible. They immediately continued operations on [Runway] XXL. Then they, the driver of the truck and ATC asked what I planned to do. I said I needed to return to the FBO, which was on the other side of the airport. ATC asked how I would get to FBO since I had shut down the engines. I said I would like to try to restart and taxi to see if it was possible to taxi under my own power or if I needed a tow. ATC suggested I do the practice taxi on Taxiway. The truck moved away because it was in front of me on [taxiway to] left. I tried to taxi slowly and it was successful, so I requested the taxi to the FBO. After verifying I was OK, the white truck left. At intersection, ATC allowed me to cross [Runway] XXL and take Taxiway to the FBO. After crossing over to Taxiway, he asked if I could see the FBO. I confirmed that I did and arrived safely.
1813959: On taxi out, Flight Attendant 1 notified we had passenger drop battery/charger and it started smoking. They had secured unit in fire containment bag and no damage or threat to aircraft. 1813963: We were taking off from ELP on Runway 22 and had an initial clearance for the TDOWN3 RNAV Departure. Tower cleared us for takeoff with revised clearance to turn left to 200 and climb to 17,000 [feet]. I was the flying pilot manually flying. As we were accelerating and getting the aircraft to a clean configuration we were issued a frequency change to Departure. Upon checking in we were immediately given further instructions which included a right turn after reaching 6,200 feet to 060. Both of us misunderstood the turn right part of the clearance. The FO (First Officer) read back 'passing 6,200 heading 060' and had no response from the controller. We climbed through 6,200 and turned left. We were about half way through the left turn when the controller saw the mistake and told us it was a right turn, but then told us to continue the left turn. He later asked us to call them for possible pilot certificate action. There are several causal factors [due to direction of turn by flight crew]. First, having a clearance for an RNAV departure that has a left turn from Runway 22 sets you up to expect a left turn out for protected airspace even after receiving a last minute change to the departure plan using radar vectors. Because the radar vectors are given last minute the old departure stays in the FMC showing the original route on our map displaying that left turn, so even though we were not following the route displayed it probably influenced our thought pattern. There is no published departures turning out to the right from Runway 22 due to mountainous terrain if you are departing east. Secondly, we also had prebriefed the engine failure procedures that have you turn out to the left for the same reason. Third, from a 200 heading to turn right to 060 is counter intuitive because it is more than 180 degree turn. All of these factors I think caused expectation bias to turn left and not hear the right turn instruction. Fourth, the controllers failure to emphasize the right turn part when it is more than 180 from current heading and his not ensuring the read back was correct. Controllers need to emphasize the direction of turn especially if it's more than 180 degrees and ensure they get a correct read back. On the phone the controller said this was normal to avoid traffic from Mexico. If this is a common procedure to use radar vectors to turn us out an opposite direction of our assigned clearance then there needs to be some notes somewhere in our charts so we can prepare for that ahead of time. This non published procedure could cause conflicts with terrain in the event of an engine failure. The missed approach and takeoff engine failure profiles for Runway 22 tell you to turn left. The TDOWN 3 SID, we were assigned, tells you to turn left off of Runway 22. The reason all of the departures turn left on Runway 22 at El Paso is because there is high terrain if you turn right. On takeoff, we were told to climb to 17,000 feet and turn left to heading 200. When we contacted Departure, the controller quickly blurted out a long, involved clearance. I responded, 'Passing 6.2, turn to 060.' He did not respond back to my radio call. On a heading of 200, the heading of 060 is to the left. As we entered the left turn to 060, the controller informed us that he had told us to turn right to 060, he also told us to expedite our left turn and continue to a heading of 010. When we rolled out on the heading, he told us to call a phone number because of a potential violation. I read the phone number back to him and asked him to verify. He did not respond because he was working two frequencies, and was talking to another aircraft on the other frequency. When we called the phone number for El Paso Departure Control, they told us that left turns off Runway 22 often conflict with traffic at a Mexican airport. So, they often vector you to the right. The Captain and I have both been in and out of El Paso numerous times, and have never gotten a right turn off Runway 22. None of our guidance for El Paso says to expect a right hand turn. Expectation bias caused us to hear 'turn to 060' instead of 'turn right to 060.' Also, the Departure Controller was working two frequencies and did not catch that we said 'turn to 060.' Here is what he blurted at us at 1,000 feet AGL while we were retracting the flaps, '[company name], radar contact, turn right to 060 and climb to 17,000.' He also had a thick, Hispanic accent. If the keyword was 'right', it didn't help that he placed it in the middle of a sentence with no emphasis or follow up. If left departures off Runway 22 conflict with Mexican air traffic, perhaps they need an updated departure procedure. The ATKNN 5 Departure off Runway 22 turns right, but it continues west bound. There are no departure procedures for Runway 22 that turn right initially, and then continue to the east. Also, none of our guidance tells us to expect a right turn off of Runway 22.

Crew talked with Duty Officer after blocking in. I called the Captain around XB30z and checked in with them. Notified them XC30Z ETD and to call crew scheduling back. 1813993: Approached Runway 28 into GMU and had the Pilot Monitoring turn the pilot controlled lighting up to max (7 clicks). The runway lights for Runway 28 did not appear to turn on. The approach was continued to 500 feet at which point a go around was executed. We joined the traffic pattern and landed on Runway 1. A third check of the NOTAMs showed that there were no NOTAMs identifying the runway as closed or showing the runway lights as out of service. After landing, we learned that several aviation [websites] such as airnav.com and skyvector.com contain this remark: ATC-CTL. WHEN ATCT CLSD ACTVT MALSF RWY 01, REIL RWY 19, HIRL RWY 01/19, PERIMETER LGTS H1, H2 - CTAF. However, the FAA Chart Supplement contains this remark: ACTIVATE perimeter lights H1 and H2--CTAF. Of note, this is listed only as a Heliport Remark, not in the general remarks for the airport. Thus, it appears that the Runway 28 lights cannot be controlled using Pilot Controlled Lighting procedures on the CTAF frequency, however, there is incomplete information is the FAA Chart Supplement. We recommend that the FAA Chart Supplement be updated with the correct information. Also, consider adding the pilot controlled lighting limitations information to the Airfield Sketch and on the Runway 28 Approach Plate, as these products are much more likely to be referenced by a flight crew while in flight.
1813994: During the final segment of the approach phase on short final, we hear gear up at 960 feet RA. Captain told Pilot Monitoring to put the gear down and decided to continue to land. We decided it was safer to land rather to do the balked landing.I believe the cause of the event was fatigue and complacency. I felt a little tired and did not scan and confirm Captain checklist items that were called for. It was night time with turbulence and at a critical phase of flight were several things were happening at the same time.I need to be more aware of confirming actual checklist items at critical phases of flight and scanning everything looks good when the Captain is focused on flying the aircraft into ZZZ.
1814060: During the boarding process, the F/O came out of the flight deck and asked me (FA 1) to go into flight deck and to let [the flight crew] know if I smelled anything.
