1814090: Aircraft was in the traffic pattern at ZZZ, downwind leg turning to base, approximate altitude 3;000ft MSL, 90 MPH. Approximately .25 mile from the approach end of RUNWAY. A small impact was heard and felt by the pilot. There was nothing observed by the pilot, no evasive action taken. There were no control issues with the aircraft, initial thoughts were that a bird strike had occurred. After parking in the hangar, the aircraft was inspected. Damage from impact with a solid object was found on the underside of the right wing, outboard wing panel and wing tip. There were scratches on the paint and a slight crease in a wing skin. There was no structural damage and the aircraft is airworthy. The damage was consistent with a hard object with a width of at least 18 inches, and suggested that the impact was with a drone. Within the traffic pattern and at pattern elevation of an airport is not an appropriate area for drone operation.
1814096: This is a recurring issue. FNL and AIA both have weather-reporting equipment on the same frequency and are only 139 miles apart from each other. Our routing typically originates east of FNL and due to ATC preferential routing, our descent into FNL typically takes us over the GLL VOR/DME. As a result of the interference between the AIA ASOS and FNL ATIS, neither station can be understood during the initial descent. When arriving into FNL, the ATIS is unreadable until we're approximately 30 miles from the airport, and by then we're already talking to Denver Approach and usually getting vectored for an approach. Likewise, descending into AIA, the ASOS is unreadable until we're about 50 miles out. I suppose it goes without saying that changing the frequency of one of these two stations seems like the best solution, but I know that reducing the power of either station could be an option as well. Personally, while I know the aviation frequency spectrum is crowded, I really hope that an effort is made to find an unused frequency for one of these two facilities.
1814136: I was taking delivery of an airplane that some friends had purchased and relocating it from ZZZ1 to ZZZ2. The first leg was to be from ZZZ1 to ZZZ3 via ZZZ4 to avoid restricted airspace. I completed the preflight and departed ZZZ1. I climbed to 6500 ft. MSL and about 35 minutes into the flight the engine began to lose power and backfire. I switched mags, switched fuel tanks, reduced power and adjusted mixture but nothing seemed to make any difference. At around 3,500 feet MSL the engine began to run smoothly again and I decided that I would land at ZZZ4 for maintenance. The engine began to run rough again and I opted to land in a field rather than overfly the city in hopes of reaching the airport. The off airport landing was made without incident. There was no damage to the airplane or myself. I secured the airplane and left a note on the nearby farmhouse door with my contact information. I was later contacted by the authorities and gave them the details over the phone. A passerby gave me a ride to ZZZ4 where I met a fellow pilot that gave me a ride back to ZZZ2. A mechanic from ZZZ1 is coming to inspect the airplane.I do not know what caused the problem at this point. The airplane had just completed it's annual inspection but had been inactive for a number of years prior. The preflight and engine run-up were normal and the airplane climbed well to 6,500 feet.I am happy with the outcome of my decision not to overfly a populated area with few options had the engine quit entirely.
1814146: I was CIC (Controller in Charge) of the Approach control facility. The Radar Controller was working North South Sectors combined, which is standard for our facility due to traffic volume not being as high as it used to be. The Radar Controller Had an IFR aircraft (Aircraft X) off of one of our satellite airports, ZZZ, climbing high with the center level at 8,000 feet northbound. The Radar Controller also had an IFR aircraft (Aircraft Y) level at 8,000 feet southbound. Both aircraft on a collision course at 8,000 feet about 5 or so miles apart. Prior to this moment an adjacent facility sector called and the Radar Controller answered the shout line. The other line left unanswered. They called again and I answered working CIC and Data combined realizing the Controller needed assistance. They requested we climb Aircraft Z to 17,000 feet. I acknowledged with my initials. Immediately after I told the Controller to climb Aircraft Z to 17,000 feet pointing at the scope at the aircraft (now 4ish miles apart.) Controller told me to 'hold on' and went to Aircraft A a VFR aircraft in the northeast part of our airspace who was descending out of 6,500 feet southwest bound towards a Aircraft B (IFR) who was descending out of 9,000 for 5,000 feet who could of been a factor but currently were 10 ish miles apart and told Aircraft A to turn on a heading of 270 (I believe) reference traffic. The Conflict Alert alert is now going off, the Controller realizing her mistake asked me what to do, I told her to crank one to the right. At this point Aircraft A got back on frequency asking 'say again.' I told the Controller to now Climb Aircraft X to 17,000 feet , she keyed up climbing him to 10,000 feet. He acknowledged the climb. I told her to give Traffic alert, to the other aircraft (Aircraft Y). She did not, and kind of froze. We did not have a hand mike plugged in to the adjacent scope so I was unable to get on the frequency myself to do anything. Aircraft X and Aircraft Y went right over one another by 100 feet. Neither knowing about each other. The Radar Controller just certified on radar and had her two RDO's (regular days off) right after. This may have played a factor on her not prioritizing the two IFR aircraft on a collision course before the VFR and IFR aircraft 10 miles apart. My recommendation would be to remind controllers working position that the CIC has say in the operation and should be listened to when they give an instruction. Because they may see something you have missed, and are trying to avoid a catastrophe. I should of been more adamant after I told the Controller to climb Aircraft Z instead of letting the Controller tell me to 'hold on.' Aircraft X was level at 8,000 feet. Aircraft Y was level at 8,000 feet. VFR Aircraft A landing ZZZ1 requesting RNAV Approach and IFR Aircraft B at 5,000 feet landing SWF were merging and I turned the VFR aircraft on a 270 heading. Due to this situation I was late to resolve the conflict between Aircraft X and Aircraft Y. Center approved higher for Aircraft X to 17,000 feet. I did not answer the line, CIC (Controller in Charge) did and advised me to climb Aircraft X. Other contributing factors were that the whole session I was working radar, the CIC was hovering over my shoulder making comments and telling me what to do. One instance was with a VFR aircraft over already radar with the adjacent TRACON sector and requested a IFR clearance to his destination. The CIC did not allow me to handle this situation how I wanted to and immediately made coordination with other sectors and was telling me what to tell the aircraft. I then went ahead and told him to take the position and for him to speak to the aircraft since he had made all the coordination. The whole session he pointed out minor things that when an actual important situation came up I could not tell he was urgent and I had not noticed the two aircraft at 8,000 feet. CIC was micromanaging me and was hindering my ability to work my traffic with his constant comments. Such as 'I didn't want to sit here and watch you'. Due to all these factors it was extremely difficult to work my traffic and focus. The one time I needed my CIC to advise me of an urgent situation, he did not until Center called to climb the aircraft. But when there were minor things in the way he wanted to work my traffic then he was yelling. This CIC took approximately over 600 hours to certify on radar and constantly had talks to during training. He also had his facility CIC waived a few months after he certified on radar. They should not have two recently checked out controllers working radar and data alone. CIC should not comment unless it is a safety issue. The CIC should allow the Controller to work traffic and only interfere when extremely necessary. I should have rerouted Aircraft Y through a less congested area.
1814160: I was listening to radar north from the Local control position due to weather surrounding the airport and seeing a medevac holding. There were 2 medevacs at the same time one with a heart transplant patient on-board (Aircraft X) and the other with the heart transplant team (Aircraft Y). Restricted Areas were hot Surface to 20,000 feet and the only clear air weather was in the Restricted Areas. I heard the Radar Controller coordinating with Center repeatedly about getting a hold of range control to try to get Aircraft Y through so they didn't have to divert because the ambulance was already waiting at ZZZ. Center stated good luck coordinating with range control because they had been trying and range control was refusing to allow the Medevac through. Aircraft X was trapped north of the line of weather and unable to get to ZZZ in a timely manner. The unwillingness of range control to stop ground training to allow the Medevacs through during 2 life critical flights caused unnecessary delay to the heart transplant patient and transplant team.Procedures should be put in place for coordination to recall the airspace due to weather, emergencies, or operational need. I've been numerous other locations where the above conditions warranted recall of Special Use Airspace for safety of flight however here there is extreme disparity between the Army's use of the Restricted Airspace and the FAA's need/ability to recall said airspace.
1814188: Aircraft X was on route to ZZZ going northbound at 7,000 feet. I took the hand off. I called out to him and the aircraft was sitting on my frequency. I called the Moderate to Extreme Precipitation between him and his destination and he acknowledged. After a talking with a few other aircraft I went back to Aircraft X to call the weather again and told him it looked as though he was going to go through an area of moderate precipitation but here was extreme precipitation to the east and west. Again, the pilot just simply acknowledged me. It looked as though the aircraft climbed about 300 feet but leveled back off, I asked how the ride was, the pilot responded bumpy. Shortly after, the aircraft began losing altitude, I called the aircraft a few times, gave a low altitude alert, no response. It also appeared the aircraft was in a spiral. A VFR aircraft could hear Aircraft X but attempts to communicate failed. I took a handoff on an air carrier that I asked to help. At that moment I could finally hear Aircraft X and he informed me he lost his vacuum. I asked if he was in control of the aircraft and if he could see the ground, he said yes and that he was below the cloud layer in VFR conditions. Afterwards, I lost communication again. I tried all my transmitters (main/standby/Backups) but was unable to reestablish communications. We watched him proceed very low towards ZZZ and I learned afterwards he did land safely. I was flying direct to ZZZ. I was IFR in clouds, rain, and turbulence at 7,000 feet approximately 35 miles from ZZZ. The plane started making turns to the right , which I corrected a few times. I was trying to figure out why it was happening. Suddenly the plane did a hard right. I noticed the artificial horizon had 'tumbled' and the 'vacuum' warning light came on. I turned off the auto-pilot and attempted to level the wings with multiple left and right corrections. Also noticed I was now in a dive. I saw the ground through an opening in the clouds and aimed for that. I broke out of the clouds at approximately 3,000-3,500 feet. Once I regained control below the clouds I tried contacting ZZZ Center. They were very difficult to hear/with broken reception. I notified them I had a vacuum pump failure, was below the clouds in VFR conditions and would call when I landed in ZZZ. Not sure if they heard me. I maneuvered the plane as necessary to stay out of the clouds and rain showers to ZZZ. Once on the ground I called Approach and Center to notify them of what had happened. I guess you can never know when a vacuum pump may fail, but it sure does affect many crucial navigation equipment. My assumption would be to have a secondary vacuum pump or artificial horizon as a safety back-up. I will be checking into that.
1814224: Continued landing from an unstabilized approach. We thoroughly briefed and flew the ILS 10L at FLL. We received a Too Low Flap GPWS warning below 500 feet and failed to execute an immediate missed approach. The First Officer was flying an outstanding approach and was stabilized in all parameters but I had missed the flaps 30 detent despite the fact that I had 'completed', the Before Landing Checklist and read, and pointed to the flap indicator. I still missed it. I set the flaps to 30 and we landed. Cumulative fatigue and startle effect were definitely contributing factors. I know better than that. I should have commanded an immediate go around. Landing 10L in FLL. Approach briefed thoroughly. Stable approach the whole way. Captain completed the landing checklist at appropriate time. Read and confirmed flaps 30 but missed that flaps were at 25. At near 500 ft we got the flaps too low on the GPWS. The captain and I immediately realized the flaps were only at 25. He selected flaps 30. The aircraft and approach were stable. Seeing that we did not have much fuel and there was a lot of traffic in the area, we decided the safest course of action was to land the aircraft. The landing was continued in a stable manner in the touchdown zone. Taxied to the gate and thoroughly debriefed that the proper course of action would have probably been to do a go around.
1814233: The night flights into PTKK should be halted as soon as possible due to dangerous situation. PAPIs on both ends of the runway are inoperative according to the NOTAMs, and have been for months. The runway is located in an area with very little illumination. According to Naval aviators very similar to landing on a carrier at night. There is no electronic means of glidepath guidance using the RNAV (GPS) Runway 4 past HIMAX. There has been a fatal accident due to lack of glide slope information approximately 3 years ago. With the lack of glide slope, and PAPIs I believe this is the highest risk airport in the system during night operations and should be stopped as soon as possible.
1814250: Departed gate dual engine power out onto taxiway. Captain was Pilot Flying. Took off [Runway] XXL heading 220 to 5,000 [feet]. It was a normal ALT-TO1 take off. Prepare for level off at 5,000, reduce power for a 24,000 1000 fpm climb. Prior to 5,000 cleared to 15,000 apply climb power. Stable climb at 24,000. At approximately 5,000 [feet] there was a loud bang and the aircraft shook, moments later the ENG 1 OUT EICAS message is presented. Captain ensured AC control, while the First Officer [advised with ATC] and asked for level off at 8,000 [feet]. Cleared as requested. Captain set a 500 fpm climb and turned on the auto pilot and the First Officer began the engine failure checklist. During the checklist, the Flight Attendant called us to inquire about the bang, told him about the failure and our imminent return to ZZZ and that we would call him back shortly. Completed the engine failure checklist. Engine restart was discussed but we decided not to attempt it because of the bang, there was likely damage. After completion of the engine failure checklist the First Officer began the single engine landing checklist. During this time we leveled off at 8,000 [feet] and received some vectors from ZZZ Departure. While the First Officer prepared the landing data The Captain called the Flight Attendant back and made an announcement to the passengers. Departure reached out shortly after that and the Captain requested an approach to [Runway] XXC and CFR (Crash Fire Rescue equipment) standing by. Transferred to approach continued vectors on course Captain and First Officer quickly reviewed the approach setup and confirmed below landing weight. ACARS message sent to dispatch to inform them of the engine failure and return to ZZZ. Around 500 ft AGL the auto pilot was drifting left of course. Turned the auto pilot off corrected and made a normal touchdown on [Runway] XXC. Exited the runway [and] directed to taxi beyond intersection and CFR was on a separate ground freq. parking break set, after landing complete. CFR confirmed there were no indications of a fire, they followed us to the alley. We parked and deplaned normally. No injuries were reported and no one requested medical attention. We departed gate with both engines running onto taxiway. Captain was the pilot flying. We executed a normal ALT-TO-1 takeoff from 10L turning to heading 220 and climbing to 5,000 feet. After Takeoff Checklist was complete and we were established in climb power. Captain prepared for level off at 5,000 feet by reducing power for a 240kt 1,000 fpm climb. Prior to 5,000 feet we were cleared to 15,000 feet and additional power was applied reestablishing a stable climb to our new clearance altitude.While climbing through approximately 5,000 feet a loud bang occurred and the aircraft shook. Moments later the ENG 1 OUT EICAS message was presented. Captain ensured aircraft control and we determined that we would climb to 8,000 feet to ensure we would be above weather build-ups in the immediate area while we continued to work through the emergency. I [advised] ATC and asked for level off at 8,000 feet which we were cleared for. Captain set a 500 fpm climb and turned on the autopilot and I began the Engine Failure Checklist. During the checklist the Flight Attendant called us to inquire about the bang. He was told about the failure, our imminent return to ZZZ, and that we would call him back shortly. During completion of the Engine Failure Checklist, a potential restart of engine 1 was discussed. Fuel, Oil, and N1 Rotation were present, however, it was determined that due to the loud bang that occurred, it was likely that substantial damage may have occurred to engine 1 and as such, a potential restart attempt would not be prudent. The Engine Failure Checklist was completed. During this time we leveled off at 8,000 feet and received additional vectors from ZZZ departure. After completing the Engine Failure Checklist, I began the Single Engine Landing Checklist. While I prepared the landing data, Captain called the Flight Attendant back and made an announcement to the passengers. Departure reached out shortly after that and Captain requested an approach to [Runway] XXC and to have Crash Fire Rescue (CFR) standing by. We transferred to approach control and continued vectors to the ILS [Runway] XXC localizer. It was confirmed that both the Engine Failure Checklist and Single Engine Landing Checklist were complete. Captain and I reviewed the approach setup and confirmed the aircraft was below landing weight. I sent an ACARS message to dispatch to inform them of the engine failure and subsequent return to ZZZ and requested a gate be assigned. We continued with the approach. Around 500 ft AGLl the autopilot began drifting left of course. Captain turned the autopilot off, corrected, and made a normal touchdown on [Runway] XXC. We exited [Runway] XXC at exit and were directed to taxi past the intersection and stop on taxiway where CFR was standing by on a separate ground frequency. The parking brake was set and after landing checklist completed. CFR confirmed there were no indications of a fire. Taxi was initiated to gate and CFR followed us to the alley as a precaution. We parked and deplaned normally. No injuries were reported and no one requested medical attention.
1814256: Flight crew smelled significant burning smell in the flight deck descending out of FL220 on descent into ZZZ. Flight crew detected burning via smell. Smell was extremely strong and smelled electrical. Flight crew [was unsure of the cause], immediately followed smoke fumes memory items. Donned masks and established communications. Crew then followed QRH and notified ATC of condition and [requested priority handling]. Flight crew descended to make landing safely in ZZZ without further incident. Through 10k feet crew assessed that masks were no longer needed as fumes had dissipated. Flight crew added difficult and different communicating via 02 masks in flight than in sims. Suggest more realistic training methods.
1814266: Upon taking the aircraft, the number 3 MFD was inoperative which, per the MEL, required the Captain to complete all flying duties. While at ZZZ the Captain noticed that the GPWS Inop, Windshear Inop, Terrain Inop, and Terrain fail message were indicated in the EICAS. The Captain called maintenance who immediately deferred the issue and the Captain completed the logbook entries. Prior to push I entered the appropriate information into ACARS which did not match the PERF INIT which the Captain entered. We verified the numbers multiple times and determined that the ACARS had to be inaccurate. We also verified our numbers with the updated AOM. After calling Dispatch it appeared that their was a fleet wide issue with ACARS. It appeared to me that some information that is generally manually input may have already been calculated in the zero fuel weight of ACARS (85lbs for crew bags). Prior to the ACARS issue we notified Ground Control to receive an off time into ZZZ1 which we were given a departure time. At that point the Captain decided to complete the paper form X. We notified the ground crew of the delay who informed us they had to leave for another aircraft and would not be back for about 30-40 minutes. The Captain decided to have them push us from the gate in the event our issue was solved prior to their return. We completed the appropriate checklists and pushed but did not start any engines. Then notified ATC of the delay to void Off Time. The Captain then called the company for approval to open the cabin window to hand the form paper copy to the ground crew. Once the form was completed we called ops, handed the W&B out the window, and re completed the before start checklist all the way through. We also discussed not utilizing ACARS W&B throughout the flight (added workload). We then notified Ground that we were ready to verify off time prior to starting engines (fuel management). They gave us an immediate wheels up time so we started the engines and taxied to [Runway] XX. I used my IPAD to verify weather at ZZZ1 prior to push which was reporting calm winds , few 050 TCU and 10 miles vis and again I checked prior to taxi which they were reporting calm winds, 046 CB, 10 miles. On departure from [Runway] XX we were given a turn to the west and eventually a heading to the north with a climb to 8,000 [feet]. When given direct to ZZZZZ for the ZZZZZ4 Arrival we had to vector around a few storms. We also had to vector around storm clouds on the arrival and were given vectors off the arrival by approach due to flow into ZZZ1. Within this period we both discussed the weather, verified the TAF, and discussed needing an alternate and potential fuel issues. After updating the D-ATIS we verified that the field visibility had dropped below 3 miles so we messaged Dispatch asking for/if we needed an alternate due to visibility. Dispatch responded that the TAF was good and we didn't need an alternate. The Captain started to become concerned because he was showing extreme areas of precipitation along the arrival and approach. Other aircraft ahead reported heavy rain. There were multiple discussion with ATC about getting in to ZZZ1 but I don't remember if they advised aircraft were going missed. We received normal vectors into the approach to Runway XYL and my first awareness of wind shear is when the aircraft in front of us called wind shear and missed. With our Windshear capabilities inoperative we were both paying very close attention to the aircraft's instruments. After intercepting the localizer and passing the Runway XYL FAF the precipitation was worsening. Somewhere between 1,700 and 1,200 feet the aircraft instruments were showing increased gains and losses and began to vibrate significantly. The Captain called wind shear and we completed the wind shear procedure up to the missed approach altitude of 3;000ft. Tower gave us runway heading and eventually turned us to the west with a hand off to approach. Prior to the handoff we began discussing fuel and alternates. The Captain suggested ZZZ2 which we messaged to Dispatch. Dispatch recommended ZZZ3. I recommend that we not go to ZZZ3 because of all the weather that was building between ZZZ1 and ZZZ3 and it also appeared weather was building at ZZZ3 per my IPAD. We asked ATC about ZZZ3 and they indicated that ZZZ3 had similar weather to ZZZ1 so we determined based on fuel and ATCs information that ZZZ3 was not an option. It seemed to me that Dispatch was adamant about diverting to ZZZ3. We also discussed other airport near ZZZ1 (off field) that could be potential alternates. After the check in with Approach they asked us our intentions which we replied stand by and began rough fuel calculations to ZZZ2. The Captain quickly determined that fuel to ZZZ2 was inadequate due to a 15-20 minute flight and approximately 2200lbs of fuel on board. (Increased fuel burn at lower altitude, storms in the area, and potential unknown issues on arrival at ZZZ2). We then asked ATC about aircraft success in to ZZZ1 which they replied that some aircraft were making it in and some were not. We then requested Runway XYR because it was the closer runway and informed ATC of our minimum fuel situation. The Captain notified the Flight Attendant, we ran the appropriate checklist (ATIS, build it, bug, brief it) and continued vectors to Runway XYR. There were two aircraft in front of us which one was able to land and another missed (aircraft in front of us) due to wind shear. After recalculating fuel requirements the Captain determined that a missed would put us in an emergency fuel situation therefore we [advised ATC]. I believe that upon intercepting the localizer we were somewhere around 1700-1800lbs. During the approach the gains and losses of altitude did not seem significant but it appeared to be difficult to maintain the localizer although I did not see anything greater than one dot. There was also added pressure to continue the approach due to the fuel situation. During the approach tower asked the aircraft that made it in where they broke out and they replied 'right at mins'. At around 800 feet I called out that I could see the ground which was not visible as we got to 500 ft. At 300 feet I called approach lights in sight 12 o'clock and continued to call out the approach lights. The aircraft began to drift right and I called the runway environment insight at 11 o'clock. Throughout this period it was apparent that the Captain was having difficulty seeing the runway. When he finally looked up and determined that he did not have adequate references, and the aircraft was not in a safe position to land, he called the missed. Immediately on the missed it was apparent the at least 90 percent of the airfield was VFR. We could see all of Runway XZ/XA, including approach paths, so we made a decision request XZ and due a VFR pattern into XZ. Tower provided we could use whatever runway we needed so we continued with XZ, entered the left crosswind, base, and landed. During the miss we did not climb to the missed approach altitude, left the gear down, and kept the flaps at nine because of the immediate landing after the missed to Runway XYR. We updated the FMS with Runway XZ and extended a line for reference because there are no approaches in our pubs for XZ. We did not rerun the performance information again because the field length was 10,500 [feet] which was longer than Runway XYR and it was an immediate landing. We also received fuel EICAS alerts during the missed and a fuel critical prior to landing XZ. All approaches were conducted with flaps 22. Emergency vehicles were on scene which we did not require. Upon taxiing into the gate the field went in to a ground stop due to lightning. In all the entire flight segment from door closed to door open was 3.4 hours. I would say that this flight provided the crew with several threats. To name a few, my PFD was inop so only the CPT could fly, windshear, GPWS, and TCAS were inop, pop-up weather wasoccurring throughout the flight route, fuel considerations, ACARS not accurate due to new AOM changes, delays prior to departure, delays in route, other aircraft encountering wind shear, and potentially an inexperienced dispatcher. There was also a significant pressure to land the second approach. I felt that we handled the situation very well as a crew and discussed and analyzed any and all potential alternatives but were cornered due to the fuel situation. I do wish I had analyzed the winds better throughout the duration and been more aware of the weather at the field during the Runway XYL wind shear event. With most of the airfield being VFR it was absolutely possible to successfully complete approaches to the XB runways and XZ/XA [runways]. The only area impacted by the weather was the XY runways approach segments. Therefore, if winds were within landing limits we could have immediately requested an alternate runway from ATC. While conducting the setup check in ZZZ, the GPWS Inop, Windshear Inop, Terr Inop, and Terr Fail messages appeared on the EICAS. Maintenance was called and the affected system was deferred per MEL. The aircraft also had an MEL for the First Officer MFD, and an NEF item in the cockpit. ACARS would not produce accurate weight and performance numbers, and Dispatch informed us that this was a known issue. We elected to perform a manual weight and balance with the Form X. The TAF for ZZZ1 was forecasting VFR and radar looked fairly benign. The First Officer obtained the D-ATIS for ZZZ1 which showed Winds Calm, visibility 10SM, Few at 5000, Scattered at 8000, with no other weather (information M). Due to this, extra fuel for weather was not considered by us or Dispatch. While in our initial descent the First Officer and myself noticed the weather in ZZZ1 was deteriorating and sent an ACARS to Dispatch asking if we should get an alternate. Dispatch replied that no alternate was needed, and we assumed that they had more up to date information than available to us in the air. Our radar was depicting areas of extreme return (red and purple) blanketing the approach and airport with other aircraft saying it was a smooth ride, but heavy precipitation. While outside of the final approach fix on the ILS Runway XYL, other aircraft were heard going missed due to windshear. ATC informed us that some aircraft were landing and some were going around. We elected to continue the approach as we were not experiencing any abnormal flight conditions. Inside of the final approach fix, I was unable to maintain positive aircraft control on the approach path due to airspeed, altitude, and course fluctuations. I made the determination to execute a windshear escape/go around. The Flight Attendant was notified of our situation. We contacted Dispatch to request a diversion and suggested ZZZ2. Dispatch replied that ZZZ3 was a better option, but ATC informed us that ZZZ3 was having similar weather to ZZZ1. I used the FMS to determine a rough fuel burn to ZZZ2 as 1400 lbs not including any deviations or approaches. We were also low on fuel, approximately 2,200 lbs after the missed approach. We discussed and agreed that we did not want to end up in ZZZ3 with such low fuel and similar weather issues. We decided to attempt a second approach at ZZZ1 after ATC stated that some aircraft were landing successfully. It was apparent that we would be below divert and possibly final divert on the second approach so we declared Minimum Fuel. We requested ILS Runway XYR due to perceived improved conditions and the closer approach for that runway. During the approach, the Flight Attendant called and said that a passenger was in the bathroom and asked if we could delay the landing. I advised her that due to our fuel situation, it would not be possible. She was able to get the passenger back to his seat before final approach. While on the approach, we overheard the aircraft in front of us go around for windshear. Our fuel level was low and a go around would put us in a fuel critical situation. We [advised ATC] and continued the approach. We experienced difficulty in maintaining the approach course and I used my PIC authority to continue the approach since a missed approach would leave us with inadequate fuel for much option. The First Officer called approach lights in sight, and we continued to 100 feet above the field. The First Officer called Runway in sight, and when I looked up, I did not see a runway and was disoriented due to the extreme precipitation and reduced visibility and immediately executed a go around. We were now showing a very low fuel level, and it was unlikely we would have enough fuel to get to another airport or reattempt an approach. I used PIC emergency authority to request a circle to land Runway XZ. We were able to maintain visual contact with Runway XZ during the maneuver. We had no time to get any type of performance numbers, and reasoned that since itwas longer than Runway XYR we could land. The landing was conducted without incident. As we engaged E/TO Reserve on the windshear escape, I entered this in the logbook and contacted maintenance. See attachments for reference if needed.Many threats existed in this incident including: pop up weather, weight restrictions, the need for paper performance calculations, an inoperative MFD, an inoperative Windshear system, and lack of an alternate. The weather and TAF looked ok during the planning portion of the flight, it was not until enroute, that everything deteriorated. I believe we acted in the best manner possible given the stressful situation and lack of backup options (fuel and/or alternate). It was a unique scenario that required a unique response. I believe we made safe decisions based on the current parameters. In hindsight, I would have been more assertive about requesting an alternate enroute. I do not believe we could have forecasted such bad weather, which is why we did not ask to remove passengers to add fuel in ZZZ. As we could not find a suitable alternate, we had little choice once we were low on fuel than to attempt to land on any runway. A third go around would have likely had us considering an off field landing.
1814273: Taxiing out from spot. Ground controller stated 'After the heavy join Lima Zulu bridge to 18L'. As trained, the FO (First Officer) read back the clearance and stated the clearance to the Captain. As the Captain, I stated the clearance back to the FO. As we proceeded to Lima taxiway the Ground Controller stated ' Aircraft X where are you going?' The FO stated you ' said join Lima...' upon to which I said to the FO that's what the Controller said. After being felt like we made a mistake. The FO and myself noticed this Controller made a few more clearance errors that needed to be corrected. The FO and I (Captain) discussed the event later on. Suggestions from our side that might have caused the event is that:1) The Controller might have been tired at the end of their shift. 2) Controller had grown complacent and had expectation bias of what Company operated aircraft doing what they 'normally' do. From the crew side of the event, we should have questioned the clearance since it was an abnormal clearance. Bring back pre- COVID staffing to ATC so proper rest can be had for ATC personnel.
1814283: Overshot parking / stop 'T' at Gate. I can't recall another parking gate that utilizes the (automated parking system) system domestically that operates quite like [this] gate at ORD. There is a 10-7 page that mentions this fact. The 'fix' as mentioned in these pages tells pilots to be aware of the parking 'T-Mark'. Problem is, there are multiple markings. Another problem is the poor lighting and obscuration of the markings due to old paint, ramp dirt, e.g. tire markings, etc. Normally pilots are watching laterally for safety area infractions and the Captain for lateral lead-in line guidance and a 'countdown' in feet to a stopping point. The system at Gate X does not provide the countdown and simply changes from lateral guidance to 'STOP'. As mentioned this is wholly unlike other gates. And, the 10-7 page is, for lack of anything else, useless, as the Captain can't see the T-Mark. If the guidance system can't be modified to provide a 'countdown' then at all times a Marshaller should be at the front of the aircraft, wands in hand, providing guidance as if the guidance system doesn't exist.
1814291: CA (Captain) on Aircraft X, ZZZ-ZZZ1 called and asked about NOTOC (Notice to Crew). He noticed that on walk around in ZZZ1 that human organs and dry ice was loaded on to the aircraft. ACARS was inoperative via MEL, but nowhere on the Load Closeout [documents] were restricted articles listed. I conference called the CA with CLP (Load Planning) and the CLP Supervisor said that there is nothing on their side they can do if the Crew Chief does not advise them. Also, usually a MEDEVAC notice from ATC would give us both a heads up about dry ice but they [did] not advise Dispatch. [Incomplete flight closeout documents issued due to] Missed SOP by Crew Chief. [Reporter recommends] not allow a flight closeout to be sent when a restricted item is loaded until CA acknowledges.
1814301: We were instructed to line up and wait while the aircraft that just landed rolled out and exited the runway. While we were in position, Tower became busy talking to other aircraft on frequency. The next radio call for us was to exit the runway at C2. While exiting, a cleared to land aircraft was heard asking 'is that an airplane on the runway?' Tower instructed them to not overfly us, that we were exiting the runway. They were never instructed to go-around, instead to offset. We observed them offsetting slightly as to not fly directly over the top of us as they continued to land.Tower becoming busy and possibly forgetting about us on the runway, and the landing aircraft not executing a go-around when they became aware of us in position on the runway, both contributed to the near miss. Query ATC when any delay in position.
1814313: I was Pilot Flying operating the ZZZ flight. On short final, we received a sink rate aural alert. My First Officer called continue, I agreed, and we continued. It happened around 100-200 feet. We never observed more than 1000 fpm on the VSI, and the PAPI indicated 2 white and 2 red and the landing was made safely in the touchdown zone. Once the runway was assured, I elected to nose down slightly coming over the threshold to give myself some more room to get the airplane safely to the ground with the given conditions. Gusty winds, and bumpy conditions made for a more difficult approach, but at no point did it seem unsafe to either one of us.After landing in ZZZ, left hand brake temperatures were relatively high upon exiting the runway and entering taxiway A. We landed Runway XXL. Visual approach, winds 250@18G30kts. Once on taxiway, left hand outboard brake temp indicated around 380C and the inboard was around 340C, temperatures still climbing. Quick decision making and thinking, I as the Captain decided to notify Ground Control that our brake temps were too high to park at the gate, and that we would like to continue taxiing around the airport to get them to cool off enough to allow us to park safely. A few moments later, temps were above 400C and climbing, and we got the BRK OVERHEAT amber EICAS message. Called for the checklist, and complied. Basically, do not set the parking brake. The highest temp seen was 495C where it stopped climbing and finally started trending back down. I elected to taxi single engine, and only use the right hand brakes (which were under 300C the entire time) in order to get the brakes to cool off and to prevent an unsafe condition at the gate with hot brakes and the possibility of having a brake fire. Once cooled off below 300C we parked at the gate, and the message had cleared prior from the EICAS.
1814314: On station arrival at ZZZ our marshaller used incorrect/non standard marshaling signals to bring us into the ramp area. Rather than marshal us into what is probably the most congested ramp in our system he continued with the move forward signal and offered little or no guidance for a turn onto the J line. Once we were parked he appeared agitated at where the jet ended up being parked. I attempted to talk to the marshaller to see what the issue was and ask that he be directive with his marshaling signals. I was intercepted by the Ramp Lead who told me that he would relay any comments I had. When I told the lead what my intent was he responded with 'you guys don't pay attention to our signals anyhow.'On our departure, the same marshaller we had inbound was used for engine start and departure. When we were ready to taxi, I flashed the landing light and got a very soft/non standard signal that appeared to be 'move ahead.' It wasn't clear that was what he was signaling so I flashed the landing light again. The marshaling signal did not change. I came forward using the marshaller for guidance and realized that he wasn't going to offer effective guidance for our turn towards the taxiway and started my turn late. Because of the close proximity of the neighboring ramp and taxiway construction and the ineffective marshaling I didn't have the energy to make a departure towards taxiway delta at idle thrust. I chose to make a right turn back towards taxiway charlie which is contrary to our 10-7 procedures. I verified that the thrust levers were at idle and the N1 rpm were at idle before making the turn.Once clear of the ramp I asked the station if there were any problems caused by the non standard turn. Nothing was mentioned.Standard marshaling is a problem throughout our system. In a perfect world, I would be able to park the jet using nothing but guidance from the marshaller. In reality, it's rare to get a marshal-er that actually marshals the jet. This leads to a combination of using the marshal-er and pilot experience to park jets. This generally works OK in stations that don't have congested ramps. Not as well in stations like ZZZ.The company needs to provide more/better training for the people marshaling aircraft and they need to ensure the supervisors enforce standard marshaling practices. As a pilot, trying to overcome a systemic problem with marshaling by using the marshal-er as a secondary source of guidance rather than a primary source, I contribute to the problem.
1814339: Yes, not a typo. Multiple trips to MIA of late. Have some today. Returning passengers barely ambulatory when boarding the aircraft. Some otherwise healthy women are wheelchaired to the plane because they basically can't walk. It appears that MIA is a destination for medical tourism for butt enhancement. We have used medical kits for leaking incisions. Most of the 'patients' board with very large pillows to sit on modifying the seat with 8 to 10 extra inches of cushion and some can not sit in the seat regardless of the crew instruction. Crew and flight attendants are frustrated by this trend. Most of the literature on-line recommends not flying immediately after this procedure for 10 to 14 days. Possible blood clots are a quoted reason. These flights seem pre-loaded for medical emergency. Some guidance needs to be published for crew guidance. We are not an air ambulance service and should not be boarding these passengers directly from the recovery room post-op.
1814363: The following narrative describes an event that took place while operating a passenger flight - the second segment of a two-segment day. For this particular flight, the Captain (CA) was the Pilot Monitoring (PM), the other First Officer (FO) was the Pilot Flying (PF), and I was positioned in the First Observer's seat as the additional crew member, aiding in pilot monitoring duties. The flight itself was uneventful and could be described as a straightforward intra-European flight. We continuously checked the weather on our way to ETAR in order to remain cognizant of the weather conditions expected for landing. Well before the top-of-descent, we pulled the final weather report, requested aero-data performance, loaded the expected ILS approach, and once all crewmembers were present on the flight deck and ready to discuss the descent/approach/landing, the PF conducted the approach briefing. All checklists were completed on schedule and as we approached ETAR, we confirmed with approach controllers that we would expect the ILS to Runway XX. As we came within approximately 20 or so miles from the field, we were given radar vectors to final. At the time, ETAR was experiencing a large number of air traffic, both inbound to the field, outbound from the field, as well as training aircraft in the traffic pattern. On the downwind leg, the PM programed the course fix intercept and executed the change with the PF's verbal concurrence. The winds at ETAR were light, visibility was great, skies had a higher scattered layer, and overall it was a nice VFR day. Due to the heat rising from the surface, we did have some convective and mechanical turbulence as we approached the runway, but nothing too far out of the ordinary for a summer afternoon. The aircraft was configured on schedule (if not slightly early to be conservative) and was stable (on speed, on path, configured for landing) well before 1,000 feet. After the 'Stable' calls were made and we continued the approach, the PF disconnected automation (as briefed earlier) and continued the approach. The approach itself never destabilized as we approached the runway, however once in the flare, I noticed we were floating quite a bit. I had preloaded in my mind that floating beyond the touchdown zone would be a 'go-around' call. As we began approaching the end of the touchdown zone (and below 10 feet RA), the PM made a comment that the end of the touchdown zone was approaching. As soon as the final touchdown zone marker disappeared under the nose and before I could make the call myself, the PM called 'Go-around!' Almost as soon as this statement was made, the main tires touched down, the PF stated 'too late' and the reversers were pulled. By the time the aircraft had touched down, the flight deck had just momentarily passed the end of the touchdown zone. The aircraft decelerated normally and we cleared Runway XX on taxiway Bravo. During taxi to the terminal building, the PF stated that we would discuss the landing at the gate, to which the crew agreed. Once we were safely at the gate with the engines secured, all checklists accomplished, and the deplaning process was well underway, we had an open discussion about what had happen and why a go around should have been conducted, especially since the call was made. The debriefing was well received by the PF, who expressed that he understood why his decision to continue the landing was not correct given the circumstances. The PF mentioned that from his perspective during the landing, he believed he had still been in the touchdown zone, whereas from my perspective, we were 100-200 feet beyond it. The PF also mentioned that he saw a low altitude balked landing as being more hazardous than continuing the landing, however we reminded him that this is why bounced and balked landing recovery are part of the Extended Envelope Training received on a bi-yearly basis. After a thorough discussion and debrief, the PF stated that he agreed that we should have conducted a go-around and remained open to any suggestions/recommendations/critiques as we conducted the debrief as a crew. We discussed the no-fault go-around policy that exists and I mentioned that the response to a go-around call made by any crew member should not, and can not be 'too late;' as this breaks down CRM, places the crew in an uncomfortable situation, and establishes a scenario similar to disregarding a statement of 'I'm not comfortable with this' where one crew member's decision to continue becomes dictating (even with deteriorating safety margins) when other crew members had already expressed concern. We discussed that, although ETAR's Runway XX was long and we had ample room to decelerate after touchdown, the decision to disregard a go-around call on a shorter runway could have drastically different results. With every critique or debriefing item mentioned, the PF was incredibly receptive, understood the points being made, and was internalizing the information being discussed. I also recommended that we as a crew file reports to take advantage of a program designed for reporting slips, lapses, and errors, as well as allow each crew-member to reflect on the event in order to further analyze what could have been done differently. This event outlines a deviation from stabilized approach criteria, simply due to the landing touchdown beyond the touchdown zone. Although the correct go-around call was made, the PF continued the landing due to the immediate touchdown occurring almost immediately after the go around call was made by the PM. Expectation bias and continuation biases are incredibly powerful by influencing decision making well into the landing maneuver. Experience of landing on runways and stopping with thousands of feet remaining can cause a false sense of security when procedural drift occurs. With this event, it was incredibly beneficial to not only take time to debrief as a crew, but to see the value in each crew-member submitting an ASAP report to simply share individual perspectives from the landing. Due to the debrief, we were able to discuss company policies, procedures, as well as determine what could have been the best course of action in order to mitigate similar threats in the future. The value of a debrief can allow for crew-members to internalize constructive criticism, rather than brush off an event as an outlier. During an event such as this, I believe a tremendous amount of learning was accomplished simply by following up and discussing the events as a crew. I recommend that the normalization of debriefings after a flight, especially after flights with an event, should be standardized among the pilots. Not only are debriefings a form of mentoring tools but setting aside ego and discussing areas of possible procedural non-compliance, performance deficits, CRM breakdowns, or unmitigated threats could reinforce learning among crew-members. This ties in directly with professionalism as aviators. Although I do not believe there was an intentional violation of regulations or disregard for safety, addressing this event as a crew served to promote learning, enhance safety, and build up colleagues rather than put them down. Emphasizing the normalization of go-arounds due to unstable approaches has also been viewed as a beneficial adaptation within the Atlas culture. However, although we are seeing a statistical decrease in unstable approaches resulting in a landing, I believe this is still a work in progress as we evidently have not reached the milestone of 100% go-arounds from unstable approaches. Emphasis can also be placed in recognizing that stable approaches can still destabilize in the last 10 feet during landing, whether drifting from center-line, landing beyond the touchdown zone, or excessive pitch during the flare. This is of course in addition to ability for any operating crew member to call for a go around at any point during the approach. The go around procedure should be accomplished assoon as the call is made, and the discussion of 'why' should be reserved for when the aircraft is in level flight with checklists completed or once the aircraft is safely on the ground, parked at the gate, and checklists completed.
1814394: Glide slope alert flying into RST. During approach phase of landing into RST. I was the Pilot Monitoring. We were cleared for the visual to runway 13. I recall we were descending and the Pilot Flying had the FAF altitude of 2,600 set, and the banana bar was indicating that we should level off at that altitude at approximately 0.25-0.75 prior to Ellie (FAF). I believe the approach mode was also activated, and we were fully configured. At the same time we were setting up for the approach there was a GA aircraft taking off, and a [air carrier] taxiing and holding short of Runway 13. I was focused outside and listening to ATC. We were both surprised when we received a glide slope alert. I believe that we were approximately 200 feet below the FAF when we received the alert. Around about this time I believe the 757 was cleared for takeoff. When we received the alert the Pilot Flying kicked off the autopilot, increased power and worked to re-establish a stabilized approach. We were still operating in visual conditions and had the runway in sight. From my perspective it seemed he had re-established a stabilized approach. Around 200-300 feet, or so, we received another glide slope alert. I do not recall us being excessively low to have activated the glide slope aural alert. The aircraft landed normally and safely. The Pilot Flying was frustrated that we had by all indications an unstable approach. In rethinking the events I am confident that we had the aircraft correctly configured and ready to fly the ILS with the aid of the autopilot. While we could not confirm this, our best guess was that the taxiing air carrier had somehow interfered with the glide slope and we began descending prior to the FAF. I felt that he had established a stabilized approach prior to 1,000 AGL, so the second aural alert was also a surprise. I believe it was the PF's first time flying into RST. After the first aural glide slope alert we probably should have called for a go-around. The alert caused a couple moments of confusion. We probably should have just gone around and removed the distraction.
1814407: The Captain and I were operating a flight to MDST from ZZZ. We thoroughly briefed and read the pertinent information for the arrival into MDST since we had never been to that airport. We briefed and expected to get the SEKAR 2P [Arrival] for Runway 11 at MDST, which we did. Upon descent, we received clearance to 6000 ft to SEKAR. Upon passing SEKAR, we were cleared direct to OMRUP and cleared approach to Runway 11. OMRUP is not on the arrival, but the approach portion going into MDST. In the FMC, we brought OMRUP up and inserted it into the line below SEKAR and verified the route. Aircraft was still in VNAV PATH and because the altitude along the route was a descent from 6000 to 4000, we selected 4000 and continued the descent in VNAV. This is where we realized something wasn't right. There is high terrain surrounding the airport and it is briefed on the briefing pages in the EFB (Electronic Flight Bag). We reached approximately 5000 and decided immediately to climb back to 6000 because the MSA along the arrival track is 5500 from RETAK to OMRUP. We climbed and maintained 6000 until we passed the high terrain. Once we cleared the high terrain, we proceeded to fly the approach without further incident. We never got a terrain alert as we didn't allow ourselves to descend further into high terrain. The Captain and I used excellent CRM to avert a potentially serious situation. The Captain's situational awareness and experience arriving at an unfamiliar airport were a tremendous asset to recognizing and correcting a potential hazard. 1814484: After shutdown checklist was completed, I deplaned to go to restroom and get a snack. When I came back to the gate the agent asked me if I knew about the flat tires. I said no. When I saw the Captain in the jet bridge he told me that our left brake fan(s) caught fire after I left and they deplaned everyone. The fire department was called. The fire and sparks were out but both left tires were flat. We noticed the left outboard tire was a little over 400C when we taxied clear of the active. So, we turned on the fans. Taxi to gate was normal with no odd indications. Arrival at the gate both left main tires blew out. Smoke and sparks were seen. I called for a deplaning. Fire department was also called. Aircraft was deplaned. No other factors. Apparently, a brake froze.
1814508: Climbing on the SID the forward Flight Attendant called the flight deck about noise coming from the main cabin door. We verified that the doors indications were all closed. No pressurization abnormalities were noted with the CPAM system. The noise was not audible in the flight deck. Shortly after the Flight Attendant called again saying the noise was louder, at which time the CPAM and doors EICAS (Engine Indicating and Crew Alerting System) page indications were checked again. Pilot Monitoring advised the Flight Attendant to verify all door securing pins were in the green position and to try and detect if air was passing through. During this time ATC amended our climb instructions from 37,000 feet to level at 32,000 feet for traffic. When the Flight Attendant called again she said she felt air coming from the right side of the door.At this point the noise was audible through the flight deck door and inter-phone rapidly increasing in volume. We then donned our oxygen masks and decided a descent was immediately required. Pilot Monitoring advised ATC that we were beginning a descent. Upon completion of the emergency descent and at a safe altitude, Pilot Flying gave aircraft control to Pilot Monitoring. At this time an announcement was given for a precautionary landing. The Pilot Flying began setting the aircraft up for a return to ZZZ, via straight in. The approach and landing phase was conducted in accordance with normal operations and checklist procedures resulting in a standard landing and taxi to the gate. Once at the gate, the Flight Attendant had difficulty opening the MCD (Main Cabin Door). This was in addition to difficulty experienced closing the MCD for departure. Both Flight Attendants reported hearing a loud pop prior to the sharp increase in sound from the MCD in flight.The risk was a complete and rapid, possibly explosive decompression of the aircraft. Suggest extra vigilance in verifying the airworthiness of MCD seals. As were climbing after departing ZZZ, our Forward Flight Attendant called the flight deck advising us that she was concerned about a loud noise coming from the main cabin door. We verified that the door was secured and all systems reported normal. We continued our climbout. She then called back and said it was getting progressively and rapidly louder and she can feel air coming from the right side. Systems were still normal. After being given an amended altitude of 32,000 [feet] from a previous altitude of 37,000 [feet], we were cleared higher. It was at this time we heard the sound from the main cabin door through our flight deck. It was very rapidly getting worse. As a crew, concerned about pressurization issues, we immediately decided to initiate a descent. We donned our oxygen masks as a safety measure. During the descent, all systems still reported normal. However, the issue with the door was still evident. Once the descent was completed and we were at a safe altitude, as pilot flying, I handed controls to the pilot monitoring.I stated that this would be a precautionary landing and to prepare the cabin. I also made my passenger announcement. We then set the aircraft up for a return to ZZZ. The return and landing at ZZZ was completed under normal procedures and checklists. We returned to the gate as planned. After talking with the flights attendants upon landing, they reported that just prior to the sound becoming very loud they heard a 'pop' further exacerbating the issue. It should also be noted that there was trouble closing the main cabin door prior to departure. There was also trouble opening the door once we arrived at the gate. Cause MCD (Main Cabin Door) seal.
1814520: Aircraft on vectors into ZZZ, NAV2 was not set correctly leading to an unexpected autopilot disconnect on intercept and loss of approximately 600 feet altitude. We arrested the descent and fixed the issue. ATC issued a low alt alert but at that point we were regaining lost alt and had the runway in sight. We advised ATC as such and continued visually for a normal landing. I incorrectly set the First Officer's RTU (Radio Tuning Unit) and did not catch it on the approach check.
1814547: During boarding Name in seat X came on board aircraft and told me the gate agent had told him to give me his battery for his wheelchair/scooter. He asked his wife if she knew what type of battery it was and she said she did not know as she looked all over the battery for an indication of the type of battery it was. She then handed me the battery and I tried to find any indication of what type of battery it was to no avail. The battery did have a hazmat fire symbol sticker on it. I let the Captain know about the battery and explained to him that the passenger didn't know what type of battery it was nor was there any indication on the battery to its type. I called the agent on the Jetway phone that was in the Jumpseat, to let them know we had an issue with this battery. The agent sent a manager down and I explained to the manager that we didn't know what type of battery it was. She then called the Ramp Manager to come up. I gave the Captain the battery to see if he could see something on the outside to indicate what type it was. When the Ramp Manager came up she told us it was a lithium-ion battery. I asked her how she knows that and she said that the passenger told her that. I then explained to the Ramp Manager and the Captain that the passenger told me that they didn't know what type of battery it was. The Captain then called someone to clarify what type of battery it was and if it was accepted on board in the cabin. The agent then pulled up a photo on her phone showing a recycle symbol similar to the recycle symbol on the battery, except the symbol on the battery didn't have the words Li-ion in addition to the symbol as the picture that she displayed on her phone did. All the symbols I have seen for lithium-ion have that addition Li-ion indicating it is a lithium-ion battery. The Captain thought that she pulled the photo from a manual that they have access to and made the decision to now close the door. It wasn't until later in the flight when I had explained to him that she just googled it and pulled it up on her phone so that she could shut the door. I was then able to find in my manual that if the agent had been told by the passenger that indeed the battery was a lithium-ion battery she should have made a notation in the passenger record with a code and instead of the passenger handing me the battery, as per procedure in the manual the agent should have brought the battery on board the aircraft and stowed it either in the overhead bin or under the seat and informed the Lead Flight Attendant and the Captain of the location so that we could inform all other flight attendants on board to then monitor the battery throughout the flight for excessive heat, smoke or other potential fire indicators. [Reporter recommends] not allowing a lithium-ion battery of that [large] size to be boarded on an aircraft or coming up with a safe location to stow that type of battery knowing that there is a potential for a fire hazard. 25 grams of lithium-ion is the max [allowed] per our manual states that we can transport. This size battery was the max. On board we have a sleeve [containment bag] for a laptop or tablet or cell phone battery that may catch on fire, this battery would not fit in that sleeve!
1814601: ZZZ MX (Maintenance) called and informed that the LH eng took 19 Quarts. MX inspected the inside and outside of the eng cowl and eng, tailpipe, inlet and behind fan blades with no evidence of a leak. The inbound crew did not write up a problem with the oil QTY. We reviewed AHM (Automated Health Monitoring) report with was posted inflight an hour prior to landing and showed good QTY and oil pressure and no high oil temp. We reviewed the oil service screen in work bench and no servicing has been done for a while which showed no oil consumption issues. We asked to MX service the oil tank and run the engine, no leaks found and a good oil gulp at start which tells us the tank is not over serviced. We put the engine oil qty on MEL for two reasons one that the oil qty transmitter was giving false readings and MX may have thought when they checked the gauge in the cockpit that the engine was full and that's why the oil screen also showed very little oil servicing of the engine. Second reason is that by putting the engine on MEL that forces the mechanic to check oil at the tank and document it. There for showing if we truly have an oil consumption problem. We monitored the take off and looked at the takeoff report and it showed good oil qty and pressure. About an hour later we got a report of the engine having high oil temp. We looked at AHM, it did show a high oil temp with oil Qty and pressure good. On post landing at ZZZ1 MX did a look at the engine and once again no leaks found. With the oil temp high that's when we asked them to pull the master oil chip detector and it had metal shavings on it. With the oil temp over limit that requires an engine change.I'm not sure we can prevent this kind of failure this was a really oddball problem we have not seen before. I think we were a victim of a failing lube and scavenge pump or gearbox the oil may have been hiding in the gearbox. If we were to do this again I may have asked MX to do a high power run instead of just an idle run, But it may not have shown the problem.
1814627: My student was preforming pattern work at ZZZ. Traffic pattern altitude being used was 1,800 feet. Conditions were VFR. My student made his crosswind, downwind, and final calls every time. At the same time a C182 was operating for a skydive operation out of ZZZ. My students downwinds were always flown to provide clearance for the skydivers designated landing zone. Throughout his 7 landings in the C172, a PT-17 Stearman joined the pattern, not making any radio communication calls so the student paid extra attention to focus on where the Stearman was operating. The Stearman continued to fly low patterns at about 1,300 feet, with tight downwinds right over the skydiving drop zone. The Stearman sometimes would not even take off from the runway. They would add power then come to a complete stop at the end of the runway and taxi back. While the student was downwind midfield, the skydive C182 was holding short of the runway and made a CTAF call they were waiting for the Stearman to to depart.When the student turned base about 1/2 mile from the runway, the C182 announced they were departing. The student then turned to final and made his radio calls. Flaps were extended about 25 to 30 degrees and the student was coming in at about 70 to 75 MPH. At about 500 feet and 1/4 mile final, the Stearman came down in front of the students C172 about 400 feet away in a rapidly descending base to final and cut right in front of the student. The student had no choice but to abort the landing and go-around since they descended to a lower altitude in front of him. The made a CTAF call on 122.8, '<tail number> going around, aircraft on runway'. Adding full throttle and waiting for a positive rate of climb the student retracted the flaps. The student's initial thought was to just fly runway heading and perform a go around but because of the lack of communication his instincts told him they would perform a touch and go. He then made a 30 degree turn to the right of the runway then turned left to fly parallel to the runway and watched below for the Stearman as he gained altitude. To no surprise the Stearman was performing a touch and go.If my student had flown runway heading the Stearman more than likely would have ascended from under him. If he was any lower on my glide slope, and due to lack of communication from the high performance Stearman, his high wing aircraft would not have seen anyone above him, and the Stearman biplanes nature would not have seen him below them and they would have collided on the displaced threshold. The student had plenty of fuel and flew to the west of ZZZ and waited for them to land before returning. The way the pilots of the Stearman were flying a high performance aircraft with no radio, contrary to the flow of traffic, and without observing Part 91 right of way rules while conducting their operations poses a significant safety hazard.
1814633: During the terminal phase of a single pilot IMC maintenance ferry flight to MRN (Foothills Regional) I requested the RNAV (GPS) Runway 21 Approach into MRN. ATC approved the request and cleared me to the CIKIS IAF. Scanning the preloaded route of flight in my G1000 PFD, I inadvertently selected the CICAC FAF as the desired steer point and turned in that direction. ATC observed the aircraft tracking to the wrong fix and directed a heading change in the direction of the IAF. At that instant, I detected the switch error and made the appropriate correct selection. The approach continued and the flight terminated without further incident. There can be no excuse for my having failed to confirm the exact GPS steer point selected, but in the interest of preventing a future incident such as this, I might question why two of the fixes on this approach would be labeled with identifiers so similar in spelling and pronunciation that this error could almost have been predicted, especially in the high workload environment of single pilot IMC during the terminal phase of the flight. I suspect that I'm not the first pilot to bite on this one, and the controller was probably spring-loaded to detect and correct my error. Can't TERPS label these fixes with less ambiguous identifiers?
1814638: Notified on XX June by ZZZ FSDO that the Aircraft X aircraft I was embarked, had a near miss at ZZZ on March XX...ALMOST three months after the supposed incident. Totally unknown, unreported to me or the other pilot who was undergoing his annual 61.58 proficiency check ride in the Eclipse. I was the PPE (Professional Pilot Examiner) conducting his final maneuver...WHICH was an RNAV to Runway XX circle to land on Runway XY. All proper reports were made on UNICOM, I especially watch the traffic on laptop and on the instruments for other traffic. To my knowledge there was no other traffic in the airport traffic pattern. We circled at 700 feet to the south of the field, turned base leg, and landed. The pilot told me that the FSDO said a Cessna 172 under ATC control now reports a near miss. I am waiting to hear what the ZZZ FSDO has to say on this matter. I suspect it is an ADS-B computer snitch or the ATC controller/other pilot have taken a long time to report the incident...OR Because the FAA folks all work from home this one got put in the 'hold' basket.This could be a dangerous time in space where an aircraft under IFR rules gets turned over to the local frequency (UNICOM) by ATC when he is established on final and does not check in or report his existence to the other traffic ahead in the pattern. It would be most useful if the other pilot writes up his report on this possible incident.
1814641: During taxi on an IFR flight plan, I was cleared to taxi Foxtrot to Sierra to [Runway] 12L at STL. I had the taxi diagram displayed on the MFD of the G1000 and was using it for reference while taxiing. I became fixated on Runway 12R on the taxi diagram and was mistakenly thinking I was taxiing to [Runway] 12L but in fact was heading towards [Runway]12R. After the turn to taxiway Sierra, I informed Ground that I would need a 1 minute run-up prior to departure. During this exchange, ATC asked what I was doing and when I looked back to the taxi diagram, I realized that I had just crossed the departure end of [Runway] 12L. Ground asked me to taxi past [Runway] 12L and then stop, which I did. I apologized for my mistake and asked ATC for further instructions and was instructed to do a 180 back towards [Runway] 12L and hold.I've flown into many Class B airports without an issue but feel that at least one contributing factor was my infrequent flying since COVID. In a normal year, I fly 300+ hrs but in the past year have logged only ~60 hours.I spoke with my flight instructor and FAA examiner about the incident including factors that led to the incursion and thoughts about how to avoid repeating the incident in the future.
1814643: I departed ZZZ on an IFR flight plan to practice approaches. Shortly before my departure, a Mooney formation group departed. There were 2 Mooney formations, a group of 2 (NAME1 flight) and a group of 3 (NAME2 flight). The names are from memory but I believe them to be accurate.The group of 2 departed approximately 15 minutes before my departure, and the group of 3 about 5 minutes before my departure. As I was being vectored for the RNAV XX approach to ZZZ, Approach called out traffic which was not visible to me. The Controller stated that the aircraft/group was supposed to be in contact with Approach, but wasn't for some reason. A few seconds later I saw a Mooney pass below me and slightly to my left. I estimate the vertical gap to be approximately 100 feet. I did not see the other plane that I believe was part of the formation. The flight continued without further incident.I believe this illustrates the hazard of formation flights in busy airspace. Since the Mooney is a low wing plane and I was in front of, and above it, I don't see how the pilot did not see me, unless he was focused on something else, perhaps maintaining his spot in the formation. He was obviously not scanning for traffic or he never would have come that close.
1814644: I met with a student and we began the preflight checks, which lasted about 1.5 hours in total. We visually verified fuel on the gauge as full and dipped the stick in the tank indicating full fuel. We began taxi and then run-up checks. We noticed fuel pressure and fuel quantity were reporting correctly.After takeoff, we did after takeoff checks and visually verified gauges were good. I vaguely remember seeing 3/4 full on the fuel tank by this point.The student [then] experienced an RPM drop. I took controls and pushed the throttle forward. The engine reacted normally and increased RPM, then shortly after reduced RPM without any throttle manipulation. I looked over and saw the fuel pressure was reducing and fuel quantity was in the yellow which indicates 1/4 tank.We were at about 4,000 ft. at this point. I squawked 7700. I called Approach who I had already been on the radio with this entire time. [We were] too far away for our glide ratio to get to an airport so I chose to land in a field. I was pitching for 73 knots which is Vg (best glide speed). We still had an operating engine at about 1400 RPM so I did not try to shut it off and restart it. At about 1,200 ft. or 1,000 ft. if memory serves me correct, the engine quit and I shut it down and secured it for landing. I applied flaps appropriately and made a soft field landing in the field. We applied brakes just in time to stop right as we made contact with a barbed fence. The fence was slightly bent, the owner came and saw as well.Our Tach time read about 0.9 so we were not up for even an hour. GPH burn is about 6 to 9 in our plane with a 24 gallon tank so we had more than enough for a full tank landing which is what we calculated before our flight.
1814651: Rapid decompression led to a rapid descent to an altitude appropriate for loss of pressurization. The landing was uneventful. A loss of pressurization while in a climb required the flight crew to initiate a rapid descent to avoid the need for supplemental oxygen. The crew coordinated intentions with ZZZ Center and leveled at 12,000 ft. MSL. We proceeded to the nearest suitable airport to assess the situation and have Maintenance fix the problem. Once it was fixed, we continued to our original destination.
1814658: At 1,900 MSL heard a thump, 20 seconds later, engine lost partial power, adding throttle did not improve power. Began a descent and located a field. Checked ignition and fuel both were on and appeared OK. Engine now making about 30% power so set up for off field landing. Crossing a fence line I struck a wire about 15 feet in the air. The aircraft shook but no other indication of control problem. Engine now at about 1700 RPM and aircraft able to climb about 100 feet per minute. I elected to head for my home base. Engine RPM still wavering but indicating 1800 so I proceeded straight to [home airport] which was now 9 miles away.Engine steady but still not making full power. I was able to complete a normal landing with no further problem. No injuries and aircraft returned to hangar. Upon inspection, found insect body parts stuck in the fuel vent. Damage confined to skin damage on gear legs and cut on right elevator.
1814681: I am the pilot/owner of Pitts S1S, Aircraft X. Upon returning to ZZZ from a short VFR pleasure flight, I was cleared for a visual approach to Runway XXL at ZZZ. The approach and landing were normal. However, immediately after touchdown, the right main tire chattered and squealed as if the brake was locked up. The aircraft began pulling hard to the right and I countered with left rudder input in an attempt to maintain directional control of the aircraft. To no avail, the aircraft continued right and as it slowed it began a clockwise ground loop. The right main tire lifted off the ground and the left wingtip and outboard side of the left aileron scrapped the ground as the aircraft came to a stop with the tail wheel about three feet off the runway and the nose pointing southbound.Tower radioed me regarding my status and I told them I was OK and will attempt to taxi the aircraft clear of the runway. I taxied the aircraft a very short distance onto taxiway, shutdown and secured the aircraft systems. I egressed the aircraft and inspected the airplane. The right main tire was flat and the tail wheel assembly was damaged and bent from the side load during the ground loop. I was not injured during this event. Subsequently, ZZZ aircraft operations met me and we proceeded to transport the aircraft back to my hanger after talking to FAA and NTSB personnel which the Tower had contacted.
1814734: I was landing and monitoring UNICOM and making callsAs I got to within 2 or 300 feet of the ground, a gyrocopter took evasive action and asked if I did not hear or see him.I did not hear or see him.I was somehow not seeing or hearing him.

1814748: Runway excursion on Runway XX at ZZZ during touch and go. 1814751: Departed ZZZ with functioning radio. Wind was calm. Enroute to ZZZ1 the radio became inop. Unable to get AWOS I observed the windsock as being limp and decided to utilize Runway XX. Scanned the area for traffic and didn't see any. On roll-out, observed another aircraft airborne that had evidently done a touch and go to the north. I quickly exited the runway at the very first possible taxiway. The other aircraft didn't appear to notice what had just happened as he continued to do touch and goes.
