1814760: As I applied brakes while rolling out from an otherwise normal three-point landing, the airplane swerved sharply to the right. I do not know whether the swerve was caused by a gust or a brake grabbing. I attempted to regain runway heading by applying left rudder and brake. When I saw I could not remain on the runway and was headed toward collision hazards, I applied full power to go-around. The airplane rolled off the edge of the runway before it became airborne but lifted off soon afterward, at which point I initiated a gentle left turn to runway heading. At some point the aircraft's left lower wing contacted the ground, damaging the paint and fabric on the underside of the aft portion of the wingtip and the outer section of aileron. 1814773: I performed my pre-flight check before flying the Mavic 2 Pro drone. My mission was to capture photos from each corner of the property and over the swimming pool area. My usual pre-flight check list before every flight is:1. Check for any airspace restrictions, TFR, NFLZ, any max altitude requirements, etc.2. Request approval with FAA if my location would be in any controlled airspace (my location was not in controlled airspace).3. Be sure all 4 propellers are secure and not damaged.4. Battery is fully charged.5. Check for any magnetic interference.6. Set my RTH.7. Make sure drone is connected to controller.8. Be sure my remote pilot license and current certificates are on or next to me before flying.9. Take off and hover drone to about 5 feet and check that all controls are functioning.10. Fly mission.I recalibrate the drone after about every 6 to 8 flights. This was my 6th flight before I would recalibrate again before the next flight or two.Before taking off, the property manager and I had people that were swimming in the pool move to a covered area temporarily for their safety.The property manager was not part of the mission and not a VO (visual Observer). I performed my pre-flight check, and I began my mission and captured a couple of photos of the swimming pool area first at 380 feet or 116 meters directly above the pool. I was controlling the drone from the ground inside the pool area.Next, I flew the drone South to the back of the property to take pictures of the playground area. As I was flying the drone to where I wanted to go, the property manager watched over my shoulder at my controller screen to see the view of the property. Once I flew over the playground, I yawed the drone 180 degrees to frame up the playground in my camera with the rest of the property. At this point, the drone was hovering at 357 feet (109 meters) above a wide open area of land with trees with the camera pointing North West. I took my photos, then I yawed to face the camera West and began flying to the next corner of the property to where I would yaw to point the camera North East for the photos. (The pool area would be the far North East corner where I was controlling the drone from this angle when I would take the photos.)About 5 seconds into this direction (West), my controller beeped, and I looked down. The property manager was still watching the controller. We saw the camera on the drone flip up at the propellers and the app froze. The Kittyhawk app (now called Aloft) displayed 'Drone Disconnected' at the top of the screen. I quickly hit the RTH button on the controller, but the app was still displaying 'Drone Disconnected' and the RTH button would not activate. At this time, I looked up to find the drone, but I could not see it anymore. Since the controller disconnected from the drone, I presumed the drone fell to the ground, and the property manager and I (and two of her maintenance workers) performed a search where we thought the drone may have crash landed in the fields.We notified the owner of the land where we were searching as well as a restaurant closest to the fields and asked them to be aware of a possible drone on the ground or in the trees and to notify us if they find it. I also tried connecting the controller to the drone while we searched, but it would never reconnect.The weather was partly cloudy, 92 degrees, and Wind 7 mph during the flight. Further south where I took pictures from the playground area were two towers, but the drone was nowhere near them.The drone did not log the duration of flight, but it was about three or four minutes into the flight when the malfunction occurred.
1814775: I was working the combined sectors as R-Side (Radar Controller). About the time Aircraft X called requesting flight following while he conducted a practice approach to ZZZ, ZZZ1 Tower called for a release on Aircraft Y. My D-Side (Handoff/Assist Controller) released Aircraft Y heading 270 climbing 4,000 feet while Aircraft X was still southbound approx 3,700 to 3,800 feet. I cannot get the replay to work properly so based on my fuzzy memory I remember multiple aircraft calling airborne for clearances and flight following as Aircraft Y called airborne off of ZZZ1. Two of the other aircraft were calling up. Aircraft Y checked on noting the transponder code he had selected. It was interesting because I did not see a transponder code, only a primary target where I expected Aircraft Y. I requested Aircraft Y ensure his transponder was on. While waiting for that I continued with other tasks including clearing the other aircraft calling. I noticed the continued primary only target and multiple times requested a recycle of the transponder on Aircraft Y. Looking back, I should have still climbed Aircraft Y to a higher altitude while we sorted the transponder issue. However, I allowed the other aircraft to distract me. Meanwhile, Aircraft X made a course reversal and was now northbound and had climbed to 4,000 [feet]. At one point I noticed the primary target headed towards Aircraft X. I believe I asked Aircraft Y's altitude. They reported 4,000 feet, the same altitude as Aircraft X right in front of them about 3ish miles. Looking back, I should have immediately climbed them but I only issued an immediate left turn to heading 210. Slowing down to the microseconds, my thought process had added complexity from an extreme precipitation cell just south of Aircraft Y, thus a few more microseconds of processing to come up with a heading far enough away from Aircraft X but not so far to have the possibility of it being too close to the precipitation and thus risking Aircraft Y refusing the heading and having back and forth transmissions to find a suitable heading. There wasn't ANY time for back and forth transmissions, I had to get it right the first time. So this caused me to pause what seemed like a long time but was probably an extra second to give the heading 210. I wish I would have climbed at the same time. I immediately went to Aircraft X and issued a left turn away to I think 320 or 330 along with an immediate descent to 3,000 feet. All I could think was I had to separate these two aircraft heading close to each other. The 3,000 foot clearance was below my MIA (Minimum IFR Altitude), But I knew I had to immediately get SOME vertical separation and I know, from being a pilot myself, a C182 can drop fast. It was the fastest way to create separation I had. Climbing Aircraft Y, while I should have done that, would have a delay in response. The headings would have a delay in response. Telling a C182 pilot to turn and descend immediately while simultaneously issuing traffic was the quickest way to pull these planes apart. It was below my MIA, however the aircraft was VFR in VMC. It was the safest option I had, with the note I wish I would have ALSO climbed Aircraft Y. To recap, I first issued an immediate left turn to 210 to Aircraft Y, then quickly issued and immediate left turn to the NW and an immediate descent to 3,000 feet while calling the traffic to Aircraft X. Then I went back and issued traffic to Aircraft Y who I believe said he had visual on the traffic. There was a combination of garbled radio and foreign accent from Aircraft Y. Looking back I technically should have used the term Traffic Alert to both aircraft, but I still got the traffic calls out as soon as possible after attempting to separate the traffic. I asked Aircraft Y if they passed the traffic, they said yes and at some point I climbed them. I told Aircraft X to resume own navigation and altitude their discretion. There wasn't time to dwell as I still had many other tasks to complete. In the middle of this all another aircraft, possibly Aircraft Z questioned why they were leveling off. I had to instruct my low time D-side to do several tasks including point outs and coordination on Aircraft Y and other aircraft. It was probably 10 minutes before I slowed and was able to report the event to my supervisor. Before the two aircraft came together I attempted at least once, unsuccessfully, to track the data block on to the primary target. I don't recall exactly why my attempts were unsuccessful and the data block stayed near ZZZ1 coast track. I may have typed the input out of order or didn't click directly on the target.I should have climbed Aircraft Y earlier and I wish I was more successful at tracking the data block on the primary target. Having the data block tracking with the primary target would have prompted me to respond quicker. Task saturation fought me on all of this. While not directly related to this event, the sector frequencies have been absolutely horrendous for weeks. Well, they've been very bad for years, but especially awful the past weeks. We have 2 transmitter sites with Mains, Standbys, and BUECs (Backup Emergency Communication System). I, and everyone else, have to CONSTANTLY switch between all 6 radios to communicate with aircraft in various portions of the sectors!! Even high altitude! My supervisor has begged us to report the frequency issues. It is a disaster waiting to happen, and I'm not exaggerating. I think even this session I had to switch multiple radios to talk to aircraft in the flight levels. Not helping the issue is bad feedback on that frequency. Its actually some other constant transmission like someone talking. You can usually hear it as soon as you unkey the microphone. Since the 2 radio sites are cross linked, the site that is receive only usually picks it up when you unkeyed. Its hard to explain but VERY frustrating. Please fix this. Someone needs to go out there and track down that rogue transmission station and either shut it down or fix it. Someone is either transmitting on the same frequency in FM or some other mode or some other harmonic frequency issue or something.
1814794: I set up for a visual approach with an ILS back-up to Runway 13L at DAL. We were in good shape from a speed and altitude standpoint at NNATE. I was hand flying. I was distracted by the localizer guidance which showed me well right of course when I was actually slightly left. I mentioned that to the Pilot Monitoring. While troubleshooting the lateral guidance, I got behind the jet for getting flaps 15 and gear down and we ended up high. As I regained my crosscheck, I subconsciously followed vertical guidance, which now was taking me erroneously higher. I called for flaps 30, and realized we were now 800 feet. The Pilot Monitoring called out the PAPIs (Precision Approach Indicators), which showed all white, but the glideslope guidance was taking me higher. I called for a go-around. My go-around was sloppy, but the Pilot Monitoring brought his A game, so it was manageable. On the second approach, a visual approach backed up by the ILS 13L, both lateral and vertical guidance were erroneous. I had to fight the tendency to cue on the vertical guidance, which again was taking me high. The Pilot Monitoring turned off both flight directors. On short final, we got an audio glideslope alert. The glideslope raw data showed me way low. The PAPIs were three white and one red. We should have also turned away from the ILS on the NAV tuning panel. On both approaches, an Aircraft Y was parked right at the hold short line in front of the glideslope antenna. I suspect we will see more aircraft stopped at the hold short line with the runway closure at DAL, and so we will see more ILS interference. I have seen similar ILS behavior at other airports with an aircraft stopped at the hold short line. We did not write up the aircraft. An ILS test was completed and passed prior to the flight. NOTAM (or other reminder) that the 13L ILS may be unreliable with aircraft in the ILS critical area. More training on go-arounds.
1814816: As our wind speed and direction reporting determines which type of approach should be flown (AOM 3.2.7), we used the advertised ATIS of LIMA (which indicated ILS XX was acceptable, if I recall correctly, landing data only showed a one (1) or two (2) knot tailwind when we used LIMA, wind 290/06). When we ran data for landing, the latest ATIS was (time), and we subsequently broke off of the RNAV5 Arrival approaching way point ZZZZZ for severe weather avoidance. We were set up for a left downwind for Runway XX (number five in the stack). We were approaching ZZZZZ1 on Runway XX shortly after the normal ATIS changeover. As we were cleared for the ILS XX, we heard preceding aircraft went around (I quickly downloaded the current ATIS to see if there was a SPECIAL).I discovered ATIS NOVEMBER was current (without being advised by the tower or approach control). I queried APP CTRL (before tower hand off) as to why Runway XX is the preferred runway, with an advertised tailwind being observed at the surface? Approach Control said 'We're keeping you on Runway XX for the sequence (or words to that effect), then he immediately handed us off to the Tower. I ran new landing data, then queried the Tower why they're landing Runway XX when ATIS NOVEMBER is advertising Runway XXR? He had no good reason. Landing data propagated around 800 feet AGL, and data showed Runway XX was all dashed lines, and we did not have the landing performance required, so I told the Tower we were going around. The Tower then asked if we were unstable on the approach as being the reason for the go-around. I said, 'No. The reason was you're landing aircraft on a runway not advertised as the landing runway, due to the wind being beyond our limits.' This wasn't a subtle wind change at the last minute, as we reported information LIMA (and we weren't corrected -- as LIMA was the current ATIS), but information MIKE had apparently occurred already, then information NOVEMBER was advertising runway XXR while on approach for Runway XX, and them knowing this, they continued to allow an unsafe operation to continue, to the extent, as we learned later, there wasn't just one go-around before ours, but three!
1814870: On the ORCKA 5 Departure, after passing the 160 SMO radial and DOCKR below 3,000 feet. We were given heading of 030 and climb to 12,000 feet as prescribed by the SID (expect vectors). As we were climbing and turning he gave us direct 'KLIPR at or above 10,000, climb to 15,000.' I could not find KLIPR on the legs pages. I checked several downline pages, went back to page 1/9 and then checked the route page to verify the ORCKA 5. It was loaded but still no KLIPR. I told the controller it isn't apparently on our route. He spelled it out. I was moving too slow. He gave us 030 heading and told us to let us know when we are heading there. I though we were heading in the right direction but the intersection is now behind us. As I was jamming the box, perhaps KLIPR got eaten or dropped out as we passed it. It's location is right by DOCKR. I can't figure out why it wasn't there initially as we turned. We were going through 10,000 feet easily so he then gave us direct KEGGS and to go to next frequency. The next controller gave us direct NNAVY. Altitudes were no issue, if anything our climb rate was quicker than my cumbersome effort towards KLIPR. What could we have done better. I had expectation bias from the old Loop departure. If I remember after DOCKR you loop back to LAX at or above 10,000 feet. With this departure giving an initial vector and our climb rate much better than my 737 experience. I was looking for KLIPR to be farther down the road than between LAX and DOCKR. I still don't know why I didn't see it because I was looking at the' top of the flight plan' legs page. I was just too slow for the expectation of the controller so he vectored us on down the line. Although I haven't been to LAX in two years I am comfortable there and fell behind unexpectedly during this event. Errors were automation Management, FMC / CDU and similarly spelled waypoints. The following narrative describes events that occurred over a very short period of time, perhaps only a few minutes in total. It is my sincere intention not to cast blame, but to offer an explanation for what happened from my biased point of view as the PF (Pilot Flying) on Aircraft X. Our flight began normally from LAX, with the exception that we were pushing back about 45 minutes late due our aircraft's late arrival into Gate 77. Preflight duties were performed fairly routine, but under some time pressure to complete everything thoroughly but as quickly as we could in an attempt to make up some of our delay. This time pressure was self-induced, as no other employee was pushing us for an on time arrival in ZZZ. Red flag #1. During the pre-departure cockpit preparations, we received notice that the passenger boarding was complete, followed shortly by ramp informing us that they were ready for the parking brake release and pushback. At this point I gave a cursory PF brief from the briefing card we all carry - too cursory. Red flag #2. Taxi and takeoff were normal from Runway 25R on the ORCKA5 Departure. I was manually flying, enjoying only my second flight as PF in over a month. We switched from Tower frequency over to SOCAL Departure, and shortly after checking in we received instructions to continue climb I believe to 5,000 feet and turn left to a heading of 030 degrees. Quickly after that we were given further climb to 12,000 and direct to KLIPR. At this point things went wrong, rapidly. The Captain, as PM (Pilot Monitoring), couldn't find the KLIPR intersection on the legs page, and informed ATC that it did not appear to be on our departure. SOCAL spelled out the intersection phonetically, and then I think confirmed that we were on the ORCKA5. Things were happening fast. While hand-flying, in the turning climb, I tried to locate (unsuccessfully) KLIPR on the 10-3 page displayed on the iPad. Red flag #3.At this point, I should have turned on the autopilot to assist with the FMC and MCP inputs, as I could detect the stress and frustration in the Captain's voice in being unable to find KLIPR on the legs page, or on the departure plan view. Red flag #4. In my divided attention between flying the aircraft and searching for KLIPR on my iPad, I failed to find it as well. I was looking too far down the flight segment to see that the this waypoint is located right off the departure end of the 25s at LAX. This was the key moment, I think, and the last opportunity to correct the error. All I needed to do was put on the AP (autopilot), join the Captain and assist with the repair. But I did not, at least not immediately. The Captain inserted KLIPR on the legs page, got my confirmation, and executed the entry. When I had looked at the route modification, I thought it was correct. The waypoint showed in the correct direction (I thought) but much further down line than it should have, off the scale of my selected range on the navigation display. Red flag #5. Passing around 10,000 feet I engaged the autopilot at the Captain's urging to finally get back in the cockpit as a crew and together correct the problem. I engaged LNAV, but we were not turning fast enough for ATC and the controller gave us a new heading of 010. I'd like to add at this point that our controller was patient, helpful and professional throughout our fiasco. The only way he could have helped us more is if he teleported into the cockpit and handed us our crew meals. Somewhere in the fray I had suggested that we reload the departure and that would bring KLIPR up, and now the legs page had a discontinuity and we had lost the LAS transition. Also we were given further climb, and now the KEGGS intersection to get us back on the departure. It was at this point I saw we had not been heading to KLIPR at all, but to 'CLIPR'! How did I miss that?! I had set up that problem by not giving proper confirmation of the legs page entry, having not used proper procedures (see Red flag #5). Further climb, and now direct to NNAVY were issued, but we first had to reload the lost LAS transition. After that was competently accomplished, our 'helmet fire' was apparently extinguished, and we were switched to the next Departure Controller. He gave us direct Las Vegas, and kindly spelled 'LAS' in the clearance for the lost crew.What followed was probably a good 2 hours of discussion and self-examination of what went wrong and why. I believe that two primary factors set us up for these errors. The first was my too-brief departure review. This was the first time the Captain had been on this departure, and only my second. Although we both verified the FMC route and legs page, and had confirmed the proper altitudes, we were not familiar with all the new (to us) waypoints, such as KLIPR. A more thorough review on the ground was paramount, and I failed to do it. The second was my desire to manually fly the aircraft during what rapidly became a complex departure. At the first sign of things getting too busy, it became mandatory for me to engage the autopilot, and thereby engage my brain in helping eliminate the threat. I failed in that regard. Adding mistakes such as 'CLIPR' vs. 'KLIPR', was due to my attention being more in the HUD than on performing proper FMC verification procedures. That was entirely on me. I still have no explanation for why KLIPR was not on the legs page. I had displayed on my CDU the Takeoff Ref page, and did not give due diligence to the ND or the legs page on the Captain's side. What I saw was '_ _ IPR', and a magenta line in the direction I wanted to go. Not good enough! Additionally, in my attempt to find KLIPR on the Jepps I zoomed in and slid the page right-to-left, taking the desired waypoint right out of sight. Using the autopilot undoubtedly would have enabled me to do this search more thoroughly. We had only seconds, it seemed, to prevent this entire undesired event.
1814892: Our company flight [Aircraft X] was given instructions to taxi westbound on TWY XX to ACM XY and to contact ground there. The crew deviated from the instructions and transitioned to XZ. By doing so, Aircraft X almost came nose to nose with Aircraft Y which was trying to enter the ramp via XZ. ATC was able to stop Aircraft Y and had Aircraft X join TWY XZ to avoid further issues.
1814989: This was in a B737-8 MAX which is not selectable on the menu. Inbound to ZZZ, deviating west of the arrival due to a severe TS over ZZZZZ and also another TS touching ZZZZZ1 along with multiple significant CB radar returns just west of our direct line to ZZZZZ1. We checked in with ZZZ Center and descended to or level at FL340. We were made aware that our deviation west of the arrival was causing the Controller difficulty in de-conflicting our descent due to departing traffic which was below us and to my understanding west of us. Very busy controller with no time to discuss options. I was approaching the west edge (absolutely as close as possible) of the last significant CB when the Controller told us in an excited tone to turn right 15 degrees and descent to FL280 (or maybe 240, I don't recall now). The CB was about 4 mile ahead and 2 miles across in both directions and 15 degrees right would put us straight through the middle of it. I started an immediate right and tried to ask my First Officer to tell the Controller we had to have farther right, but he saw me turning and read back the 15 degree instruction. The Controller was immediately on to two or three other calls. I asked my First Officer to tell the Controller the heading that we needed to fly and about then the Controller noticed that we had turned a bit extra and shouted at us because apparently another aircraft was departing in the corridor between the last CB and the big TS. I immediately corrected back and flew through the middle of the CB I was trying to avoid which was where the Controller wanted us in the first place. I also paused my descent very briefly to verify with the Controller that we were going to be safe still and we agreed on a heading of north as we passed directly through the cell. Fortunately, despite passing though the small cell with a solid yellow return, there was no significant turbulence and no injuries. I don't believe we caused loss of separation and my intention was to coordinate and return to the desired heading as soon as possible. The frequency was too busy, departures probably should have been pushed farther west, I was trying to comply with the Controller's guidance as best I could while not creating a dangerous turbulence situation for my flight attendants and passengers. The B737-8 MAX radar might be overly sensitive. Had the Controller asked 30 seconds sooner we would have had time to coordinate, or a minute later we could have taken any heading. In retrospect, we should have said we were unable to turn for another 6 miles, but given the urgency in the Controller's voice, I thought I was doing the right thing.Whenever an airplane is cleared to deviate for weather and is operating around thunderstorms and significant CBs, it seems like the Controller should always ask if you can accept a turn, not just assign a heading into the direction of the things we are avoiding. Also, if there is any way to make these frequencies less congested, that would help also. And finally, the other company's aircraft was apparently flying outbound and closer to our assigned arrival than we were comfortable with flying inbound. Maybe ZZZ Center should develop and publish alternate Departure and Arrivals that could be assigned for weather avoidance as widespread thunderstorms are so common in this area.
1815045: We were cleared for takeoff on Runway XX in XXX and completed the before takeoff checklist. We lined up on the runway and I gave flight controls to the First Officer as it was his takeoff. He initiated the takeoff roll and all was normal. I called 80 knots and a few seconds later we noticed a large bird flying in front of the aircraft, flying at engine height from left to right in front of the aircraft. We presume that we were around 90-100 knots of airspeed. Upon the bird flying past the right side of the aircraft we heard a loud bang with a simultaneous shake/vibration. (Between seeing the bird and the noise/vibration was about 1-2 seconds) As this happened I called for the reject and applied braking and reverse thrust. We came to a stop on the runway and I advised the passengers to remain seated and the First Officer advised ATC. The engines were idling normally, (although the vibrations on the #2 engine were briefly amber) and our brake temperatures were below then amber range. We exited the runway at exit and stopped as CFR (requested by us) evaluated the exterior of the aircraft, we had shut down engine #2 prior to them approaching the engine. They reported some damage to the engine but no other visible damage to elsewhere on the aircraft. I elected to taxi to the gate and we parked at Gate XX without issue. I had briefed the passengers and FAs about the situation and everyone was kept informed. While parked, I was advised by the B-FA that in addition to a loud bang and vibration (presumably when we hit the bird), there was a bright orange/yellow flash on the right side of the aircraft at the same time as these noises/vibrations. Upon inspection of the aircraft at the gate it was obvious that a bird was ingested into the #2 engine as there was debris inside of and damage to the engine.
1815139: Engine failed on takeoff and climbout at about 300 to 400 feet, busy trying to get a restart, switch fuel tanks, backup fuel pump, ignition, carb heat, mixture, throttle, all to no avail, just had to land straight ahead. Confirmed after towing back to hanger that fuel and controls all have continuity, aircraft had been filled with 25 gallons 100LL at ZZZ, 10 in port tank 15 in starboard tank. 21 gallons each tank, confirmed fuel in carb bowl, no ignition. Commercial EFII aircraft ignition system.
1815151: While approaching 7NM initial at ZZZ AFB under Runway Supervisory Unit ops control, my 3 ship of military aircraft were told that tower was going to have control of the runway for commercial traffic at 20 mile final. My 3 ship were instructed to carry through the overhead and go around the pattern. We executed that and once we were 90 to initial at 2,800 feet we picked up the visual to a commercial aircraft (Aircraft Y) approximately 200 feet above and descending to the runway.. I initiated the turn to initial early and offset the runway to the west to avoid the commercial aircraft. During the turn my wing men got perhaps 3,000 feet from me and they were not squawking in accordance with with our procedures. I was told that Aircraft Y had previously gone around and this was their second attempt to land. I was also told they received a TCAS advisory. I do not recall hearing a TCAS advisory, however my system was on 'TA' and it is very common to receive multiple traffic advisories in the pattern. I believe they were flying the RNAV Approach that does not have a hard altitude of 2300 feet at the final approach fix, like the ILS and TACAN approach does. We do that to avoid the VFR pattern traffic at 2800. I would suggest a review of all approaches at ZZZ AFB to avoid this situation again, or for the commercial traffic to have been assigned a hard altitude of 2300 feet until Final Approach Fix.
1815153: We were holding short of Runway 21 waiting for traffic landing [Runway] 21. A Warrior pulled down to Runway 3. I asked multiple times what he was doing and no answer. He finally said he's going to takeoff [Runway] 3. I advised him that there are 3 aircraft (2 planes including us and a helicopter) for patterns for [Runway] 21. A moment later he pulled onto the runway and started to takeoff. He called that he was taking off after rolling halfway down the runway. There was an experimental on a short base to final for [Runway] 21 that had to cut his base really short to evade the aircraft taking off [Runway] 3.
1815154: I was in communication with Center. Engine ran rough briefly then plane shook violently. Immediately assessed flight situation and started to run through checklist of potential issues. Switched fuel to most full tank and started fuel pump. Pushed in mixture and prop to full. Looked for a place to land. By then we were directly over a private landing field. I asked the Controller could we land there. He was not aware of that airfield and suggested [another airport] just north. By then I had lost about 1,000 ft in altitude. When I applied throttle, the plane shook. By my engine monitor it appears that we lost cylinder 1 and cylinder 6 was not performing. As I turned to the north, the passenger door then popped open, most likely from extreme vibration. This added to distraction and increase in ambient noise. I located the airport environment and made preparations for a 'normal' landing. When I began to slow plane down for gear extension, I began losing more altitude than normal. I could not apply throttle to regain altitude. I extended gear and then waited until I had airport made until I put in 10 degree of flap to slow us down to landing speed. Once on ground, I contacted Center and cancelled flight plan. Kudos to Controller who helped guide me to safe landing.
1815159: This was an engine fire that occurred after a hot start attempt. We tried to start the plane normally with the fuel pump, and then attempted again without the fuel pump. After the first attempt we decided to let the starter cool down for 20 seconds and cranked for another 10 seconds with the mixture lean and the throttle half way as the hot start [procedure] said. The engine almost started so we decided to pump the throttle. We let the plane rest, but soon after, the engine started smoking and we rushed out of the plane, cut off the mixture, and got the closest fire extinguisher to extinguish the flame. We should not have pumped the throttle as this could have been the cause of the engine fire, especially with a hot engine. Upon attempting to start the aircraft, we went through the normal before engine start checklist and cranked the engine, it almost started but did not. We then tried the flooded start procedure with full lean mixture and full throttle. The aircraft still sputtered but did not start. We then turned off the electric fuel pump and waited 20 seconds for the starter to cool down. Then we tried once more with no start and still the flooded start procedure. After that we decided to let the started cool off for longer and turned off the battery master to save battery charge. Shortly after turning off the electrical switches we noticed smoke coming out from under the cowling. We set the mixture to full lean and vacated the aircraft, confirmed the presence of flames under the cowling, retrieved a fire extinguisher and put out the fire
1815173: I was performing touch-and-go's during a supervised solo flight. On my final approach (GMU Runway 19), the other aircraft, who was told by ATC to continue flying through the final, took a northbound turn straight in front of me, flying directly towards me. I took evasive maneuvers by dropping down to the right. The other plane, only after being told by ATC that he had cut someone's final off, also took evasive maneuvers and started flying to his right and upwards. Following the evasive maneuver, landing on Runway 19 was uneventful.
1815189: Aircraft X [requested priority handling] while enroute to KTN from an airport in the lower-48. The pilot reported a loss of navigational avionics including the heading indicator, and could navigate solely by compass heading. Using a series of no-gyro vectors, I attempted to guide the aircraft over the airport in order to establish visual contact with the ground to allow for a visual approach or cancellation of IFR. Without the use of navigational equipment, I assumed that all instrument approach procedures would be impossible.During the initial vectoring, the pilot reported a momentary loss of engine power. He was able to restart the engine, which remained functional for the duration of the flight. When the pilot was over the airport at the minimum IFR altitude but could not make visual contact, I guided him to an area with a lower MIA in the hope that he would find visual conditions. After a descent in the lower MIA area, he indicated he was beneath the cloud layer and I gave him further instructions based on the aircraft being in VMC even though he had not cancelled IFR. This included allowing the pilot to continue a descent below the MIA while I continued a series of no-gyro vectors utilizing the terrain map on my display. I attempted to keep the aircraft over the water while maneuvering to enter the Tongass Narrows from the north. This stretch of water leads directly to the airport and is regularly used by VFR traffic operating locally. While maneuvering, the pilot lost visual contact with land. I issued a climb instruction to regain the MIA altitude, 060, over the airport in order to recover adequate separation from the terrain. Shortly thereafter, with the pilot level at 060 and flying over the airport, a Company A pilot [in] Aircraft Y called on frequency with weather information and indicated he could see the aircraft as it passed overhead. Additionally, a local frequent flyer, Aircraft Z, was instructed possibly by KTN FSS to abandon its VFR approach to Runway 11 and continue southeast toward the aircraft [with priority handling] and [to] join my frequency. I utilized that aircraft as an airborne spotter to aid in guiding Aircraft X into the airport from the south below the MIA.At this time, the pilot of Aircraft X advised he had approximately 13 gallons of fuel remaining and was exhausting it at a rate of 18 gallons per hour. Given the limited fuel quantity, lack of navigational options, and uncertain weather, I determined I would have to take the aircraft on the most expedient path to the airport. The pilot of Aircraft Z was VMC in the same area, having climbed from less than 1,000 ft. north of Runway 11 to nearly 4,000 ft. all while over terrain. Depictions on the Company A RNAV M 29 approach plate indicated that the terrain was no higher than 3,000 ft. in the area Aircraft X needed to fly across in order to reach the airport. Using the information provided by Aircraft Y, Aircraft Z, and the approach plate, I felt it was the last reasonable option to guide Aircraft X north toward the airport, over terrain at 4,000 ft.Aircraft Z established visual contact with Aircraft X about 10 miles south of the airport and remained in close proximity. The pilot of Aircraft X reported the airport in sight while heading north over Gravina Island near Nichols Passage and Blank Inlet at about 4000 ft. Shortly thereafter, we received confirmation from KTN FSS that the aircraft had landed safely on Runway 29.I am not sure there is much I could recommend that would prevent future [priority handling] of this type. It is not uncommon for pilots to encounter difficulty in Southeast Alaska, particularly those unfamiliar with Alaska flying. Perhaps more robust outreach to pilots from the lower-48 concerning the multitude of factors that present greater risk in the area is warranted. Weather, procedural and service limitations, lack of suitable landing sites, and the need for greater safety margins could all be presented to summerleisure flyers who visit our airspace.The pilot of Aircraft X performed incredibly well during a challenging situation. The pilots of Aircraft Y and Aircraft Z were crucial to my situational awareness and contributed directly to the successful resolution of this incident. KTN FSS and my colleagues at ZAN provided timely and useful assistance. All are to be recognized and commended for their efforts.
1815248: Beginning taxiing from gate had to come to a stop avoid a collision with a company vehicle. Fortunately, I brief this as a threat in ORD and DEN, so I was able to stop smoothly. The disturbing part of the event was how reckless his driving was. He didn't even slow down. Instead he or she took a hard left turn towards the terminal and continued on the parallel road. Ramp frequency was too busy to make a timely report.
1815304: At GS intercept, 2000, on the ILS XX and as I was setting the missed approach altitude, 2,500, the outer ALT ring was in 1;000s increments. I intermittently set 3,000, reset 2,000, twisted outer ring to 100s increments, and set 2,500. In my haste twisting the outer ring, I unknowingly tugged the ALT select knob. We had just begun the descent on the GS. The engines went to climb power, destabilizing the approach immediately and the Captain called a go-around. I called the GA to Tower, and their instructions were runway heading to 2000. Since we were almost already at the GA altitude, the Captain stopped the go-around configuration at go-around flaps. We assumed a very quick return/rejoin was about to happen so he maintained gear down, flaps 2, and 170 kt.During our vectoring back to final with Approach Control, an ECAM was triggered simultaneously with autopilot disconnect cavalry audible alert, and the Captain said, 'TOGA LOCK?' He immediately accomplished a match/mash. ECAM showed AP (Autopilot)/ATHR (Autothrust) OFF, SLATS LOCKED and WINGTIP BRAKE. He maintained PF role as it was now raw data, with zero PFD (Primary Flight Display) information beyond airspeed, altitude and VSI. There were no characteristic speeds and no min/max symbols, Vls, Vmo, etc., apart from the blue-selected speed caret. I ran the QRC, the QRH, and LAND APP procedures, as well as comms. The Captain elected to not declare an emergency, as Approach had broadcasted we were priority. We verified the approach was the appropriate one and reloaded it, a quick cursory brief about speeds, and we were cleared for the approach. One attempt was made to cycle the FDs for some guidance, to no avail. Autothrust would not engage. The Captain had to hand-fly the approach raw data. He successfully landed, we cleared the runway, and taxied to the gate.Slow is smooth and smooth is fast. In my haste to correct a simple mistake, I made a blunder. No fault go-around policy is great! There's no way of knowing if we'd have seen the slat lock if the first approach was flown to a landing. I had approximately XX hours on type.
1815316: [The] flight departed ZZZ, [runway] XXL and at 400 ft. we were given a heading of 360. As soon as the turn was initiated a loud bang was heard from below and behind the cockpit. The noise then went away. A few moments later FA (Flight Attendant) 1 called up and reported a loud banging noise from 2R. There were no ECAM or any other indications in the cockpit - all displays were normal - nor was the noise audible from the cockpit. After getting the airplane stabilized and the after-takeoff checks completed, I sent the FO (First Officer) back to investigate. It was confirmed that a loud banging was obvious in the cabin. A return to the field was planned, ATC notified, [priority handling was requested], FA's briefed for a precautionary landing, Dispatch notified and CFR (Crash Fire Rescue) requested. Runway XY was requested as this was an overweight landing, and the QRH procedure was followed. A smooth landing followed, the aircraft was brought to a stop after clearing Runway XY and the airplane inspected by CFR crew. The comment was that, 'A door was missing.' No other damage noted, and the flight taxied to a gate uneventfully. A walk-around revealed the 2R slide door departed the aircraft, followed by the slide. The noise was from the inflation supply line which was banging against the fuselage and wing root. A write-up for the missing door and raft was entered into the log along with the overweight landing notes. [The cause can be found through] perhaps confirmation of all maintenance items accomplished during the inspection at ZZZ immediately previous to this event. [I suggest to find the] determination of why the slide/raft door failed and [to find] appropriate remedies [to be] taken to preclude future issues. I was assigned FO (First Officer) on [the] flight. I arrived at aircraft and the Captain was already at the aircraft. I performed the preflight walk-around and noted no issues. All checks for preflight were normal. We were cleared for takeoff on Runway XXL, initial climb to 5000 and heading 290. Takeoff was normal. The Captain called for AP (Autopilot) on and pulled heading at turn altitude. Climb power reduction and clean-up was normal. We were handed off to Departure and checked in. Departure gave us a climb to 7,000 and 360 heading. I confirmed 7,000 with ATC and the Captain set 7,000 and I confirmed it. As he turned the heading knob to 360, a loud bang was heard from behind the flight deck. The #1 FA (Flight Attendant) called and reported the bang and a clunking noise near 2R door. No ECAM or warnings were displayed.The Captain retained the aircraft, leveled at 16,000 as cleared, and set speed to 245. We completed all checks and asked ATC to remain at 16000 as we needed to check out something. They approved that and asked if we were [requesting priority handling]. We replied not at this time, but we will need to check some things. The Captain then asked if I was OK with going back and checking things out as the sound could not be heard on the flight deck. The FA came forward and I went to the cabin and inspected the area and heard the banging she described. I returned to the flight deck, described what I heard and what I felt was happening and suggested that we return. The Captain agreed and formulated a return plan. He completed all notifications [and] reviewed all procedures with me. We [requested priority handling] and returned to base for an overweight landing.The Captain performed the landing as per QRH procedures. He brought the aircraft to a stop on the taxiway as CFR (Crash Fire Rescue) could inspect the aircraft, and they informed us that there was a door open and everything else looked OK. We taxied to the gate, followed shutdown procedures, and then went down to inspect the aircraft. At that time, we found that the 2R slide door and slide were missing and the inflation hose was hanging down and had struck the fuselage. The Captain the entered entries in the AML for the damage and overweight landing.My concern is that when we checked the system pages to see if we had any systems issues, there were none indicated. The doors page showed all the slides green and the white 'slide' indications. I.e., normal armed condition. Had the green box that indicated the 2R slide shown amber, we would have been alerted that the door was in fact open - in this case gone - and would have had a better idea of what we were dealing with.
1815317: After a 2 hour maintenance delay I was taxiing from gate XX to spot XX. My First Officer (FO) was just back from furlough and [was] a bit behind. He was having trouble with the ground frequencies so I diverted some of my attention to helping him with the frequency. In doing so I taxied across the line and my nose was out on taxiway Kilo. There were no other airplanes in the area but Ground did point it out to us (when we finally got the right frequency) that we were on taxiway Kilo. I've been doing this a long time and I violated one of my own rules- stop the aircraft and sort out the problem. I also did another thing that I strive not to do- micro-manage my FO. Causally speaking it was a wake up to me. Stop the plane.
1815340: During the preflight, I had a jumpseater come to the cockpit and ask to ride in the jumpseat to our destination. This was my first time having someone occupy the jumpseat in over a year due to Covid, and this was my first experience with an Additional Crew Member (ACM) in the auto-closeout passenger counts. The First Officer performed the W&B and Takeoff calculations. Neither of us noticed that the jumpseater was missing from the ACM data that was pushed to us from the gate agent. As a result, we took off with an improper W&B and Takeoff performance calculation. During the climbout I realized I didn't double check the W&B for the ACM before departure and found the ACM was missing. I was chatting with the jumpseater and did not double check the First Officer's work to make sure the jumpseater had been added into the W&B. I should have remained focused and double checked the W&B for the ACM. Full flight with jumpseat access granted from gate agent, jumpseat would be occupied. Received auto closeout thinking everything was taken care of including ACM in jumpseat. After departure, the Captain asked if the takeoff data included the ACM, after review, it did not. Cause of this event was being in the mindset that passenger auto closeout took care of all people loading considerations without double checking that the ACM was included. Recurrence of the event can be prevented by verifying ACM is included when they are occupying jumpseat instead of relying on auto closeout.
1815360: While passengers were boarding I was notified by Flight Attendant A that a passenger had a smart bag that they could not put on the cart because they could not remove the battery. Flight Attendant A told me that it was a fairly full flight and there might not be a seat to put the bag in because it was not going to fit in the overhead compartment in the cabin. She asked me if we could put the bag in the forward cargo compartment with the flight crew bags since we have access to it inside the cabin. I told her to standby and proceeded to request a supervisor give me a call to help interpret the rules on this situation. In FOM it says that smart bags must have the batteries removed prior to being stored in the cargo compartment, but it does not reference anything about cabin storage. The supervisor, Name, and I decided that the bag was okay as long as it was placed in the cabin and not in a cargo compartment (including the forward cargo). There was an open row that the bag was placed in and we determined that it was in compliance with the FOM guidance and departed as scheduled. Improve and clarify guidance in the FOM and flight attendant manuals on this topic. There is currently no guidance on smart bags in the cabin of the aircraft, only in the cargo area. After being notified by ground service agents and flight attendants that one of the passengers has in his/her possession a smart bag, both Captain and I reviewed the FOM regarding the smart bag policy (FOM page #), and the Captain called the supervisor. We all agreed after reviewing the FOM that the bag may stay with the passenger in the cabin, because FOM stated that battery from the bag shall be removed prior to the storage in the cargo compartment. It did not state that battery needs to be removed prior to the storage in the cabin. FOM should be clarified to state that smart bag batteries shall be removed prior to the storage in the cargo compartment and in the cabin, or more simply, anywhere on the aircraft.
1815434: I was enroute from the south and was to the west of the Washington DC airspace when I was given a new route which was direct ZZZZZ, then direct ZZZZZ1, then T291 to ALB, then V489 to GFL. I was advised that my read back was correct. I was in IMC and slowly entered the new route into the navigator. As I was trying to enter V489 from ALB to GFL it became apparent that that segment of V489 no longer existed as the VOR was decommissioned several years ago and I discovered later that the ALB - GFL segment was removed last fall. I did not make an issue of it because I knew I would be asking for and getting vectors to final for the ILS 01 at GFL long before arriving at the ALB VOR. My question is whether the folks that give these routes are using outdated charts or have preferred routes that should have been updated. In any case, the routers need to be made aware of the changes to the Victor airways that used GFL in them as they all have been modified.
1815448: I was coming back to my home airport after a fuel stop, there was weather coming in and I was trying to land before the storm got to the airport. I entered pattern at a 45 degree entrance to the downwind of Runway XX and flew the rest of the pattern. On short final, I was at landing speed of 90MPH. I landed long on the runway and tapped the brakes on landing which entered my aircraft into a porpoise. Being too far down the runway, I knew I could not pull out of it and needed to keep the airplane on the ground. I pulled the power to keep it down and the prop struck the ground which then collapsed the nose gear and brought me to a stop. Analyzing the situation, the first mistake I made was trying to beat the storm. This was the root to everything that happened. Next, I was coming down too fast and landed too long. I also tapped the brakes, which commenced the porpoise. If I was put into this situation again, I would have diverted to another close airport and waited for the storm to pass. What I have learned from this is to never try to beat a storm, along with don't rush to get down and go around when you need to go around. I am very lucky to have walked away from this situation and it will forever be an experience to learn from and never repeat.
1815459: We were attempting to land at the FOK airport. We attempted to use the pilot controlled lighting system, and made several attempts to key the microphone to turn on the lighting for landing. However, the runway lighting did not illuminate.We contacted a person on the ground attempted to activate the lights for us using a radio, and reported that they were unable to activate the lights. Air traffic control vectored us directly overhead the airport. We attempted to activate the lights again while we were overhead the airport, and we were able to successfully activate the lighting.We made a normal approach and landing. We unloaded our passengers, and prepared to takeoff. While on the ramp and during the taxi for departure, I tried to adjust the runway lights intensity, and we were unable to do so. We took off before the runway lights turned off, and reported this issue to ATC. I checked later that day, and a NOTAM had not been issued regarding the issue that we experienced.
1815460: Enroute to ZZZ, I tuned to ZZZ's UNICOM and it sounded like the pattern was very busy. [I] decided to change plans and go to ZZZ1. I got airport information from the sectional map and noticed *RP. As I approached the airport, I could hear transmissions from a Piper Pawnee departing Runway XX towing a glider. I announced entering a right downwind for Runway XX, then base Runway XX, and final Runway XX. About mid-final, the tow plane announced left downwind Runway XX. I saw the tow plane heading [towards the] opposite direction above me at about my 11:00 position. I looked inside for a few seconds to complete my final GUMP check. The tow plane announced left base Runway XX. I saw the tow plane about my 9:15 to 9:30 position approximately 300 ft. laterally and 30 ft. to 40 ft. above me. At that point I realized I must not be transmitting. As I started to do a go-around, UNICOM announced, 'You have traffic.' He replied, 'Thank you;' and immediately entered a climbing right turn. I did not try to troubleshoot the radios at that critical phase of flight. I did not feel it was safe to go around and enter the traffic pattern considering the other aircraft in the area and not being able to transmit.When getting airport information from the sectional I failed to notice the asterisk next to 'RP' and assumed right traffic. Right traffic is for gliders and gyrocopters. Airplanes use left traffic. At airports where both left and right traffic exist, I would suggest simply putting 'TP' for traffic pattern. That way neither can be assumed and would require further research. After entering CTAF in com1, I noticed the 'com1/com2' transmit selector was already in com1.I failed to adequately research airport information. I failed to manage my radios. I failed to ensure communication with UNICOM and traffic. It won't happen again. I enrolled in a ground school and I am getting additional instruction.
1815480: We attempted to activate the pilot controlled lighting, and then conducted an ILS approach to Runway 24. When we were clear of clouds on the approach and observed the lighting, the approach lights appeared to be on full intensity, but we did not observe runway edge lights. We attempted to adjust the pilot controlled lighting system to get the runway lights to turn on, but were unsuccessful. At approximately 500 feet above ground, we executed a missed approach. We contacted the Fixed Base Operator and they tried to activate the lights for us with a radio on the ground, but they reported that they were unable to activate the lights. We then diverted to a nearby airport and landed normally.
1815538: We were operating with MEL 27-XX, Pitch Control Disconnect Advisory Message, which requires other MELs, including MEL 22-XX Autopilot System. Approach Control turned us onto final for a visual approach to Runway XX and instructed us to contact Tower. After tuning the #1 com radio to the Tower frequency, we began configuring the aircraft for landing when we received the autopilot warning along with the AP (Autopilot) Fail and Pitch Control Disconnect EICAS messages. This was a bit distracting because the autopilot was not in use nor had it been used the entire flight due to [the] MEL. After determining all systems were okay to continue, we then started receiving the EGPWS glideslope warning. I determined this was due to ATC having the ILS for Runway XY turned on. The FO (First Officer) had established a normal visual approach angle so I told him to continue. I then reset the frequencies in both nav radios to silence the errant warnings. After landing, the Tower issued taxi instructions and said that next time we should contact Tower for a landing clearance.[The cause was] multiple distractions. Don't let minor distractions dominate the flight deck.
1815560: It was written up in the maintenance log. Repeatedly, hex screws [were] missing from main gear wheel wells. Multiple screws, multiple aircraft. This is a serious safety issue that needs to be addressed. [This] needs to be addressed in [the] training of aircraft maintenance personnel. Policy and procedures need to change at all levels of quality assurance. Process within the company.
1815573: First Officer was the Pilot Flying. Three minutes after level off at FL350, Engine 1 stall ECAM [was displayed] with loud banging from the #1 engine. Followed the Non-Normal methodology. Ran the ECAM action. With power on the #1 engine at idle we were unable to maintain altitude. Descended to FL240. Finished the QRH follow up procedure. #1 engine showed all indications normal. Landed without further incident. Startle factor was in full effect. Took me good minute to wrap my head around the event. It was mechanical so I doubt [I could suggest] anything. Add it to a training event perhaps.
1815593: After landing Runway 13 instructed to Taxi K, Runway 22, P3 to gate. Turned on to Runway 22 and noticed blue marker to our right. Asked ATC about them and was informed that is the taxiway for Runway 22. Transitioned so as to be between those. There are no NOTAMs regarding a designated taxi lane on Runway 22. Only NOTAM listed is Runway 22 closed taxi only. I feel that the NOTAMs need to be corrected to indicate Runway 22 has an established taxilane and ATC not use the term taxi Runway 22 to P3. Instead join taxilane on Runway 22 to P3. Apparently there have been numerous people doing the same thing. Markers are not lighted and very short with only reflective tape. Instructed to taxi to the gate after clearing [Runway] 13 via K [Runway] 22 P3. After entering Runway 22 we noticed unlit blue markers on the runway and transitioned between those. NOTAM doesn't mention that runway has been modified to a temporary taxiway that is on part of the runway with unlit nonstandard markings. Provide more info in the NOTAM and taxi instructions that highlight the change. The taxi instructions should not reference Runway 22 but call name it a temporary taxiway which is what they have constructed over Runway 22.
1815598: Arriving in TUS we had briefed the RNAV RNP Y Rwy 11 approach. Our clearance was for the ZONNA 1 arrival which took us from SSAND to OTUKE. Just outside SSAND we were cleared to fly the lateral course for the RNAV Y. We cleaned up the box and turned on to the course. The next fix was LUYEG, our clearance was to cross at 11,000 feet cleared for the RNAV Y approach. We slowed to 240, went flaps 1, did the LAVS procedure. The FMA went to PATH and looked normal. We read the Approach checklist. I checked the FMAs again, it indicated SPD not PATH. There was no VNAV scale to indicate high or low on the path. I selected V/S and slowed the rate of descent. Before I could enter the next stepdown altitude in the MCP, ATC called with a low altitude alert. There was no EGPWS warning. I disconnected the A/P and initiated a climb. We were in VFR conditions. We reengaged the A/P and selected 9,500 feet for a crossing altitude at HODPU. We did the LAVS procedure outside of HODPU. The FMA went to PATH and looked normal until it crossed the fix and then it went to speed. After that we used the A/P to fly the lateral course put each crossing altitude in the MCP. On final I disconnected the automation [and] flew a visual approach. First Officer did an excellent job monitoring, calling out deviations, and analyzing the problem. We delayed reading the approach checklist until the FMS was correct for the approach that we intended to fly. I was distracted by the checklist reading and that caused a delay for me to recognize that the FMA for the vertical mode was no longer in PATH. We had asked the ABQ Center Controller to clear us onto the approach [but] he told us to make our request to Approach Control. It meant that we were making changes to the FMS just before turning on to the approach.First Officer and I discussed the FMS setup, the approach, our procedures in the debrief. We were unable to determine what error caused the airplane to not fly the RNAV approach correctly. It would have been helpful to do everything earlier, complete the changes to the FMS and read the Approach checklist well before we were cleared onto the approach path. That would free both pilots to monitor the automation and catch deviations sooner.
1815642: While setting up beverage cart, myself (4), 2, and 3 all at the same time noticed an abnormal smell. It smelled electrical and went from a level 2 to a 10 within seconds, and haze was also noticed. I pulled galley circuit breakers, turned chillers, and coffee makers off while 3 called flight deck and informed them of the situation. We diverted to ZZZ1. The entire incident was approximately 30 minutes. The three of us (2, 3, 4), experienced headaches, nausea, and dizziness.After deplaning in ZZZ1, we, as a crew, needed to debrief. We had NO place to do so. Ultimately, we all sat in the one restaurant that had seating. We politely had to request the loud music be turned down, as we didn't feel well, as well as needed to debrief. Scheduling had only called number 3, and was having her relay our account of what happened through her. Scheduling should have called EVERY crew member for our account of the incident from us DIRECTLY. Tracking was called and said 'we heard two of you want a [day off]'. None of us had any idea where that came from. In the meantime, Name 1 from safety had text or called us. He told us You all need to get out of your uniforms IMMEDIATELY, take a hot shower and wash our hair IMMEDIATELY '. He said to contact him if the company gave us any sort of push back. The company did give us a hard time. They told us in order to get a hotel, that we would be removed and coded as a sick call, using our sick time. Our Captain, was listening to this on speaker phone, and he told the company that this was a diversion due to fumes, and questioned why our crew would or could possibly be charged with a sick call and sick time taken away. Keep in mind, there were still approximately 50 passengers that were unable to be rerouted for one reason or another. It was our impression, that after FIVE hours sitting in the ZZZ1 airport, the company needed us to work the flight back to ZZZ to get said passengers back. I called tracking back, and after a very long wait on hold, told her that we took Advil and wanted to be reinstated to work the flight back. The agent had indicated to us that there were NO flight attendants laying over that could relieve us. We had also gotten back in touch with Name 1 from safety, letting him know we had no way of showering and getting out of the fume filled uniforms. I believe the only reason we were reinstated to work the trip is because the company wanted to get the passengers back to ZZZ without any regards to how we felt or the ordeal we went through. Each crew member should have individually been contacted by scheduling. We were dealing with two different people, and neither seemed to know what was going on."
1815668: On initial climb out 600 ft. AGL, [an] airplane climbing from [the] parallel runway turned left crosswind in front of me with no ATC clearance, causing me to level off for collision avoidance. ATC was supposed to call our turns but the other aircraft did not follow instructions. I, [the] Flight Instructor, took a private pilot, whom I have never flown with before, up in the traffic pattern to 'kick off some rust' as he hadn't flown in the last 60 days. We had done 8 touch-and-go's prior and were completing one more to end the lesson. Upon takeoff, Tower called and stated, 'Aircraft Y continue upwind, I will call the crosswind.' We continued the upwind and I began talking with the private pilot to do the right traffic, etc. At this point, Tower called up to unknown aircraft and states, 'Turn left crosswind.' I did not hear the tail number clearly and could not confirm it was for our aircraft. [The] private pilot states the call was for us and was given to turn left crosswind. I stated I did not hear the call and cannot confirm. I began to second-guess him and asked 3 times, and each time the private pilot stated yes, we have the okay to turn left. [The] private pilot turns left and Tower called and stated, 'Aircraft Y, turn right crosswind.' [The] private pilot got on the mic and stated, 'We are in the wrong downwind and made the incorrect turn.' Other aircraft later transmits it was a 'close one' to Tower.To avoid this from happening in the future, I believe as Flight Instructor I should have called the Tower due to the miscommunication. At the end of the day, I have more experience and it is my duty to make sure the aircraft is operated correctly and safely. I also believe the private pilot should have recognized they were unsure of the radio call and [to] call to Tower as well. If the communication was better in the cockpit and we were more authoritative to speak with Tower, this situation could have been avoided.
1815669: Came in to land on Runway XX. Upon landing student applied heavy left brakes. I applied right rudder to counteract. I applied the handbrake and there was no pressure. I had to use the handbrake because the Cherokee doesn't have brakes on copilot side.Ended up off the runway and in the grass. Taxied off the grass back to parking.
1815680: Short Final to S95's Runway (RWY) 23 - a motorhome and trailer crossed the runway. Executed a Go-around as I was just crossing the threshold. I thought I was making calls on the CTAF of 122.8, but I had failed to select the proper radio, and was actually making calls on the [wrong frequency].
1815691: [We] departed HNL for a training flight. This was both a biannual flight review and a night currency flight to be shared between us. It was an uneventful flight with training completed as needed. Upon returning to HNL and accordance with the Approach Controllers, we held over Ford Island for sequencing. We were then given clearance to land on Runway 8L. The landing was uneventful.Taxi instructions were then given to us - turn right on taxiway G, left on B, right on E, and hold short of Runway 4L, the left seat pilot read back the instructions verbatim and confirmed the hold short instructions. We began to taxi, and then I took the the flight controls midway down Bravo. The intersection of taxiway B and E is listed as Hotspot 3 on the HNL Airport Diagram. Before we arrived at E, Tower made another call to confirm the hold short instructions and they were read back correctly, again from the left seat pilot. As we made the turn from B to E, we did not see the Runway 4L hold short lines and unknowingly taxied onto an active runway.This near 30 feet horizontal runway incursion put us directly in front of a departing [aircraft]. The [aircraft] was at rotation speed when they spotted us in front of them and [they] were able to lift off and bank the airplane to the right, overflying us.I had control of the aircraft from the right seat at the time, but the responsibilities between the two of us were unclear and controls were exchanged on the ground, but radio were handled from the other pilot. Also adding to the confusion was a lack of experience and recency with night operations in general, night operations at HNL, never having landed on runway 8L or taxied from 8L - I only had one other night flight at HNL X months prior. All of these factors contributed significantly to this inadvertent runway incursion and near miss.
1815717: During take off, the decision was made by the PIC(self) to abort owing to a bang and the aircraft pulling left requiring extreme right rudder use. It was later determined by the PIC this was due to the spring loaded rudder trim jumping to the left from the right. It had previously been advised by the other flight instructors at the school to leave the rudder trim in the right side position during all phases of flight, owing to a extreme left turning tendency. However, by doing this it put undue stress on the rudder trim spring and when left rudder was used during take off the spring gave way and released the trim fully left. At the time this cause was not known to the PIC, hence the decision to abort the flight. Later it was advised that this should be in neutral, as per the POH, however incorrect local guidelines had been advised. PIC will revert to the POH for all future use in Aircraft X.
1815722: I received an invite to fly my drone over the residential property to determine damage to the roof of the detached garage. I normally check Airmap in order to determine airspace before flying. I did not check airspace before this flight. My Manager upon doing reviews, determined that I flew in a Class D of ZZZ Airport without prior authorization. Future flights, I shall check airspace before flying my drone and obtain authorization prior to flying in controlled airspace.
1815752: Cleared by Ramp Tower to taxi. We had switched to Denver Ground frequency when Company came racing southbound and cut us off. I had to jam on the brakes to avoid a collision. We returned to Ramp frequency. They confirmed that Company had been instructed to give way to us.
1815770: Assigned the Visual XXR backed up by the RNAV XXR Approach (which was advertised on the ATIS). ATC assigned 170 or 180 knots to ZZZZZ. I used LNAV/ VNAV with the autopilot engaged, speed intervention to maintain assigned speed. VNAV reverted to VNAV SPEED and began to get high on the approach. At 400 feet high, I disconnected the autopilot began correcting. Approaching the glide path we were still four white bars on the PAPI and visually looked much higher than we should have been. I began to fly the approach visually but became low in reference to the RNAV. The resulting approach produced descent rate warning approximately crossing the threshold. Upon coming into ZZZ we were set up and expecting the RNAV XXR. We had that loaded into the box. Somewhere outside ZZZZZ1 if I recall right we got cleared for the visual and backed it up with the RNAV XXR. Captain started calling for flaps and the aircraft began to slow to the selected flap speed. ATC gave us a speed of 180 knots so we had to open the speed window and reverted us into VNAV SPEED. We ultimately ended up being high on the approach. I told the Captain the path is not matching with the PAPI and he started to correct. Ultimately we ended up getting the 'don't sink warning' on the aircraft and the Captain corrected.
1815850: On PHLBO 3 arrival to EWR, approximately 5 to 10 miles south of PHLBO, level at 6,000 feet, 250 KIAS. Saw a bright yellow drone off the left side of the aircraft, maybe 200 feet below our altitude and 100 feet lateral. Reported the drone sighting to ATC, New York Approach Control on 120.15.
1815851: APU (Auxiliary Power Unit) bleed was on MEL (Minimum Equipment List) so we had to start Number 1 engine at the gate. After engine start all parameters were normal with engine stabilized. The external air and electric were disconnected and jetway removed from aircraft. Shortly after ground crews notified us via intercom that engine was on fire followed by saying that continuous flames coming out of the back of engine. Engine was shut down immediately and QRH was performed. No cockpit indications of fire and ground crews confirmed no fire after shut down of engine. Fire Department were called only as caution and we asked jetway to be reconnected to the aircraft for normal deplane. Entry was made in AML (Maintenance Log) and Maintenance was notified. We never had any indication in the cockpit of fire. We treated the ground crews alert as an ongoing fire and took action based on that. Safety is always top priority and in this case our external resource being our ground personnel played an important role by alerting us of the possible fire.
1815867: As we were en-route at cruise altitude FL360 feet 80 miles northwest of HMN VOR when we started to experience degraded navigation performance in the form of ATC fail alerts and an increasing ANP (Actual Navigation Performance) number relative to RNP (Required Navigation Performance). We notified ATC and were informed of GPS jamming somewhere north of El Paso. As we proceeded west, the navigation performance of our aircraft degraded more to the point where we received an UNABLE RNP message along with a GPS amber message. Once we got west of ELP and the TCS area, the navigation performance gradually improved and came back within normal parameters. Route track and actual position of aircraft were unaffected and there were no deviations from the planned and cleared routing. Not really any way to avoid other than don't jam GPS. But considering ATC was aware of it and able to keep aircraft notified of where and when the jamming effects would abate, it is not a huge hazard.
1815895: Started up the right engine and as I began to lean the mixture to stabilize the engine I heard a loud bang from the area of the right wing. As I looked out the right window of the cockpit I could see the wing had been severely damaged with flames coming out. I had not yet started the other engine and the airplane had not moved from its original position. After seeing the flames I immediately shut off the mixture to that engine and evacuated using the crew hatch. Once I was a safe distance away I call 911 to get the fire department and then notified supervisors.
1815921: [Passenger] has a large blow up pillow in exit row.Passenger in [exit row] has a air/blow up pillow that she put her arms in holes through the bottom, placed on her lap, and head through a hole in the top. Was not connected to the plane but larger than a regular air pillow. C and D flight attendants didn't know if this was allowed and asked me to let them know what I find out. Larger than a normal air pillow but was not connected to any part of the plane. Is this an obstruction of the exit or could it be popped or thrown forward was advised. Is this air pillow allowed in the exit or is it an obstruction of exit?
1815931: Pilot report that his right inboard brake was not actuating. Supervisor in Charge, Name, decided to change the right inboard brake. Assignment was given to Name 1. I, Name 2 was behind the desk that day printing all necessary paper work, Name 1 calls for assistance due to having brake jack issues. Name 3 and myself arrived at Aircraft X to help Name 1. Name 3 was in the cockpit monitoring hydraulic system and brake temp. I assisted Name 1 with lifting and changing the right inboard brake only due to the brake jack having issues and the weight of brake. Name 1 told me he was good from there and he will take care of the rest such as brake fittings, brake lines and brake temp sensor. I received a call from my Supervisor, also I sent pictures of what happened. After spending nearly an entire year without touching an aircraft due to the pandemic it is a possibility that Name 1 might of had a relapse reading the job card. After hearing about the incident from the Supervisor I was upset, frustrated that having done the job in the past, this could have happened. But I was more relief to know that problem was caught and rectified before something serious happened that could have put our customers, crew and aircraft in jeopardy. To read and ask as much question as needed in order to perform our duties in compliance with company and FAA policies.
1815932: I was in the process of landing at ZZZ and upon landing lost directional control after over rotating and striking the tail tie down and rudder, causing the aircraft to roll 30 yards off the right side off the runway after skidding about 500 feet on the main gear and tail on the runway without striking anything else and proceeded back on the runway and taxied to ramp.
1815943: Was on final approach into OSU landing to runway 27L. On final at less than .25 NM from end of runway, encountered a drone approximately 1 foot X 1 foot at same altitude and had to veer to right to avoid strike. As soon as I realized what it was, I contacted tower and notified them of location and all data that I could pass on incident.
1815953: With just 0.9 hrs of PIC time YTD, I arrived at my flying club's towered home field, ZZZ, rested and eager to shake off some rust. My first sign of how much rust I had came when I accepted a Ground instruction to RWY XX but taxied to the nearer RWY XY. After completing my runup, Ground advised me to taxi to RWY XX. I thanked Ground for 'that catch' and received a double-click 'you're welcome.' I paused, ensured I was focused and not letting myself feel rushed, and proceeded to RWY XX. I completed four takeoffs and landings, and after reviewing LiveATC recordings I believe that my radio communications were professional and crisp. Ground did request that I confirm one hold-short instruction, and Tower asked that I confirm a 'give way to helicopter' instruction as part of a 'hold short' read back. However, I acknowledged and complied with all instructions promptly, including hold-shorts, midfield reports, extended down winds, go-arounds, no delay etc., using proper phraseology. A midair near-miss occurred when two Cessna's with 'XXXX' in their call signs began to turn base at the same time -- Aircraft Y from Right Downwind, and I, Aircraft Z, from Left Downwind. I mistook a 'cleared for the option' instruction for Aircraft Y as being intended for me, and radioed my acceptance for a full stop. I believed Tower had cleared me to land. The conflicting traffic had been advised of 'that Cessna on Left Downwind;' from which I further inferred my own landing priority over this newcomer to the pattern. Upon review of the recordings, it is clear to me that Tower attempted to clarify that the landing clearance was for Aircraft Y, and that the call out to my position was purely advisory for Aircraft Y -- and not a reaffirmation of a clearance for Aircraft Z to land. However, someone stepped on the frequency, and I missed the clarification. It was only after Tower instructed me, 'You need to turn right now' that I saw the conflicting traffic approximately 1/2 mile turning right base. Tower then instructed me for the first time that I was #2 for the field. I attribute this near-miss primarily to my own lack of recency, but secondarily to additional factors. I lost situational awareness of other similarly-[call] signed Cessna's entering the pattern from the opposite direction. ATC could have clarified our landing sequence earlier, or verbally emphasized the differences in our call signs. (A minute later, Tower itself briefly confused two call signs, instructing me to turn Right Base when I was already on Short Final from Left Base, Tower quickly corrected itself when I advised of my position.) It was also a very busy pattern in which to shake off rust -- for pilots and ATC alike. Simultaneous radio transmissions obscured instructions that might otherwise have been sufficiently clear.
