Stress was apparent: After landing, I complied immediately with Tower's instruction to exit without delay -- only to be told urgently to 'stop right now' to avoid a jet on its takeoff roll. (I appreciate Tower's urgency: I had acknowledged the hold-short instruction and was already preparing to stop, but to their eyes I was still in 'no delay' mode as I transitioned from RWY to Taxiway.) Tower similarly expressed frustration with another pilot for requesting 'a turn around a point;' a term that Tower did not recognize, they doubtless would have preferred 'a 360' or 'a circle.' When I was finished with my pattern work, I briefly expressed my appreciation to Tower and received a friendly 'no problem' in response. I think we all did what we could to be as clear as possible (urgently if the situation demanded it), and to correct our mistakes. Although it will be frustrating at times, on balance I think this is a good set of attitudes to have, especially as the entire National Airspace System shakes off varying degrees of rust coming out of the pandemic. The dangers here were addressed, but a slightly more intransigent attitude, or a slightly more congested frequency, might have tipped the balance to a midair collision.
1815968: On above time and date at SJC I taxied from FBO to 30L at intersection C for departure. Upon completing the run up at about a 45 degree angle to runway facing departure end, I switched frequency to Tower frequency and immediately heard tower call me asking if I was ready. I responded in the affirmative. Tower's response was partially stepped on but I thought I was given take off clearance with an advisory of traffic on 2 1/2 mile final. Since with Tower's initial call to me asking if I was ready I sensed possible urgency and in my attempt to assist in that perceived urgency I quickly ran through pre take off flow and turned aircraft perpendicular to runway which placed the aircraft partially over the hold short line. Upon becoming perpendicular to runway I looked for the said traffic on final and saw the traffic not on 2 1/2 mile final but on short final. I immediately stopped the aircraft at which time Tower urgently advised me to hold short. I believe the tail of the aircraft was approximately at the hold short line with of course the rest of the aircraft beyond the hold short line. The Tower did advise the landing traffic to go around. After take off I was given a phone number to call. Immediately upon landing I called said phone number as requested and discussed occurrence with Tower.
1815972: During the approach to LAX Runway 25L, between the IF and FAF, we had a TCAS resolution, the traffic was shown 400 feet below us, to the right side, so we had to perform the TCAS maneuver, first it told us to reach steady flight and then ascend, so we had to interrupt the approach and maintain 2000 feet, then we had to perform another approach through [Runway] 25L without any issues.
1815979: The instructor and I were on a checkout flight in a flight school C172. After the training flight, we returned to ZZZ for 1 touch and go and 1 full stop landing. It was VFR conditions, but hazy with scattered clouds about 2000 feet above the airport. The airport was very busy with multiple training aircraft in the pattern using both runways. We were assigned Runway XXR. We completed our touch and go and were instructed to fly runway heading. After several minutes, we advised ZZZ Tower that we were still runway heading, at which point the controller advised us to turn right crosswind for right closed traffic to Runway XXR. While on the downwind, the controller advised us to extend downwind and he would call our base. We read back the instruction.When we were approximately .75 statute miles northwest of the airport, the controller changed our clearance to fly a close approach and we were cleared for the option. We read back the clearance and turned right base. Because we were high, we extended flaps to increase our descent rate. As I was about to turn final, the controller (a different voice this time) advised us to extend downwind, which we read back. I began an immediate climbing left turn. The controller immediately followed that clearance by clearing Aircraft Y to fly an immediate left 360. Aircraft Y was on final to either [Runway] XXL or XXR. There were multiple flight school aircraft with similar call signs in the pattern. Aircraft Y mistakenly made a right 360. I gained a visual contact on Aircraft Y, who was at my one o'clock low. I continued my left turn and climb to avoid collision with the aircraft. We extended downwind and were then given clearance to land. We landed without further incident. I believe that the hazy conditions, busy controllers, controller change or controller training, and multiple aircraft from the same flight school and similar call signs created confusion leading to this incident.
1815991: VFR flight, Aircraft Y approached from our left. Did not see plane until it was very close. Fortunately, our course did not intersect.
1816005: Air carrier descending via BAINY STAR, at apx. 8,300 feet reported near collision with a drone over the downtown Minneapolis area. Pilot estimated drone passed overhead by about 10-30 feet. Pilot stated it was a quadcopter type with red lights. 4 or 5 other aircraft passed through the same area over the next half hour but no other sightings reported.
1816007: Aircraft X was issued 3,500 ft. by my Trainee and we heard a good read back of 3,500 ft. I observed the aircraft at 3,100 ft. and I issued a climb immediately as the aircraft was a few miles from a 3,500 ft. MVA. The aircraft continued to descend further before he was able to climb. To be honest I let the Trainee go too far in running his own sequence. Had I been working I would typically not have the aircraft that low and close to the airport if he wasn't number one for the runway. I think this may have contributed to the Pilot mistaking thinking he was cleared for the visual approach.
1816010: I had Aircraft X in LUAW (Line Up and Wait) Runway XX waiting for Aircraft Y to complete a Touch-N-Go Runway XXR. While the Aircraft Y was around short final Runway XXR, a Helicopter (Aircraft Z) called ready to depart from west side of the airfield. I also had 2 helicopters (Aircraft A / Aircraft B) inbound who were 2 - 2.5 miles out to land. I quickly responded to Aircraft Z to depart and proceed outbound.Based on memory, I don't recall giving Aircraft Z any traffic about Aircraft X in LUAW. My memory feels like about 1-2 minutes now have passed and Aircraft Y is now upwind Runway XXR and crossing the intersection of Runway XX. I tell Aircraft Y to continue upwind. I then clear Aircraft X for take-off Runway XX. As I'm scanning the runways watching Aircraft X start his departure rotation, I noticed a helicopter going east about to cross the departure end of Runway XX. I thought that helicopter was Aircraft A which was supposed to land and according to our Letter of Agreement (LOA), would make him restricted west of Runway XX. Finally, I reached out to Aircraft A and told them to turn base now to land. Aircraft A then responded that they were still 1 mile west. I then realized my mistake and that the helicopter crossing the departure end was my helicopter outbound. I became flustered and a bit panicked and tried to reach out to that Aircraft Z, but accidentally called them the 3rd helicopter's call sign, Aircraft B, adding even more confusion to the whole scenario. At this point Aircraft X passes below Aircraft Z by maybe 50 to 100 ft. I apologize to Aircraft X about the close aircraft, he responded that he had the helicopter in sight. I then later reach out to Aircraft Z and apologize, and they said it was OK. Aircraft X did not report a RA and neither aircraft reported having to take evasive maneuvers.
1816018: Aircraft X was issued pilot discretion descent to 9,000 ft. He started down and I was busy working other traffic and had large differences in altimeter settings between ZZZ and ZZZ1 areas. I saw him go down to 8,900 or 8,800 ft. and thought it may just be a bad altimeter setting or since I had several frequencies that maybe he got stepped on trying to tell me he had airport in sight and wanted to cancel IFR. So I gave him altimeter setting for the closest airport, then asked him to verify altitude. On the next radar sweep he was still descending so I issued a low altitude alert and had him climb back up to 9,000 ft. He climbed back up and let me know about some forest fires in the area.
1816033: I was working a Radar Sector with a Radar Associate controller. I was informed prior to the event that I would be very busy and over numbers for the sector. I was working multiple, 8 plus IFR arrivals into ZZZ using the ILS approach. The volume and complexity of arrivals/departures/and overflights in the sector was high. After an initial descent, I had cleared Aircraft X to cross ZZZ1 at or above 14,000 ft. and cleared him for the ILS approach. I inadvertently issued this clearance in a 14,600 ft. MIA (Minimum IFR Altitude) area. Once my Associate Controller alerted me to the MSAW (Minimum Safe Altitude Warning) alert, the aircraft was already exiting the 14,600 ft. MIA, and as a result I did not issue a low altitude safety alert. The aircraft continued on the approach. ZZZ has shown a pattern of having very high peak demand in respect to arrivals. These spikes in demand are usually left up to the Radar Controller to take care of with little outside assistance from the Center TMU (Traffic Management Unit). This has resulted in numerous errors and other safety events as the Radar Controller is saturated. This high workload is also due in part to multiple transmitters for overflights and ZZZ arrivals and high terrain around ZZZ. I would suggest that preemptive procedures be developed for times that ZZZ is experiencing peak demand. Another possible long-term solution would be the stratification of Sectors into a high/low configuration so as to reduce the added complexity of overflight traffic. Frankly, with the volume ZZZ sees on a daily basis, especially in peak seasons, I am surprised it does not have an Approach Control. I was working the Assistant Controller position dealing with communication with Tower and point outs with adjacent sectors. Aircraft X was level at 15,000 ft. above a 14,600 ft. MIA (Minimum IFR Altitude) area when the Radar Controller issued a crossing restriction and clearance to Aircraft X to cross the ZZZ VOR at or above 14,000 ft. and cleared the aircraft for the approach. The aircraft descended below the MIA to 14,000 ft. before the Radar Controller realized the low altitude. No low altitude alert was issued. Spacing from adjacent sectors for ZZZ arrivals. And rerouting aircraft not landing into the sector around the airspace assisting in lower work load on the Radar Controller. The job was doable.
1816083: This is an informative report to highlight an issue that could be a safety and or planning concern. We were planning our takeoff data for departing ZZZ and were receiving MTOG [Maximum Take Off Gross] limitations that seemed unusually restrictive. We were a full flight from ZZZ - ZZZ1 reasonable fuel load. The advertised runways in use for departure were Runway XX, XYL. We were unable to receive takeoff data for Runway XX at our weight. The restriction on MTOG was listed as Obstacle Limitation. We tried various adjustments to get a number that would work. We were able to get takeoff data for XYL but that was limited also. We were required to do a TOGA takeoff even at a medium weight in a 319. We were concerned why the takeoff was so limited on a relatively average day with moderate weight and favorable winds. It took several calls to Dispatch to confirm that the numbers were accurate. The Dispatcher was unable to find a reason for the restrictive data. As we found out later with the help of another flight that had departed ZZZ also that morning, there was an obstacle that seemed to be the reason. Although we read the NOTAMs for the field and noted the cranes, etc, construction obstacles for the various runways, what we didn't see was that these obstacles had a significant effect on takeoff data calculations. Normally we understand that when the review is done for takeoff performance evaluations the message is that if engineering has looked at it you are good to operate as normal with the possibility of effects on takeoff data. But this was a rather significant change to the takeoff data. We were concerned that as we were quite limited to which runway we were able to use safely it could become very restrictive if conditions were less favorable. For example, heavier weight, tailwind, hotter temps. Our main concern was that there was no information to pre-plan for this restrictive data. The point of this report is to provide the information from our experience for future flights. It seemed like information from operations would have been appropriate to help us plan for and minimize threats to our takeoff planning. We wanted to encourage a further look at this threat with the intent to warn other crews of the more complicated takeoff restrictions departing ZZZ. Preflight planning had us plan for Runway XX departure. ATIS confirmed that. Computer came back with MTOG of 127.0 max for Runway XX. So we planned for Runway XYL. Also got an error for 151.0 weight on that runway. We finally got a valid takeoff condition doing TOGA takeoff at 148.5. Called Dispatch and they saw the same limits in computer. If the wind was stronger out of the west I [was] sure we would be able to takeoff. Meanwhile we saw 2 A319's from other airlines takeoff Runway XX.
1816084: Descending in to SNA on DSNEE 4 arrival between CARZZ and KADYN somewhere between 13,000-15,000 ft. we had a near miss with a glider. I was flying, never saw it. We got a primary target only, no mode C, 30 seconds or less from when the CA actually saw the glider, he guesses maybe 100 ft. vertically and 500 ft. laterally. The glider was right on the arrival path. It startled him, and even though I never saw it his reaction startled me. Great CRM, professionalism, training for us to get our focus back and not get distracted and become an unstable approach statistic in to the challenging SNA, especially after having hot brakes climbing out of ZZZ1 and having to lower the gear, it felt like a true multiple threat simulator session! Great scenario for an IOE. Operating flight from ZZZ1 to SNA. Cleared to descend via the DSNEE 4 Arrival. Between CARZZ and KADYN Intersections at approximately 13,500 ft., we received a 'Traffic, Traffic' TA with only a primary yellow circle popping up as a target with no altitude or trend information. The TA occurred about 20 seconds prior to us and the target converged. Center called 'traffic at 12 o'clock, altitude and type unknown'. The weather was VFR, but it was hazy. We scanned the immediate area above and below and did not see it.Then I looked to my left and I saw a white colored glider passing less than 500 ft. laterally and within 100 ft. vertically. I did not pick it up until it was at our 8 o'clock position and as we were descending on the arrival. We must have NEARLY HIT HIM! He was heading southeast bound.This occurrence made the hair stand up on my neck and it really shook me up. Just as I reported the near mid-air, ATC gave us a frequency change to Approach. I was so taken-aback by what had just happened, I had to ask Center to repeat the frequency. Just as I was trying to re-establish contact with Approach, I heard Approach calling us on Guard, which I thought was strange as we had only been off of Approach for less than 30 seconds. There seemed to be either a late hand-off from Center and they were looking for us, or they saw the near miss and were trying to call us. I mentioned that we had just missed a glider and we were trying to regain our composure but we had switched over in a fairly timely manner.After a busy, but uneventful approach and landing to 20R at SNA, during the taxi-in to Gate XX, SNA Ground alerted us that Approach was requesting that we call them once we parked.I called and spoke to a Supervisor. His first question was am I going to file a NASA report. I stated that I would. He took my name and number in the event that this occurrence needed further investigation. That glider was sailing on the main ridge-line just prior to entering the area. HE HAD NO MODE C transponder at an altitude that should have required him to have it. The glider was sailing on the direct arrival path of the STAR, and we are lucky that we hadn't arrived at our point of convergence 10 seconds sooner. When I saw him he was about 100 ft. higher than us at 8 o'clock as we were descending.
1816163: The five of us crew members boarded Aircraft X at ZZZ just as soon as the inbound flight fully deplaned. The inbound flight crew left the APU and APU Bleed ON. Upon stepping aboard and entering the Flight Deck (FD), I noticed an odor that wasn't quite normal. As I was setting up, one of the flight attendants (FAs) called me to the back to check on something. She was standing approximately halfway between first class and the emergency exit row, and as I walked towards her the odor became readily noticeable and more intense. I recognized it as an odor I haven't smelt in many years, that of burning oil coming through the APU driven pack. She asked, 'do you smell that?' which confirmed my thought. I said I certainly did and that we were not going to take this aircraft. She said 'it's that old dirty sock smell' referring to a common term used many years ago (6-8?) pertaining to a period when there were many bad and noxious odors on the Airbus 320 fleet. I told her I agreed and explained it was likely APU oil that was getting into the air conditioning system. I took a few steps further aft and noticed the odor intensified the further back I went. I believe she went to the back of the aircraft to tell another FA as I made my way to the FD to turn the APU Bleed OFF. I briefly explained the situation to the FA in the fwd galley, and told her we were not taking this aircraft. After turning the APU Bleed OFF, I called Maintenance and informed them of the situation. I grabbed the AML and my iPad and headed out to the jetway to fill out the forms. All 3 FAs were now in the jetway and my FO (First Officer) was outside doing his walk-around, preflight inspection. I advised the cleaning crew they should also exit the aircraft, though 2 of them remained aboard as they wanted to finish as they were almost done. The odor dissipated within a few minutes of turning the bleed OFF. I then called my Dispatcher and advised her of the situation, explaining the noxious odor we just experienced, and that some of us already had noticeable symptoms. Per the first items of the online Smoke/Odor/Fume Report in [the] checklist, I asked how everyone was feeling. The 3 FAs and myself had throat irritation, a foul taste in our mouths, and varying degrees of a headache. Mine was slight at that time, hardly worth noting as I began filling out the S/O/F form. My FO had been outside, therefore had minimal exposure and no ill affects. The 4 of them then went up to wait in the terminal while I remained in the jetway to fill out the S/O/F form and AML. A few minutes later, an FA came down to inform me that another FA was feeling light headed and nauseous and that they were contacting their Inflight Coordinator to seek medical assistance. A few minutes later, my FO came down to inform me that FA was now looking faint and had vomited. I gave him the number to Med-Air to give to the FAs. After completing the S/O/F report and making an AML entry, I put the AML back in the FD, shutdown the aircraft and left, intending to go with my FO to another gate (D3?) for a replacement aircraft to complete the flight to ZZZ1. As I was walking up the jetway my symptoms intensified, particularly the headache, and upon entering the terminal it was strongly suggested I have my condition assessed. I called the Chief Pilots [office] to confer and advise them of the situation, then I went with the FAs to [the] hospital. The 4 of us each had POC Blood Gas, arterial tests done, and were monitored. We were discharged shortly after midnight. I contacted an FA to see how she and the rest of the FAs were doing. She reported a new symptom of watery eyes, still with sore throat and headache. Another FA still had a dull headache, and the one who vomited was still not feeling well. The first FA contacted me again later in the day for an update stating no change with her, the other one was now down to a dull headache, and the one suffering the worst now reports body aches. My own symptoms have improved but not yet gone away, still with a mild throat irritation, a nasty taste in my mouth, and almost negligible headache. I have been on the A320 fleet for overall XX years and have experienced many of these events, particularly during that long ago time period when there was a rash of these incidents, many before the cause was determined or rectified. I was rather surprised at how quickly and intensely the symptoms came on during this event. This was by far the most intense experience I've had. As mentioned above, I haven't experienced this in many years. It is my understanding that maintenance procedures had been put in place to prevent these from occurring. I recently read a bulletin message regarding recent events occurring and a new operational procedure to remedy the situation. I am curious as to what may have changed to cause the recent events, as it seemed to me this had been under control. If it is a design flaw it must be fixed. If it is a procedural matter, we must figure out what works for the health and safety of our passengers, and particularly the crew who have potential exposure many times per work day.
1816217: Prior to boarding aircraft crew noticed pungent smell of urine. Captain advised report showed this smell was reported two times prior to this flight. Gate Agent and Supervisor noticed smell. We received spray from catering. I sprayed entire cabin. Crew hoped the smell would dissipate. While in flight, smell of urine became suffocating. When landing in ZZZ1 Maintenance came and discovered urine was leaking behind the aft galley causing odor. While inflight, I was nauseous and dizzy. Symptoms continued through the evening. I threw up, and had no appetite. When crew arrived I called OSHA spoke with [name] who advised to call Supervisor and he will call inflight nurse. After speaking with [name] I was given a number to advise the inflight nurse. After speaking with the nurse, I decided to do 'self-care' and continue with planned flight for the remainder of the trip. Upon reporting to Aircraft X in ZZZ, the crew noted a smell of urine in the passenger cabin. I figured the smell would subside once we had some airflow in the cabin as the aircraft had been sitting for a little while. The air onboard was hot and stagnant. I started the APU soon thereafter. In addition we requested some deodorizer to spray in the cabin. I informed the supervisor to hold boarding for a minute while we deodorized. The crew did feel as though the smell subsided enough to board at this point. After departure, it was apparent that the urine odor had returned and was intermittently present during the flight. I'm surprised that I didn't hear any passenger complaints post flight. This issue was documented 2 prior times in the AFML (Airplane Log). The corrective action block on each had stated an inspection was made and found nothing. I initially figured that maybe a pet onboard a previous flight had caused issue and that the smell had resurfaced. Assuming the issue was resolved, we departed. Upon arrival in ZZZ1, I notified Supervisor and Maintenance of the issue along with an entry in the AFML. I did contact the pilot on duty who in turn notified the Manager on Duty that it seemed to be more than just a cabin cleanliness issue and that at more than 1 member of the crew would be unable to continue working on the aircraft until the smell subsided as it made them feel sick. I was told by the Chief Pilot that Maintenance would be finishing up shortly and that I would be using the aircraft on a revenue flight to a maintenance base. A maintenance inspection revealed there was a leak from the lavatory system and that it had been leaking into the insulation in the lower fuselage for some time. At that point I was swapped to another aircraft to use. I do understand some of the challenges in our operation and I made the initial effort to clear up the issue in a timely manner to ensure an on time departure out of ZZZ1. It is frustrating to know that this aircraft was sent back into continued service after numerous complaints, smelling of urine.
1816253: Air Traffic Control requested that Aircraft X fly a heading of 110, and maintain 3,000 ft. until established on the localizer for Runway XXL ILS approach. Once established on the heading of 110, and stabilized, Air Traffic Control advised the crew of opposite direction traffic. Traffic was within 500 ft. of Aircraft X, and when the traffic ascended to less than 400 ft., the Traffic Advisory warning initiated, 'Traffic. Traffic. Climb.' The autopilot was immediately disengaged, and the advisory was followed to climb, then updated to bank left. Final deviation altitude was 3,200 ft. MSL, and was quickly corrected to the assigned 3,000 ft. when traffic was no factor. Air Traffic Control was advised of the deviation. We were on a heading to intercept approach path for Runway XXL into ZZZ. Approach gave us heading 110 degrees to intercept and maintain 3,000 ft. until established on the ILS XXL approach. As we turned to 110 degrees and established Approach also mentioned traffic opposite direction while were looking outside we told Approach LOOKING FOR TRAFFIC. Once we were established on heading received Traffic Advisory warning advise to turn and climb at approximately 400 ft. closing to 200 ft. I disengaged autopilot as I turned and climbed following traffic advisory warning. My First Officer advised ATC about traffic advisory and deviation. We then returned to 3,000 ft. and established on approach.
1816271: I have not been to MIA for many years except for a few times recently and not in the X terminal pocket at all. We were pushed from gate X to spot Y. When the tug turned us loose all I saw was spot Y still ahead of us. Ground control told us to wait for an aircraft to pass, then taxi on taxiway P to [Runway] 8R. I thought it was prudent to continue to spot Y while we wait for the aircraft to pass. On the way to Y I noticed we were encroaching on taxiway P. I stopped to let the other aircraft pass. I did not understand how I could have gotten to close to taxiway P while still short of spot Y. I was using the 10-9 page and did not see an error. Upon further review using 10-9 page I saw there are three taxi lanes that are only depicted on this page. Spot Y lane to the North, spot Z lane to the South and one in the middle that does not lead to either spot. There is a large Y painted on the ground further out that is not depicted on any chart. When the tug turned us loose I believe we were stopped on the middle taxi lane very close to the hold line. The hold line and the close in spot number were not visible from where the tug stopped us. Neither of us saw them. The Y painted further out is the only one visible from my vantage point. If not familiar it is a very confusing situation. Even though I reviewed terminal and taxi charts this still happened. Next time into Miami I will be more aware of ramp layout.[Suggest] depicting the hold line on 10-9 chart and tug driver not stopping aircraft so close to hold line that it cannot be seen in wide body aircraft.
1816282: After FILPS Intersection we were given a heading of 150 and 4,000 feet for radar vectors, visual 27 SWF. We were in the vicinity of Gardiner PJA, just north of SWF, when I spotted the twin engine jump plane at our 11 o'clock high and one mile in a steep descent parallel to our course. A few minutes earlier we did hear jumpers away. ATC tried repeatedly to contact the jump plane when it suddenly dove to the right and rapidly towards us. I banked the plane hard right, 45 degrees, with a descent. We Simultaneously received a RA for the same. We leveled off at 3000 feet and did a visual landing at SWF. the Jump plane probably came within a few hundred yards of us, I could clearly see it up close passing under our belly to the rear. The Jump plane finally answered ATC and sounded a little excited. We briefed the pax after landing, they had no idea of the event as we are a smooth bunch up front. They were appreciative. All is well.ATC vectored us through the Gardiner Jump area which would have been fine if the Jump plane had been more attentive to the radio at the time. Maybe ATC should keep us out of there in the future? I know we'll be more attentive.
1816397: Flying Pilot thought he was cleared for visual approach.ATC then gave us a low altitude warning and instructed us to climb back up to 3,000 feet.During descent the Flying Pilot asked the Monitoring Pilot to ask the ATC Controller how to cancel our IFR flight plan. The Controller then gave the Pilot Monitoring instructions on how to cancel our IFR flight plan. Upon hearing this, the Flying Pilot mistook it for cleared for a visual approach. The altitude alerter was then changed and no communication was exchanged to the other Pilot about the change.We complied with instructions.Suggestions - Verify you heard what you thought you heard. Always keep other Pilot informed of altitude change in altitude alerter if self changed or have the other Pilot change it. During descent, Controller went over canceling procedures. Pilot thought we were cleared for approach. Altitude was changed without confirmation and was told to climb back up. Lesson learned.In approach mode, confusing instructions, did not verify altitude. Lesson learned.
1816581: On final coming into [Runway] XXL I began my touch down and made contact with the runway, a moment after, a gust of cross wind picked the aircraft up forcing me to bear left and causing me to veer off the side of the runway. Throughout, I maintained back pressure and ensured the wings would remain level and once I had the aircraft under control I taxied back to the runway while staying in communication with Tower, ATC gave me a phone number to call when I reached the ramp, they checked to ensure my safety as well as the condition of the aircraft. Once stopped, I did a post flight inspection and determined there was no damage to the aircraft or airport signage. Called the owner of the aircraft and his Mechanic will take a look at it in the morning.
1816594: Flying from ZZZ to SLC IFR, I was given the Cargo 1 Visual approach to Runway 32 (over the top) by SLC Approach 135.5. After my descent from 11,000 ft. to 7,000 ft., while leveling off at AMENR way point, Tower called traffic at my 12 o'clock and 5 miles at 7,000, Aircraft Y. I assume the pilot was doing a VFR transition north over I-15 which runs directly below the approach path. I did not see the aircraft, however, he reported to see Aircraft X. Tower told me to stay on the profile and he would call my base turn for Runway 32. The profile has you level at 7,000 until DUECE way point. In-between AMENR and DUECE I spotted Aircraft Y at my 1 o'clock slightly lower within 400 ft. heading for a collision course. I immediately performed a climbing left hand turn to avoid the traffic, while he did a left turn at the same time. We narrowly missed each other. I called Tower in my turn to advise them of the deviation for traffic. Finished the flight with no other incident.I would advise that VFR transitions north while the Cargo 1 approach is being used stay below 6,500 ft. MSL, or refused entirely.
1816611: On take off, Runway XXR, the aircraft was generating 2,100 RPM, 60 mph, and climbing slow due to the high temp and low Barometric pressure at max gross weight. At crosswind the aircraft accelerated to 65 mph and 2,200 RPM but still climbing slowly. On my turn to downwind, the engine rolled back to partial power approximately 1,400 RPM. I looked to see if the student was pulling power back as I was holding it forward. He was not, and I pitched for best glide and immediately turned for the Runway XXL. Advised ATC and landed on the XXL numbers. As soon as I pulled power to idle on the ground, the engine quit.
1816615: During an initial flight lesson with a student, I was landing on Runway XX with a slight crosswind. Upon touching down, right at the point of adding brake pressure, a gust of wind picked up the left wing. The wind also caused us to drift aggressively to the right of the center line and pointed the nose off of the runway. I felt that I did not have enough energy to go-around, but also felt the aircraft was moving too fast for an aggressive left rudder input. I decided that the best option was to apply maximum braking in hopes of stopping before reaching the runway edge. Unfortunately, I was unable to stop the airplane before it struck a runway edge light and rolled approximately 10 ft. off of the asphalt. The aircraft nor anyone on board received any damages or injuries. Upon reflection of the event, I suspect that my failure to apply full opposite aileron for proper crosswind correction once touched down may have been a leading factor. If I had made that input, the initial uplifting left wing may not have occurred, which would have kept the aircraft pointed in the right direction. I do not regret my judgement in solving the problem after it had occurred. I believe that an attempt to go around would have caused us to strike multiple objects off the side of the runway, and an attempt to steer back towards center line could have causes the aircraft to skid/flip.
1816627: Lost a cylinder coming into ZZZ. Experienced severe engine roughness and a 500 RPM loss with my engine. Notified Tower and requested priority. Landed safely.
1816628: After starting engines on the ramp at TEB, Aircraft X received the following instructions from the combined TEB Tower/Ground control: 'Aircraft X, Runway 24 taxi via Papa, Lima, hold short 19.' Upon receiving this ATC instruction, both crew members briefed the taxi route to include a left turn from the ramp onto Papa, a right turn on Lima, and hold short of the crossing runway. Shortly after turning left from the ramp onto taxiway Papa, Aircraft X received amended instructions from Tower/Ground: 'Aircraft X, cross Runway 19 at Lima.' Shortly afterwards, another aircraft (Aircraft Y) received a clearance to takeoff on Runway 24. Upon reaching the intersection of Papa and Lima taxiways, Aircraft X turned right onto Lima and proceeded to cross the runway. All aircraft lights were illuminated, the Pilot Flying (from the left seat) announced 'clear left;' and the Pilot Not Flying announced 'clear right' after a visual inspection of the runway environment. When Aircraft X was approximately halfway across the runway, a small-to-midsize jet passed low overhead after rotating from its takeoff roll on Runway 24 (the runway Aircraft X still believed, at the time, to be Runway 19). Among the resulting radio chatter, the departing aircraft asked what Aircraft X was doing on the runway, and tower responded 'They were not supposed to be there, sir.' Aircraft X responded with the assertion that we had been cleared to cross. Only after the tower responded did the crew of Aircraft X realize that we had been crossing Runway 24 instead of 19 as assigned. Aircraft X continued clear of Runway 24 and continued taxiing at ATC's instruction. Improper/incorrect taxi briefing between crew members. Both crew members failed to properly identify the branch of taxiway Lima that leads to Runway 19, and instead improperly concluded in the pre-taxi brief to make a right turn, rather than the correct left turn, at the Papa/Lima intersection. In reviewing the event, both crew members concluded that the taxiway diagram used to plan the taxi route had been zoomed in too far to properly identify the entire assigned taxi route. Combined Tower/Ground frequency. After receiving the clearance to cross Runway 19 at Lima, Aircraft X did not hear any corrective instructions or warnings from ATC following the improper right turn at Lima. Additionally, ATC did not specify a left or right turn at the Lima intersection. Acute angle between taxiway Lima and Runway 24 limited visibility of oncoming traffic. After turning right onto Lima, the approach end of Runway 24 was partially obscured by the sharp viewing angle behind the left-seat pilot's left shoulder. Misinterpretation of ATC instruction to 'cross Runway 19 at Lima.' This instruction was received as Aircraft X approached the Papa/Lima intersection, after which both crew members concluded that we had been instructed to turn right onto Lima and cross the runway. Failure to identify runway identification markings. Neither crew member noticed the Runway 24 identification markings while making the right turn onto Lima. After completing the turn onto Lima, all runway identification markings were behind the crew's field of view. During our takeoff roll, (Runway 24) I was the Pilot Monitoring. As we passed approximately 105 kts indicated Pilot Flying stated 'he's not stopping ' l looked up and noticed an aircraft from right to left had entered Runway 24. Without hesitation Pilot Flying rotated the aircraft. Our track took us directly over the other aircraft.
1816636: Prior to entering the traffic pattern at UAO, I could hear over the radio that it would be very busy with all the air traffic and could sense the air traffic controller was not taking his job too serious because he had had a comedic inflection in his voice, which I've never heard any other controller use. I was told to enter left downwind for 'A' taxiway and report when abeam the tower. I entered the left downwind and reported when abeam the tower. Nothing was heard from the controller. After thirty seconds had passed I made another call to the tower and the controller instructed me to pass behind the traffic that was on right base for Runway 35. During the downwind approach I got multiple 'Traffic' advisories. This became a distraction and I reported back that I had the traffic on final in sight because I had been focused on that aircraft. This was not the correct aircraft that I was supposed to pass behind and my transmission was not corrected for by the controller so I turned for left base. As I'm turning I am getting another 'Traffic' annunciation and look out my right door. Down below I see Aircraft Y 500 feet under me. By the time the controller comes up on the radio and questions my intentions it is already too late. Luckily the Cessna saw me and began descending or else we would have been a much closer incident. I maintained my altitude and requested a descending right 360 because I had overshot 'A' taxiway. This in turn caused a fixed wing that was departing to the south from the right downwind to make a left 360 to avoid me. I proceeded down to the taxiway to park on the company ramp. I should have not got so caught up on the aircraft on final that caused me to not read back the proper clearance back to the tower. I was also distracted from the multiple 'Traffic' annunciations while I was trying to locate where these aircraft were in particular. I feel that had the controller also done his part in correcting my incorrect read back that the situation could have easily been avoided.
1816640: We took off from Runway 30R at SJC with TEKY3 Departure, before reaching the SPTNS fix, we were instructed to climb to FL190 without restriction, seconds after the plane gave us a TA of an airplane that was 100ft below, seconds later we had a RA with said traffic performing the evasive maneuver which was to climb, we notified the ATC about the resolution, once clear of conflict we were instructed to resume our climb to FL190.
1816657: Descend via STAR. We didn't know we were in trail and aircraft must have been far enough ahead of us that we didn't see it on TCAS. Encountered wake turbulence. Approx 25 degrees of roll and a 5 degree pitch up. We were at max landing weight, close to Vref speed. I manually flew the aircraft, co-Captain increased power, as requested, and we recovered. Returning to altitude we encountered it again, but not as bad, plus we were faster. We told the controller we were taking a heading. The controller initially balked, then canceled approach clearance and gave us a heading and then vectors to rejoin the approach. The combination of events left us slightly high and slightly fast, but the airport was seen from about 10 miles out. We stabilized and landed normally. After landing I asked the Ground Controller type of aircraft had caused our wake turbulence encounter. '737', without the variant number. I believe it was a 737-700. As big is my aircraft is I didn't think a 737 could cause as much roll and pitch as it did.
1816661: I was flying Aircraft X. I was incoming to SQL from the north for [a] full stop landing, exiting the SFO Bravo, heading south towards the airport. SQL Tower initially asked me to enter a left downwind for Runway 30, keeping 101 freeway to my left, and they would call my left base for Runway 30. A couple of minutes later they asked me to turn left, overfly the runway and enter a right base for Runway 30. I crossed the runway at 1200 feet and began to descend to pattern altitude. SQL Tower told me to follow Aircraft Y that was on an extended right base for 30. As I was searching for Aircraft Y, I began to turn right downwind for 30 right as I noticed Aircraft Z cross in front of me....both of us executing an evasive maneuver. I told Tower that I had a near miss with Aircraft Z....and Tower responded that this aircraft was not on frequency. I was able to land safely. Upon reviewing ADS-B data and ATC recording of the event, it appears that Aircraft Z took off from Runway 30 and was asked to follow Aircraft A, Aircraft A was told to proceed to KNBR [radio station] antenna and then proceed on course, which they did. Aircraft Z however did not follow Aircraft A and turned too early into downwind. The tower also gave Aircraft Z a very early frequency change so they were not on frequency at the time of [the] near miss. It seems to me that the failure of the Tower to verify that Aircraft Z had Aircraft A in sight was a factor in this near miss, as well as the Tower's early frequency change for Aircraft Z.
1816665: On this aircraft, annual inspection is current and the most recent oil change had happened less than 2 flight hours prior, with the mechanic noting that the filter cut check was normal. I had flown the aircraft uneventfully for about 0.9 hours previous to this. Preflight was normal and showed good fuel quantity in all tanks and no evidence of water or sediment in any fuel cell or the main sump. Engine oil was full and run-up checks were normal. I executed a straight-in approach [planning on a touch-and-go]. I conducted my descent check in accordance with the checklist along with a 'GUMPS' check. Final approach and landing were normal. I pushed up power for the 'go' portion and the aircraft initially responded normally. Shortly after takeoff I heard the RPMs drop and felt the airplane experience a partial power loss. I checked mixture, prop, and throttle all in the full forward position (they were) and maintained landing attitude until touchdown. During this time I announced (incorrectly) 'engine failure' on Tower frequency. Once the aircraft was down, the engine was still running and I was able to taxi clear of the runway. At this point, after continued power manipulation the engine stopped. I maintained radio contact with Tower until a tug arrived to taxi the aircraft back to the hangar. I documented throttle/mixture settings, fuel quantity indicators, and checked the sumps. There was no apparent damage to the aircraft or any property, and no injuries.
1816666: Was flying on Los Angeles Special Flight Rules (LASFR) northbound at 4500 [feet] when my ADS-B in system gave me a traffic warning coming from the right side. The traffic was ascending into me on a current collision course. [It] looked like a Cirrus or Bonanza and were much faster than me. I tried to call them on LASFR frequency to no avail. They continued on about a 75-degree angle directly towards my route of flight. The scary part was that they were heading directly towards me but also ascending into me at the same time. They were traveling much faster than me and guessing from their speed and my speed we were on a direct collision course. I was on a special use airway in Bravo airspace and was originally nervous to descend due to possible on-coming traffic from the opposite direction as well as fear of violating Bravo airspace. Since they were ascending from underneath me I had no visual contact with them (I was in a low wing aircraft). My ADS-B system continued to give me hazard and collision warnings. I turned left to avoid them, but they seemed to turn left immediately after I did and now again were on collision course. My ADS-B system warned me that they were now within less than half a mile from me and were at the exact same altitude as me, going much faster. I still could not see them visually so at the last second I cut my power and dove about 400ft and hard left to avoid them. I now immediately saw them visually, pass overhead right above me. Since I had dived a few hundred feet they were a bit higher now and were no factor. The whole experience just overall shook me a bit but I am doing fine now. I believe one of the biggest issues of this possible collision was that nobody was warning them for traffic, as well as them not looking for me. Since I was on an uncontrolled special use frequency and was not on flight following during the Bravo transition (it is not provided there, although I was squawking 1201 which is mandated), nobody was warning me of traffic. Since I was higher than the oncoming aircraft and they were coming from my right side, if it were not for my ADS-B in system, I absolutely would not have been able to see them visually. I believe a human factor involved that did startle me more was that my ADS-B system kept beeping and flashing and trying to warn me which only incited more fear, although this was good at the moment because I took evasive action, it made me feel more startled afterward. If the oncoming plane was on flight following or an IFR flight plan, then they absolutely should have been warned about me, if they were simply flying VFR then they failed to scan for traffic and failed to see me. Overall, the incident was just more startling/scary than anything, I wouldn't usually expect anything like this to happen in such well-controlled airspace, especially since this happened within Bravo airspace (to note, they were not on the special use corridor that I was on, they were departing to the west over the ocean, so they were flying in Bravo airspace on non-special use airspace.) I wanted to just report this to get it off my chest, as well as a few friends of mine recommending I do this.
1816677: During a training flight with a student who was preparing for solo operations, the student made his second approach to the runway in calm conditions. During the flare, the aircraft yawed to the left and he attempted to correct it using right rudder. Shortly thereafter the aircraft touched down, at which time it immediately exited the runway to the right. The aircraft crossed a grassy area, then an adjacent taxiway and another grassy area, before coming to rest. As the Instructor, I had taken control once it began exiting the runway. Once the aircraft had stopped, we exited the grassy area back to the taxiway and held short of the runway. I exited the aircraft and took a visual review of the aircraft for damage. Having seen none I asked the student if he would like to continue and while he said he was shaken, he was OK with continuing. I then took control of the aircraft and proceeded to demonstrate an approach and landing. Upon finishing the lesson and reviewing the aircraft, I noticed a slight nick in the prop. In hindsight, I should have shut the aircraft down and suspended operations immediately, to do a more thorough review of the aircraft as well as allow my student to gather his thoughts and focus.
1816689: I was flying RNAV 24 into LKR with a student. We both each made 2-3 radio calls on CTAF once we were 10 miles out to make sure our locations were clear on approach, and we checked to make sure we were on the correct frequency multiple times. Winds were calm, so we planned to land on runway 24, and suddenly I saw a plane taking off of 6 while we were 3 miles out on the approach. The plane never made any calls, and only slightly broke off to our left on departure. I took controls and broke off the approach to the right some while he was passing by. It seemed he knew where we were, but still decided to take off the opposite runway and squeeze past us.
1816701: While flying out to the practice area outside of the Bravo, I was attempting to maintain an altitude 100 feet below the shelf of the ORD Bravo airspace. There were some up and downdrafts during the first portion of our flight. Based on the altimeter reading in the aircraft I had thought I had caught it in time, but while reviewing radar/ADS-B data on an aviation website, I concluded I did enter the airspace. It was only for a few seconds, but I do take this quite seriously. I believe an additional factor is a lack of flying currency related to the pandemic. In the future, when I feel unstable air, I will select an altitude even lower to provide more of a buffer. Flying with a private pilot to help him get recurrent. Departed ZZZ and climbed to intermediate altitudes to avoid the Bravo airspace. Pilot selected 3,500 [feet] and acknowledged he would stay clear of the Bravo. He leveled at 3,500 [feet] but then caught an updraft and allowed his altitude to surpass the 3,600 foot floor of the ORD Class B momentarily. He called out that he had allowed the aircraft to climb 100 feet high and I immediately commanded a descent back to the selected altitude. No other aircraft were in the vicinity. Lack of currency, having been out of the cockpit for months, turbulent conditions, and the distraction of instruction as we were reviewing G1000 operation led to the momentary altitude excursion.
1816732: Shortly after touchdown on Runway XX the plane began drifting to the left, controllability was deteriorating rapidly. The SIC was attempting to correct the drifting, I (the PIC/PM) stated we're drifting left and applied Full, Authoritative, Firm pressure to the right rudder. The plane began to straighten out and correct right. The left tires were on the edge of the runway next to the grass and water runoff, causing hydroplaning. As the plane decelerated I was able to regain control and corrected back to the center of the runway. The SIC further assisted in maintaining control of the aircraft as we could feel the tires slipping and hydroplaning. With team work and crew coordination, we regained full control of the Aircraft again and we're able to stop and clear the runway onto a taxiway.Contributing factors include, but not limited to: Weather, rain, winds/crosswinds, darkness/night, unfamiliar airport, wet runway, uncontrolled airport, fresh grass clippings and water pooling along edge of runway, long duty day greater than 12 hours, consecutive long duty days, multiple flights in a duty day (4th), human factors, pilot/crew exhaustion, crew dehydration due to extreme heat and humidity throughout the day, high stress loads throughout the day, get there itis, external pressure from passengers, crews desire to succeed and make everyone happy by completing the mission. After touchdown the aircraft began to drift to the left. Control correction was applied as the aircraft was drifting but with very little effect. As we neared the left edge of the runway the Pilot Monitoring (PM) assisted the Pilot Flying (PF) and applied full right rudder. Due to the water collecting on the runway the aircraft did not respond very well to the rudder input until we decelerated. At that point we had drifted slightly off the runway edge onto the grass. With crew coordination we were able to recover the aircraft back to the runway center line. We excited the runway without further incident.Contributing factors:Weather, fatigue, hot temperatures and humidity throughout the day, dehydration, lack of nutrition, end of a long duty day (arrived at ZZZ on hour 13) preceded by multiple long duty days.This event has opened my eyes a little wider to the complexity of risk assessment. In the future more emphasis will be placed on assessing external pressure, fatigue, and physiological needs. Also more assertiveness towards these areas of risk assessment. ADM is a very complex system of checks and balances and awareness to even the slightest deviation can prevent future contributing factors to this and other events. A lot could be benefited from a personal assessment matrix to pair with a flight risk assessment matrix to help with mitigating a go/no go decision.
1816744: Landing at ID24 (short grass runway) to the North which meant there is a large hump in the middle of the runway- about 15 feet high but with a short but smooth run up to it. Asked student if I could do the landing as this was the second time I had landed on a grass strip and the first time on a runway with a pronounced hill in the middle and that hill was only about 700 feet past the threshold- I knew we would be rolling over it. If you rolled over too fast it was possible for the plane to want to become temporarily airborne. There were some very tall trees on final and it was a good idea to touch down as close to the threshold as possible. The idea was to fly a very stabilized approach as low as possible over the trees and then get into the flare just as we were crossing the shore of the lake where the runway began. Set up a long straight-in over Garfield Bay, crossed the shore when I realized I did not recognize the landmarks at the lower altitude we were at, and was already descending to what I thought were the tops of the trees on final. I think we were below the legal altitude limit a few times when considering how far from the airport we were so I climbed a little so as not to bother residents and get a better view. Then my student who knows the area well spotted the landmarks I needed. Set up the steep approach and the rest went better than expected. Contributing factors were [the] challenging approach and landing in the type of plane we were flying had me anxious- would have been really easy in a Aircraft X. More challenging to me than landing at Telluride with a 25 gusting 35 crosswind during light snow (Aircraft Y). I did not pick out my landmarks for the approach with the idea I could not orient so well when down low. Did not do a low approach to check out the runway where I wouldn't be so worried about getting stabilized on the approach early- we just overflew the airport at pattern altitude having taken off from Timber Basin about 40 minutes earlier. Did not just do a left downwind/base/final because I was worried about being super-stabilized for the short/soft field landing. I could have just done a longer downwind and my orientation would have been very good. The high terrain on the left downwind had something to do with my decision. How to avoid [is to] do a better job of picking out landmarks for making an approach plan to challenging airports. Fly the pattern as long as it is safe. At short unprepared strips with tall trees all around it do a low approach and check things out, ensure safety and make a good plan.
1816745: Have been a 107 UAS pilot since 2016 - haven't flown in 3 years. New drone. Recently updated 107 recency, now current. Flying at dusk and tiring of practice getting manipulation skill back, decided to site see thinking I could maintain VLOS (Visual Line of Sight) further with lights.Lost situational awareness - gone further than I realized and unfamiliar with new software program map as I had only flown for getting manipulation skill back (requires tap to open and change to orientation from thumbnail map. Started getting high wind warning. Tried a different direction, and still high wind. Saw a ball field that I thought was close to house on video screen - it was the High School. Fumbled with map enough to get orientation and dropped to 200 feet to avoid high wind at 400 feet (was very little wind at ground level).Personal assessment - I was stupid to push the VLOS via lights. Training said stay closer at night, but range of drone was tempting to see. Secondly, storms coming in later so higher wind at altitude could've likely been seen if I'd looked at the weather. But weather was still and pretty on the ground. I will be back to my smaller world of VLOS without aid of aircraft lights. Truly frustrated with my normally disciplined self.
1816751: Aircraft X departed [Runway] XXL and I requested that they make an early turn to the north so I could depart an IFR small transport behind them. Shortly after clearing the small transport for takeoff, I hear MAYDAY on the frequency, and it was Aircraft X with an engine out. They requested to land Runway XY. I was working the Tower all by myself, so the first thing I did was go and cancel take off clearance for the small transport, and then left them in position on the runway. In order to alleviate frequency congestion, split responsibilities, have oversight, and just have one person on break to keep a minimal rotation during our high traffic volume hours we need the following:opening shift- 2 CPC7am shift- 2 CPC9am shift- 2 CPC1pm shift- 2 CPCclosing shift- 2 CPCThe above plan will allow us to have Local Controls, Ground Control and Controller in Charge all decombined and with someone on break to have a rotation that avoids anyone going over 2 hours. This plan is 10 Certified Controllers each day, and our current MOU (Memorandum of Understanding) is 7 Certified Controllers each day. To cover 10 Certified Controllers per day and to allow for just one or two people to have bid leave each day, we need at least 17 Certified Controllers. Keep in mind if we have 17 Certified Controllers we can still lose them yo transfers so you may consider a larger number than that. So it wouldn't be a surprise if we may even want to regularly decombine clearance delivery eventually.
1816752: Aircraft X went NORDO on the downwind. There was no reason given as to why the aircraft went silent. They entered into a 3,500 foot MVA (Minimum Vectoring Altitude). I tried to reach the aircraft on emergency frequency and back up radios.

1816773: Aircraft X is a MAX 8 aircraft. It was my understanding that I flew it on its first revenue flight on this flight. 1816790: It was a hot day and the Flight Attendants (F/A's) were continually reminding us that the cabin was warm. We were also running about 30mins behind schedule so we felt rushed to make up time, and at the same time, cool the cabin as quickly as possible. Upon receiving our takeoff data at the gate we noticed we were going to have to do a bleeds off takeoff. It's been a while since either of us had done one so we took the time to look in the manual and review the procedure so we would properly execute the procedure. The aircraft was already warm and having MAX's long engine start sequence didn't help. After pushing back, with our departure runway practically right in front of us, being in a hot aircraft and 30 minutes late, we definitely felt the pressure to get things moving. After waving off the crew, our MAX engines finally got started. After the start during the First Officer's (F/O's) flow, he stopped at the air conditioning panel and realized we discussed the procedure for takeoff but not re-configuring after takeoff, nor had we discussed configuration taxiing to the runway. So while we waited for the MAX's engine warmup we discussed reconfiguration after takeoff as well as deciding to keep the air panel configured for takeoff, since it would be a very short taxi. After our discussion the F/O called for taxi. I released the brakes and since [the runway] was so close, I decided to do my pre-take off flow coming out of the ramp. So I chimed the F/A's and did a throttle burst all at once right out of the ramp area. And the mistake was made. We got the Takeoff Configuration Warning and horn. I stopped the aircraft, advised ATC we stopped, set the brakes and we accomplished the QRH items and with a successful throttle burst, did the Before Taxi Checklist and made an info only in the logbook. We then called for taxi and departed for an uneventful flight.Flows need to be accomplished and completed before any briefing discussions or questions take place. We both feel if we had waited to have the discussion after the FULL before taxi flow, we would have caught our mistake. After the Before Push Checklist, Captain stated it would be an Engine Bleeds Off takeoff. (First Officer was in the Yellow.) I replied it has been two years since I preformed this takeoff procedure. To mitigate this risk, I read the Engine Bleed off Takeoff procedure in the MAX AOM [Aircraft Operations Manual] to Captain to be familiarized with the procedure. We pushed back [and] started the engines. During the engine starts, the Captain stated for me to call Ground after a minute and thirty seconds passed, after engine start, because we were so close to the runway. I performed my after engine start flow when I got to the bleeds, I stopped and I asked the Captain how he would like to configure them. Once configured we agreed enough time had passed to call for taxi. As we taxied, the Captain performed the before takeoff flow. We heard the Takeoff Configuration Warning. We stopped the aircraft and performed the proper checklists to reconfigure the aircraft for takeoff. Additive conditions involved in this event: First Officer (F/O) unfamiliar with Engine Bleeds Off takeoff. Very hot cabin. Short taxi to runway. Flight Attendant (F/A) PA about the hot cabin. Once I heard the announcement. I told the Captain I had not made announcement to the passengers about the hot cabin and if he wanted me to keep the right engine bleed on before takeoff as stated in the AOM.On my next Engine Bleed Off takeoff, I will complete my normal flow so the Captain will hear 'Standby Flaps', then go back to re-configuring the bleeds properly. [I will] become more familiar with this procedure prior to my trips in the summer months.
1816819: The chart for the complex special procedure for an engine failure departing [Runway] 8L on the RATPK Departure from LAS airport shows a turn at 12.7 DME LAS to the heading of 050 degrees or continuing on the SID depending on altitude. The turn point seems to be more closely aligned with SCAAR, which is different point on the SID for departing [Runway] 8R. 1816825: Starting with the descent into ZZZZ we were cleared the arrival and a descent to FL190 with thunderstorms and lightning on both sides of the route. Turbulence was light to moderate with intermittent rain and ice pellets. We were instructed that an airplane had gone around on the RNP Runway XX for lack of visibility although we could not get any exact information on what the conditions at the field were. ATIS was not operating for the station and we were relying on Approach Control to pass us that information. METAR through ACARS showed that the conditions at the field were OK with a few low clouds but high ceilings and almost no wind. Further complicating matters was the fact that enroute we received a message from Dispatch that the ILS for Runway XX was unserviceable thus forcing us into the RNP Approach with higher minimums and higher visibility requirements. Shortly after being told by Approach that an aircraft had gone around at ZZZZ we were instructed to hold at ZZZZZ as published at FL190. This hold was in airspace that was mostly clear from severe weather but with thunderstorms mostly to the north and east in close proximity to the hold. At this time we calculated a Bingo fuel to our filed alternate of ZZZZ1 which was 95 miles away. Fuel upon entering the hold was 10,200 and we calculated a BINGO for ZZZZ1 of 8,100 lbs. which would get us from a missed approach to ZZZZ1 with about 6,000 lbs. remaining. Requesting the METAR through ACARS showed the weather at ZZZZ1 was VMC. With little knowledge of the actual field conditions at ZZZZ other than that visibility may have been poor we elected to commence the arrival and attempt the RNP for Runway XX. Approach was still reporting that the conditions on the field were good but that an airplane had gone around about a half hour ago. We were then cleared a descent in the hold and then cleared for the approach. This was only after making many radio calls to ZZZZ Control to determine what their plan was for us. Other than being told to hold they provided no EFC (expect further clearance) time and we were given no options. We informed Approach that if we needed to execute the missed approach we would then need to proceed directly to our filed alternate, ZZZZ1. It was at this time we were informed that this was not possible and that ZZZZ1 was not accepting any more aircraft. I instructed the FO to contact Dispatch for clarification. Dispatch informed us that ZZZZ1 was in fact accepting aircraft but that the nearest alternate beside ZZZZ1 was ZZZZ2, which was over 300 miles away. During the approach ATC told several other aircraft requesting a diversion to ZZZZ1 including 2 other [Company] aircraft and a [Airline] heavy that they were not accepting aircraft. After Approach switched us to ZZZZ Tower they informed us that there was 'no visibility'. They also told us that they 'cannot see the runway from the Tower' but they had the lights full up. We flew the approach to minimums and I did not see the runway and started the published missed approach. The FO said he saw the runway just after we started the missed approach. During the missed approach we once again asked for vectors to ZZZZ1. This was a very high workload environment at night, in the weather with terrain and still burning fuel. Approach told us that ZZZZ1 was not accepting aircraft. He repeatedly told others the same thing. At this time we were looking for further options but in my mind we could not afford to hold and did not have the fuel to go to ZZZZ2. Exacerbating this problem was the fact that my years old iPad, although sufficiently charged was at times very slow to respond to my inputs. Several times I had to look across the flight deck at my FOs iPad to confirm information. After telling Approach that we needed to divert to our filed alternate they would again insist we couldn't go there then started talking to other aircraft. At this time I instructed the PM to tell approach that we were proceeding to ZZZZ1;that we were minimum fuel, and we put that at the top of the LEGS page and began heading that way at 10,000 ft. Approach was still being unhelpful and he was saturated with other aircraft and radio calls. I instructed the PM to remain on ZZZZ Control frequency and selected ZZZZ1 Approach on VHF2. After contacting them and relaying our position and intentions they said they would make room for us and to proceed direct the field. I told them we were still in contact with ZZZZ control and that we would be back with them shortly. Switching my attention back to the flight deck the PM had set up the FMC for ZZZZ1 and I sent the Diversion message to Dispatch and informed the Flight Attendants and passengers that we were proceeding to ZZZZ1. While proceeding direct to ZZZZ1 I used Captains Authority to deviate west and south for more thunderstorms between ZZZZ and ZZZZ1 as ZZZZ still wasn't responding to queries in a timely manner. The PM informed me that he could not get a word in edgewise with ZZZZ Control but they had reluctantly cleared us to ZZZZ1 at 12,000 ft. I instructed him to switch frequencies to ZZZZ1 Approach since we could not get ZZZZ to respond or give much helpful information at all. After the weather deviation ZZZZ1 approach was very helpful and accommodating and cleared us for the VOR DME Runway XX at ZZZZ1. The approach and landing were uneventful. After landing we held on a taxiway for about an hour waiting for a gate. There were at least 4 other diversions there in similar situations. At this time I called Dispatch and told them what had happened and we decided that we would attempt to refuel with a ZZZZ2 alternate and go to ZZZZ. There was no response with ZZZZ1 Operations so coordination was done with Ground and Operations personnel there. They were very helpful. The Flight Attendants also informed us that several passengers were asking if they could disembark at ZZZZ1. After seeing the situation I said that this was not possible.... we didn't even have a gate or jetway driver let alone Customs personnel or ground handlers to retrieve bags. After coordinating the short flight back to ZZZZ we departed and landed relatively uneventfully at ZZZZ a little over 3 hours late. The only issue upon arrival was that although METAR said that conditions at ZZZZ were CAVOK upon switching to Tower we were once again informed that visibility was poor and that they could not see the runway from the Tower. ATIS was still not updated or even operating. We saw the runway at about 800 ft. AFE. There was significant low level fog but the approach was safe and uneventful. Taxi in and shutdown was also uneventful. A few things to note here: The ILS being unserviceable significantly impacted our ability to land in poor visibility. ATIS was not operating and Approach and Tower were passing conflicting, ambiguous field conditions. There was a significant problem in understanding what the conditions on the field actually were as METAR said one thing while Approach said another and then Tower advised there was 'no visibility' with no concrete data on what the visibility really was. The runway has no centerline lights, no distance remaining markers, and no grooves even though it was wet. ZZZZ Control was far less than helpful in all regards. We had to 'push the rope' to get any kind of clearance. They didn't even provide an EFC (Expect Further Clearance) time in the hold. They appeared task saturated which is completely understandable. However, his insistence that nobody could go to our legally filed alternate led to a lot of confusion. Ultimately we had to just be forceful and tell them that's where we were going. They provided us a clearance there but no handoff. We felt like we basically had to affect our own rescue. Flying around in bad weather, at night, in terrain, with a developing fuel situation with little help from ATC was task saturating. The PM (the FO), although with low time and on probation, was excellent and we could not have accomplished the mission without him.

1816941: Last day of 3 day trip. Started both Engines and joined the long line of departures. Had a closeout, completed all the checklists and taxied J, K7 short of Y. We also requested numbers for tailwind takeoff (10 knots). Somewhere in between we received an ACARS that closeout had been deleted. 1816945: FO Flying / AP on in Nav mode. Just as we were making our turn to transition from the arrival to the approach. FO selected APP mode on FCU the LOC & GS captured simultaneously . Initially the GS indicated below us but as soon as the aircraft went to capture mode the GS indication jumped above the 1/2 scale deflection up. The aircraft followed the GS as it moved up to 1/2 scale high until the aircraft pitch was approximately 20 degrees nose up. 1816958: On Date, I was assigned as the Captain of Aircraft X, an Company flight with scheduled service from ZZZ to ZZZ1. The aircraft was Aircraft X. The scheduled departure time for the flight was XA:37 local time and we had all crew members present for an on-time departure. On the day of the flight, I had come on duty as a short call reserve at XA:00 AM local time in ZZZ. The reserve day that I was working had been picked up as an overtime shift due to short staffing in the base. At the time of this flight, I had already flown two previous legs and was fit for duty to conduct the round trip flight to ZZZ1.As I settled into the flight deck to perform my preflight routine, I noted that the left side window of the aircraft was suffering from de-lamination. At the time I estimated that the de-lamination was approximately 4 inches tall and 18 inches wide on the bottom side of the window. After speaking with my First Officer, I consulted the Company standard operating procedure manual for the CRJ 700 aircraft. The SOPM states de-lamination and/or cracking is allowed two inches from the edge of the windshield around the entire periphery with four inches of penetration in the corners. Later on I was able to take pictures of the de-lamination and I used a takeoff and landing data card as a measuring tool and determined the de-lamination was approximately 3.75 Inches tall. The width of the de-lamination was approximately 18 inches but was not measured. I checked the maintenance log for the aircraft and found multiple previous write ups by Captains who had believed that the de-lamination exceeded standards. In each instance I found that Maintenance had signed off the window as being within standards and not a problem. I phoned ZZZ Maintenance Supervisor Name and told him that I would have no choice but to write up the window again. He said that was not a problem and they would come out and sign off on the window. When Maintenance arrived the A&P looked at the window from the jet bridge and began the process of returning the aircraft to service without taking any measurements or further inspecting the damaged area. I was standing in the jet bridge at the time an observed a copy and paste from a previous write up stating that the window was still within limits per CRJ700 CMM 56-11-02. At that time, I was not satisfied with the return to service an asked to see they see CRJ700 CMM 56-11-02. When Maintenance pulled up the section it had a picture that exactly described what is in the standard operating procedure manual for the CRJ 700. It clearly states that the limit on de-lamination is 2 inches from the bottom of the window which we already knew had been exceeded. At that point Maintenance agreed with me that the aircraft could not be returned to service and called his supervisor. Name1 from ZZZ Maintenance came out to the aircraft and showed me in what I was told is the PPG windows manual a section that states the following.'Allowable de-lamination is two inches from the edge of the daylight opening around the entire print and four inches in the corners. Localized areas of de-lamination are allowed to exceed the continuous peripheral limit as long as pilot visibility is not impaired'. Name1 told me that localized is any one side of the window. Believing that localized should be a defined term I asked for any documentation on what exactly localized means in that statement but was unable to get a written answer from any available manual. At that point we reached an impasse where I along with my First Officer was not willing to take the aircraft in an un-airworthy status and outside of the limits of the standard operating procedure for the CRJ 700. Name1 stated that they would find another crew.I contacted my dispatcher for the flight and told him that I would be unable to accept the aircraft as airworthy and would need a replacement aircraft. Around that time Maintenance was communicating with someone in ZZZ2 that the aircraft was airworthywhich further complicated the situation where a flight crew was saying it is not and maintenance is saying that it is airworthy.Approximately 2 hours later with the same aircraft still assigned to the flight I was removed as the Captain due to my refusal to take it and the fact that I was now up against duty limitations. I was replaced by another reserve Captain. At that point I was still sitting next to my First Officer who was not comfortable either taking the aircraft. He called crew support and informed them he could not take the aircraft and was then transferred to the OCC Coordinator. I overheard during the conversation that the coordinator told him that in 25 years with the company she had never had a crew refuse an aircraft due to window de-lamination.Shortly after that a new aircraft was found to complete the flight with the remaining crew members.When I completed my drive home, I looked at the flow board and found that the aircraft had been returned to service and was now completing a flight to ZZZ3 with an entirely different crew.In conclusion despite every attempt at talking with Maintenance and getting a satisfactory resolution or answer on why the aircraft was airworthy my entire crew ended up believing that the aircraft was not airworthy. I also had a major financial incentive to complete the flight as it would have paid 150% had I completed it. Despite the pressure that I received from maintenance and the financial loss from refusing the flight I simply could not determine the airworthiness at that time.Most of the things that we find wrong with an aircraft are either deferrable or are not deferrable. Very few things have ambiguous statements like it's okay if it's localized even though it's outside of the standard operating procedures manual for the CRJ 700.Most of the things that we find wrong with an aircraft are either deferrable or are not deferrable. Very few things have ambiguous statements like it's okay if it's localized even though it's outside of the standard operating procedures manual for the CRJ 700.It goes against the safety culture of this airline to make attempts to bully a flight crew into flying an aircraft that is not airworthy. It is my belief that Maintenance has become accustomed to signing off de-lamination that is outside of standards despite not being able to clearly define what localized means. This is known as the normalization of deviance and has resulted in numerous fatal accidents in aviation.
1816970: On descent into ZZZ, we set up for the visual to XX backed up by the ILS. I was the pilot flying. We were given a runway change from Runway XX to XY. We made the necessary changes and briefed them. The ILS frequency for XX and XY at ZZZ are the same. After we were not receiving a good signal on approach to XY, we asked Approach if they had switched from XX to XY. He responded roger and sent us to Tower. He sounded busy and both the Captain and I agreed that he had not really processed the question.Once with Tower, we asked the same thing and they advised us to let them know if we ever got a good signal while on approach. We didn't have good ILS guidance and the Captain suggested I click off the autopilot and hand-fly it down. I did so and was working to maneuver myself on final. I overshot final while continuing to descend. I was worried that this would trigger a GPWS warning as I could see that I was near high terrain to the south of the field. I adjusted my vertical speed as I corrected toward final, but still got a GPWS warning. I responded to the warning as I continued correcting back to runway centerline.We were immediately out of the GPWS threat and elected to continue the visual approach but we were left high after the response.
