It was here that I should have seen we were not in a good position to continue and should have gone around. As we continued down final, we were at idle thrust and flight spoilers were out as we continued to configure the aircraft. I don't believe that we were fully configured below 1000 ft., which was outside of stabilized approach criteria, and we still had the flight spoilers extended - which, after review, was against company limitation. By 500 ft. we were fully configured but still fast and slightly high. Another opportunity to conduct a go-around. The power remained in idle for almost the entire approach. We landed on Runway XY.Due to poor maneuvering to final while on visual approach, an overshooting final resulted in a terrain warning. Rather than make the decision to terminate the approach there, we continued, which resulted in an unstabilized approach that continued to a landing. [The cause was also] failure to call a go-around when that was the appropriate course of action. When you think you should go around, go around. Don't wait for someone else to call it and don't continue an approach that isn't stable. Follow SOP and your training. GPWS warning followed by an unstable approach into Runway XY in ZZZ. We were descending into ZZZ and were set up for Runway XX. Approach advised that winds had shifted and asked if we would like Runway XY. We accepted and began to set up for XY. When we had the airport in sight, we were cleared for the visual. As we armed the approach for the autopilot, we were told by Approach that the localizer and glideslope may not be working. My First Officer turned off the autopilot and began hand-flying the visual. He became distracted by configuring the airplane and was flying through the localizer when I informed him he needed to start his turn. As he began the turn he started descending, which caused a GPWS warning for a couple seconds due to terrain. We were confident of terrain clearance but leveled off until we were back on the localizer. Once we were on the localizer, we were high. We began our descent and continued configuring. We weren't fully configured until about 800 ft. AGL. We proceeded with the landing without further event.I think fatigue played a factor in our poor decision-making to continue the approach. We had a [before-dawn] wake-up call that morning and this was our 4th leg of the day. We had been dealing with thunderstorms and delays all day long.
1816979: ATC slowed us to 210, 190, then 170 KIAS, and then vectored us at 4,000 feet on a base leg for the visual approach to [Runway] 34L. As we rolled out on our base leg vector heading, a B737 was 3 miles ahead, at our 11 o' clock and about 1,000 feet above. ATC had us follow that traffic, cleared visual approach 34L. In the flight deck, we discussed the options to increase our separation, and reduce wake turbulence, behind the preceding aircraft. We decided to make the turn as square as possible without blowing through the localizer (visual approaches were also being conducted on the parallel Runway 34R), and stay one dot high on the glide path. We made a square turn to intercept the localizer, but the aircraft was still only about three miles ahead. As we began our descent below 4,000 feet, we encountered wake turbulence. Significant control inputs were required to correct for the resulting 'Dutch Roll' motion (wing lateral roll/rocking motion coupled with tail wag directional motion). The turbulence lasted for approximately 15-20 seconds, as we raised our glide path to about one dot above, which allowed us to exit the wake turbulence by about 3,000 feet. We maintained a higher glide path for the rest of the approach, keeping us clear of the turbulence for the rest of the visual approach to landing. Although the aircraft remained under positive control throughout the turbulence encounter, and within stable visual approach parameters for the entire approach, the motion was very uncomfortable and noticeable to everyone on board. Checking with our flight attendants after the event, no one in the cabin was injured, but a lot of passengers were understandably giving the flight attendants weird looks. Both flight attendants had recognized the motion as wake turbulence as it was occurring.A busy airport can present challenges with aircraft separation and wake turbulence avoidance, especially on visual approaches. ATC requested a specific speed for sequencing, presumably to fit us in behind the B737 and in front of other arrivals. Under other circumstances where the preceding aircraft is at the same altitude or lower, three miles of spacing behind a B737 may not have resulted in wake turbulence. It is a larger aircraft but not a heavy. However, in this case, the higher altitude of the preceding aircraft guaranteed that we would start out below its glide path, at least until we could cross its glide path to become established on a higher glide path. Therefore, the spacing really was not adequate for wake turbulence avoidance, since additional time should have been allowed for the vortices to dissipate prior to our crossing of the preceding aircraft's glide path (and those vortices). We suspect ATC was not accounting for the higher altitude of the preceding aircraft when they stacked us in so close behind the preceding aircraft. In the future, we will be more assertive and ask ATC for a lower speed, or for delay vectors, prior to the visual approach, even if that means ATC has to work harder to fit us in somewhere else in the sequence.
1817102: I was instructing. Trainee issued a descend to 040 from 090 to Aircraft X. Aircraft X descended through a 055 and 047 MVA. Trainee anticipated descent rate wouldn't be a factor. I was researching a TEC route for an IFR overflight, and failed to prevent Aircraft X from descending through the MVAs.Do not allow trainees to anticipate descent rates. Issue altitudes that satisfy MVAs.
1817125: Captain and FO (First Officer) experienced multiple additive conditions/factors that led to not completing checklists fully [and] briefing, that led to taxiing without selecting takeoff flaps. For example, use of opposite flow runway for takeoff, bleeds-off takeoff requirement, MEL that appeared to be corrected, ATOG and minimum required fuel to include MAX warm-up requirements, bleeds-off takeoff requirement, possible delay of 45 minutes for Ground to coordinate opposite direction takeoff from taxi call, i.e., fuel concerns, trying to make push time, [and] single-engine taxi necessity. These additive conditions took us out of our normal flow and led to us taxiing without selecting takeoff flaps or running the Before-Taxi Checklist.We captured the error and threat during the Captain's Before-Takeoff Flow, with the Configuration Warning horn. We had not crossed the hold-short line, but the time it took us to run the QRH, correct the aircraft configuration, and then run the Before-Taxi and -Takeoff Checklists, Tower canceled our takeoff clearance, due to opposite direction requirement. We were shortly thereafter cleared for takeoff. We thoroughly debriefed what happened and how it happened, as we are both very experienced operators. Due to multiple distractions and additive factors - opposite direction, full-length takeoff on XXL and coordination involved with fuel issues - an MEL I spent too much time getting an explanation from Maintenance, discussions managing minimum takeoff fuel and ATOG requirement, bleeds-off takeoff discussions, being fairly new to ETOPS and not fully in sync with my ETOPS flow, and allowing myself to get rushed to make push time, took us away from our normal flows and mistakes were made, culminating in a taxi without takeoff flaps set.Our error was captured with the before-takeoff flow throttle burst, as Tower cleared us for takeoff. We got the horn, and that put us in the yellow. We ran the QRH, reset the flaps, and ran the Before-Taxi and Before-Takeoff Checklist to ensure we didn't miss anything, and got back in the green. As we taxied toward the hold-short line, Tower cancelled our takeoff clearance. Tower re-cleared us for takeoff shortly thereafter. The rest of the flight was solidly in the green.
1817128: I was provided with two NOTOC forms late in the boarding process which I reviewed and signed. I kept a copy of each and OPS kept a copy of each. Distracted by a delay in boarding bags, I forgot to verify a NOTOC statement in the remarks section of the Dispatch Release per FOM. The error was realized once airborne when Dispatch contacted us to verify we had the NOTOC. We communicated with Dispatch, amended our release, and asked them to communicate with ZZZ Operations to add the pen and ink change to the release as well.
1817205: Takeoff was normal until rotation. Rotated at 75 knots, but didn't lift off until 100 knots. Verified flaps were at takeoff. Climb-out was at 100 knots. At around 400 feet AGL, started a turn and was scanning the instruments when the stall warning went off. The airspeed had dropped to 77 knots. almost instantly. I performed a stall recovery and proceeded to climb to 3,000 feet MSL. At cruise, I noticed all 3 airspeed indicators were showing different airspeeds and the altimeters were different as well. The true airspeed and ground speed were displaying higher than indicated. I pulled the ALT static air and pilot airspeed dropped about 15 knots, but I could not tell which reading was correct. I informed ZZZ Departure and returned for a visual landing. I verified my altitude with ATC and the pilot altitude was correct but the PFD2 was showing about 200 feet lower. On approach airspeed was showing 120 - 130 knots, but the pitch attitude was too high and the controls were mushy. Post-flight walkaround found pitot and static openings OK, but the static system drain lock open.
1817208: Talking off out of ZZZZ on Runway XXL. On the takeoff roll we got a NAI over-temp on engine #2. No master warning. We continued the takeoff and after rotation we got engine fire #2. We let it produce thrust due to a high climb gradient. We ran the Quick Action items followed by the engine fire #2 checklist. After doing so, the fire indication went away. The aircraft was above max landing weight so we decided to tell ATC that we needed to return. We proceeded to run the jettison checklist and climbed to 6,000 feet. We got vectored around the missed approach area of Runway XXL. We talked to the company and Maintenance and advised them of the situation. We got time and initials for a re-dispatch back to departure airport. We requested priority handling to return for landing. After landing and clearing the runway, [it was determined it was safe to taxi] to our gate. After we got to the gate, Maintenance opened the cowlings and determined there were a lot of melted wires.
1817229: We were flying ZZZ1 to ZZZ, a XA00 report in ZZZ1. It was the First Officer's (FO) initial trip back from a 10-month furlough. We were on the ZZZZZ RNAV arrival from the northeast. I was the PF. ZZZ was landing north. ZZZ airport had an overcast layer obscuring the airport. At the appropriate time, I briefed the ILS XXR approach. We set up the FMS and tuned/identified the NAV radios for XXR, the normal approach for this arrival. When we checked in with ZZZ Approach, we were advised to expect the ILS XXL. I briefed the approach and we tuned/identified the NAV radios. We were being vectored to intercept the localizer. It looked like we overshot the localizer on the NAV display, so I turned to intercept. ATC advised us, 'It looks like you are lining up for the wrong runway;' and turned us off of the approach. There were no conflicts with any other aircraft. They then told us to expect the ILS XXR. We flew that approach successfully to a landing. While we were setting up for the XXR approach, we discovered we never set up the FMS for the ILS to XXL. [I believe the cause was] early sign-in. Overcast skies obscuring airport. [It was also the] FO's first trip after furlough. [I suggest] verification that both the NAV radios are tuned and identified and the FMS is set for the proper runway/approach. Planned and briefed approach for ILS Runway XXR and was given ILS Runway XXL. The CA (Captain) set up and briefed new approach. I verified the frequencies and inbound course but neither of us set the new approach into the FMS. Was getting vectors to the ILS XXL [and] we had the correct ID for the ILS. When the CA looked at the ND and saw himself flying through the course for what was ILS XXR, the wrong approach, he corrected the heading to go back to intercept the course on the ND. The Controller said you are turning to line up for wrong approach and told us to go around.I have not flown since [last year]. I also do not have much experience in the aircraft. Was first flight since furlough. [I plan on] getting more flying in and becoming more comfortable in the aircraft, getting back into the rhythm of the flights.
1817230: On approach on the ILS for 18R at 1,500 feet we passed a drone hovering about 50-100 feet off the left side of the aircraft. We did not have to deviate to avoid it, but it was close by. It was black and white with four propellers. It did not move over as we went by. It just hovered in the same spot. We notified ATC tower controller. Upon landing the controller asked us more in depth questions about the drone. Being on localizer and glide slope was key here because a deviation to the left may have hit the drone. Suggestions: Not sure what to do to stop this action, except for strict enforcement of the law when these operators are caught. Had I been left of course a bit a half dot, this could have been worse.
1817242: On approach into [Runway] [27C] in Chicago it was by all accounts a normal day. A storm had passed about 2 hours prior giving way to the benign conditions usually experienced after the passing of a storm. The wind was hardly noticeable I had nearly no crosswind correction in on the approach. As we approached the final approach fix Tower cleared a 777 to cross our landing runway. We continued, the aircraft was fully across the runway by the time we reached 1,000 feet AGL and parked on Taxiway TT. I assume he was waiting for a clearance from Ground to continue further. We continued on the approach and right as I was bringing the thrust levers back to idle a sudden jolt of firm left aileron and right rudder were needed to continue a safe ground track and land the aircraft. I am not sure exactly what bank angle was achieved but the proximity to the ground made it seem like quite a lot. My guess is around 10-12 degrees of bank at 10 feet off the ground. Some comments from passengers sounding the alarm that things where not correct when they got off the airplane make me think things where perhaps worse than I know due to the speed at which this all happened. The incident all happened approximately 10 ft AGL. Due to the suddenness and nature of the incident the best course of action was to land the aircraft. I had plenty of runway available to safely execute a full stop landing. Had the event happened at say 50 or 100 feet, a go-around would have certainly been necessary. The landing overall was completed without further incident. We taxied to gate, deplaned. And other than a few comments from Flight Attendants and passengers it was a normal operation. The cause of this sudden change and necessity for rudder and aileron was due to the 777 parked on Taxiway TT attempting to taxi right as I was landing. He was headed out for takeoff so I assume he was all loaded up and needed a lot of thrust to get moving. This is what caused such a dramatic necessity for correction very close to the ground. I hope out of this pilots and Controllers are made aware of the possibility of incidents like this in the future if we're not operationally prepared in some way. The cause of the event was the new taxi procedures and runway configuration due to the addition of 27C in Chicago. When cargo carriers taxi on TT they're putting anyone landing at risk of jet blast. At least a note could be added to our company pages alerting pilots about the possibility of this happening. But maybe even a change in how Chicago does taxi operations. There is a significant safety threat to aircraft landing on Runway 27C in ORD, due to jet blast from aircraft crossing 27C on taxiway TT. This taxiway is approximately 1,100 - 1,200 feet from the departure end, so it is perfectly situated to impact aircraft in the landing flare. To make matters worse, aircraft that cross 27C are instructed to contact Ground on TT and are therefore not on frequency when given an instruction to continue their taxi. In this particular case, a 777 had crossed 27C, then stopped on TT, presumably awaiting further taxi instructions from Ground. They were not on our frequency. At under 10 feet we were hit with a really bad amount of jet blast from the 777. The First Officer did a fantastic job of getting the roll event back under control for a safe touchdown. We advised Tower of the event. Something with regard to the above needs to change. Either, aircraft should cross somewhere else, Controllers should advise aircraft crossing 27C at TT to use minimal power when resuming taxi, Controllers advise pilots of the jet blast potential, or at the very least, there should be a note on a chart.
1817247: Wing Fuel Imbalance exceeded limits. Advised ATC, landed in ZZZ, overweight landing.Cause - Bad fuel transfer pumps/valves. Fix the old airplanes.
1817312: I was seated at XX on approach to EWR. We were going in and out of large clouds. I saw what at first appeared to be a balloon just to the left, under wing level. I watched as it climbed. I could see that it was not a balloon, but a large drone. We were under 10,000 feet, as the captain had signaled such. The drone was yellow and black, black rotors. I estimate that it was 50-75 yards away. I took a time stamp on my phone about 10 seconds later. It was XX37Hrs Eastern Time. The pilots had left the aircraft before I could make my way to the front of the plane.
1817315: The crew waited on the jet-bridge during the plane cleaning and electrostatic spraying process. The crews aren't being allowed even 30 seconds after spraying completion to wait boarding the airplane. As we board the plane there is still the overwhelming smell of chemicals in the cabin. It would be helpful if policies were put into place that allows time for the smell of the chemical to dissipate before we have to board the plane.
1817353: I was instructing a Student Pilot on traffic patterns and full stop taxi back landings this morning at IYS off of Runway 04. We had been working in the pattern for over 30 minutes, making all radio calls: 'upwind, crosswind, downwind, base, and final'. For over 30 minutes we were the only ones in the traffic pattern and landing at the airport. We made frequent position radio calls the entire time we were there. We were on our 4th landing, on the final leg for Runway 04, when a multi engine aircraft overtook us from behind and underneath. Not only had we made a 'turning final' call but I also personally made a 'short final' call. We were already established on a stable approach and on glide slope. We had not heard any radio calls at all from any other aircraft for PAWS or the surrounding area while on that lap in the pattern. We believed we were the only ones in the traffic pattern or attempting to land at the airport.After I made my short final call, I saw them at my 2 o'clock position underneath us. They heard my call and finally made a radio call with their position, and made a hard right 360 to avoid traffic. We started a shallow climb on our present heading, responded over the radio and informed them we would continue our final heading to also avoid conflict. We came to a full stable stop on Runway 04 and taxied to the parking area where I shut down the plane and had my student and myself take a break. The other aircraft continued to fly multiple approaches, only ever making a call when on their own short final. We waited for them to leave the area before starting the plane up again, taking off, and leaving that airport.
1817354: During cruise flight at 3,500 feet and 106 knots ground speed. Aircraft was in straight and level flight. I noticed a 3% torque spilt between the #1 and #2 engine, with the number 2 beginning to slowly decrease in torque. N1 remained steady at 93% which is normal reading with both engines at 80% torque. The number 2 motor rapidly declined in torque causing a larger torque split to occur. Once the torque split became 15% difference, the N1 on the number 2 engine began to decrease. It went from 93% down to 73% causing an even larger torque spilt by 60%. At that time I decided to transition to single engine flight (OEI) and make a mayday call requesting vectors to the nearest airfield. Approach vectored me to ZZZ. I kept the engine at idle, since it was still producing minimal power. I figured some power is better than no power. So I used what power the number 2 engine had coupled with my good number 1 engine. Preformed a low power roll on landing into ZZZ and taxied onto the ramp. Upon visual inspection of the engine and discussion with the director of maintenance it was decided that an attempt to start the #2 in manual fuel control mode was the next course of action. Thinking that the fuel control was the culprit. The engine was started and sustained power along with the number 1 engine. The flight was then resumed in manual mode to our hangar in ZZZ1 where maintenance was performed. After inspection of the engine a borescope revealed that the #2 had suffered a near catastrophic failure. With multiple hot section blades missing, broken off, cracked, and folded over. Along with significant sized holes in the combustion cans.
1817361: My student was on his solo cross country flight from ZZZ, ZZZ1, ZZZ. Upon returning to ZZZ, student experienced a gust on crosswind after touchdown, his wing lifted and airplane ran off the runway into the grass. ZZZ ATC checked in with my student and asked if he was OK or any damage. Student reported OK and no known damage. Received instructions to taxi back to FBO and was able to do so under own power. I called the airport Tower to check in after (as I was on another flight in the general area) and also debriefed and filed report with student. Student was understandably a little shaken up, but is OK.
1817367: This was a practice approach to ZZZ RNAV XX. I was the Instructor in the right seat. We had requested the practice approach from ZZZ Departure and was cleared for the approach and had changed to the ZZZ CTAF frequency. We had made several radio calls of our location. Our airplane has a Garmin 530W with ADSB and Traffic. Also onboard was an iPad with Foreflight and a Status 3. At no time did we get any traffic warning or observe Aircraft Y in the pattern at ZZZ. We were on short final at about 1/2 SM and 500 MSL. When my Pilot (Student) spoke out of the near aircraft, as I looked out the right window I observed Aircraft Y within 100 feet. I immediately took the flight controls and made a descending right turn towards the south away from the aircraft. I then transmitted that we were turning to avoid the aircraft that had just flown over us. There was a long pause when a female voice transmitted that they didn't see us. We circled around and re-entered the pattern to land. The other aircraft had continued their approach and landed. After we landed and taxied around for another takeoff, I observed the plane parked at the fuel with two individuals standing near the aircraft doors. When the aircraft departed, our equipment showed the aircraft but no display of a tail number. Prior to this incident, our equipment had been reporting other traffic.
1817379: Weather was very good, a few scattered clouds at 6,000 feet with no real ceiling, visibility was over 6 miles. I was north of the field and called my position at 10 miles. I heard some aircraft that were landing and taking off and was looking for them. About 2 miles north I think I recall one of the aircraft declaring crosswind for [Runway] XX and was still looking for him. I got a little distracted with setting up for the downwind and my visual search was a little interrupted. I still could not make visual contact and thought maybe the other aircraft was close to base or had left the pattern. I called entering downwind [Runway] XX and the other aircraft responded that they were on downwind as well. At that point I responded that I would leave the pattern and circle and re-enter. It turns out the other aircraft was just below me and I couldn't see them. A later conversation with the pilot after we landed was that he saw me just above him probably less than 100 feet and pitched his plane down just as I turned out. I normally won't enter the pattern or will leave the pattern if I don't have visual contact with other known aircraft, but maybe cause of other distraction I did not this time.
1817391: Student went on first solo cross country to ZZZ. After touchdown, student lost pedal control and veered to the right into the grass. He proceeded to shut the aircraft down, inspect for damage, and call his instructor. He was able to push the airplane out of the grass and fly it back to the base
1817442: A little over two hours into the flight, I was informed via ACARS by our Dispatcher that five pounds of Class 7 Radio Pharma HAZMAT was loaded onboard the aircraft in Bin A. The Dispatcher had just been informed by ZZZ Ops. This was news to me as I never received a NOTOC or saw any notes about hazmat on the Release. I acknowledged the discrepancy from Dispatch. Flight continued uneventfully to ZZZ1.
1817538: This was a FFOD flight. While completing the hydraulic test, Hydraulic Pump 3B would not work. While writing this up, cabin boarding commenced. The associated circuit breaker 1A2 remained set in. Because of this problem, along with the emergency lights not working, and in consultation with Maintenance Control, it was determined that the airplane would be deplaned because it was unknown how long the flight would be delayed in getting maintenance personnel to the airplane to resolve the maintenance issues with the aircraft. I left the aircraft, still prior to the original departure time, and notified the ramp agents and gate agents. The passenger gate checked bags were brought back on the cart to the front of the plane so passengers would be able to have their things in the terminal. I made the announcement to the passengers face-to-face via the Flight Attendant's (FA) inter-phone explaining that we would be deplaning due to the aircraft needing maintenance and the time required for them to complete their job to ensure the airplane was safe for flight. It was also due to the hot temperatures making it uncomfortable in the cabin of the aircraft.As the passengers deplaned, there were a number of passengers saying that they would rather be late, but fly in a safe airplane. I kept assuring them their safety is our top priority. A couple expressed discontentment due to the strain placed on their travel plans and possibility missing their connections. I told them I that I apologized for the inconvenience, but that I needed to make sure they were completely safe on our flight and directed them to the gate agent to see what could be done to help them. I did not see anyone making a video or taking pictures with their phone. There were a couple of people talking on the phone.While I was greeting the passengers as they deplaned, the first officer notified me that the R PACK HI TEMP caution message came on and shut the PACK down by itself. This was then written up in the ELB.During the approximately 1 hour and 55 minutes delay, I made several trips into the terminal (about every 15-20 minutes) to make announcements to the passengers providing up-to-date information regarding the time frame of the delay, the status of the maintenance process, and to express sympathy for the inconvenience and disruption to their travel, but that their safety is our first priority.Maintenance came out to the airplane and resolved the hydraulic pump issue and verified the emergency lights had been charged long enough by the APU and the R PACK was deferred.By the time Maintenance had completed their items, several passengers had rebooked to a flight leaving for ZZZ just an hour or two later. Some that were just flying to ZZZ opted to drive instead saying the trip would be quicker. Again, I did not see anyone appearing to be making a scene or social media post, video, or taking photos. There was one man who expressed his displeasure at not making his connection in ZZZ. I expressed my apologies for his inconvenience, but told him that his safety was our top priority.As Maintenance had returned the airplane to service on their part, we elected to board the airplane while waiting for Dispatch to return the airplane to service. I made the announcement in the terminal that the maintenance issues had been resolved, again expressing apologies for the inconvenience, but telling them that their safety is our top priority. At that point, boarding commenced. I called Dispatch and verified that I had the the amended release, with its associated limitations on the cruise altitude. They then returned the airplane to service, which we saw verified in the ELB.After boarding, the flight deck crew and cabin crew complied with all procedures and we pushed out of the gate for taxi. After contacting ATC, we had a 5 minute wait for our flow time at the end of the runway. After waiting, we departed climbing on departure, with me acting as Pilot Flying (PF).As we climbed throughabout 7,000 feet, the L PACK HI TEMP caution message illuminated. A couple seconds later, the PACK fault light illuminated and the cabin depressurized slowly. I told my First Officer that we were going to level off at 9,000 feet, which we did.I verbalized that this was an unanticipated threat and that I was flying the airplane. I stated that there were no QRC procedures or memory items. I then told him that I was going to have him fly the airplane, holding a general orbit over the airport within the confines of the airport. I made the radio call at that point to ATC that we were leveling off at 9,000 feet and would be making turns over the top of the ZZZ1 airport for what I approximated to be about 15 minutes. ATC asked if we were declaring an emergency. I declined declaring an emergency and told him that when I got back with Center, that I would want vectors back for the approach. Center responded with 'roger.'I then proceeded with the QRH abnormal L PACK HI TEMP (Bleed source is engine) procedure. The procedure did not resolve the problem and the caution message remained illuminated. Because I did not have any operative PACKS that negated the ability to transfer the bleeds from the engines to the APU.I contacted Ops on COM 2 and notified them of the problem and that we would be coming back to the airport. They responded and understood. I called the Flight Attendant and notified her of the problem, but that this was not an emergency, just to clean up the cabin and configure for landing. I told her that she had 10 minutes.I then made a PA announcement that we had lost pressure in the cabin and that we would be returning to ZZZ1 after I had completed a couple of procedures. I expressed my apologies of the continued problems and the inconvenience to them.Because of the slow depressurization of the aircraft, the CABIN ALT caution message came on while I was running the L PACK HI TEMP QRH procedure. This was expected and I ran the abnormal QRH procedure for CABIN ALT after finishing the procedure for the L PACK HI TEMP. The CABIN ALT caution message persisted, as expected. My next procedure to run was the abnormal QRH for Unpressurized Flight Procedure (PACKs off). I completed this procedure, confirming the guarded switches with my First Officer. During this entire time, my First Officer had been making CTAF radio position calls. Another airplane had flown up underneath us and was staying 1,000 feet below us. Because of this, the other airplane would get within 800-900 feet below us and kept tripping TCAS traffic alerts. My previous instructions to my First Officer were to orbit the airport, which he was doing. I had to stop the QRH procedures and redirect where to put the airplane to avoid the continued TAs. I changed my instructions to him that he could outline the geographic exterior of the valley to avoid the other airplane. We never heard any radio calls on CTAF from the other airplane of what they were doing or any intentions. These radio calls are not required in the ZZZ1 area.I finished the QRH procedures.I called the passengers again and attempted to assure them that, although we had lost pressure, the airplane was still flying fine and the flight crew was working to get the airplane on the ground safely and we should be on the ground within 10 minutes.I contacted ATC and they told me that unless I could climb higher than 10,000 feet, I would not be able to get vectors. Because the weather visibility was virtually unlimited and there were no clouds, I called the airport insight and cancelled IFR. In hindsight, I should not have canceled IFR, but I was still given traffic advisories from Center until we were clear of the conflicting targets.I directed the FO to fly east over the desert area that had lower terrain obstacles that would allow us to descend to land on Runway XX.I explained to my First Officer that we didn't have cabin pressure and that we would need to plan a slow descent rate.I heard the FA's jumpseat click and I called her to verify that she had been able to complete her duties, which she affirmed. I then made a PA announcement attempting to assure the passengers that the procedures were complete and we would be landing in about 5 or so minutes. I went on to explain that because the airplane was not compensating for the lack of pressure that they would feel the pressure change in their ears.Inside the airplane, it did get very hot. Even with the RAM AIR open, we were not able to cool it off. I did have concern about some of the elderly passengers we had onboard. The ECS page said the cabin temperature was 34 degrees C, but it felt hotter. The QRH procedure talks about keeping the speed up to 250 knots for cabin cooling, but that was not possible due to landing and having to keep the airplane confined in the valley and maneuvering for landing.We landed normally, besides the pressure, and taxied into parking at the terminal. We opened the door, which immediately allowed cooler air into the cabin, and I made another passenger announcement, again expressing apologies for the problems and that they could talk to the gate agent to make further arrangements.I wrote up the L PACK HI TEMP caution message in the ELB, called maintenance control and finished up with them. Operations then wanted to move the airplane to an adjacent FBO to open up gate space for flights expected later. Maintenance Control made a note in their record of the location of the airplane being moved to the FBO and stated that they were fine with the airplane being relocated.As passengers deplaned, they were frustrated with the return of the flight.After everyone was deplaned and safe in the terminal, the plane was pushed back and we repositioned it to the FBO. I called Dispatch and had them close out the ELB, as the program had locked me out from being able to close out myself. Old equipment on a hot day.I cannot entirely control the effectiveness or reliability of an airplane or its systems. The Captain was flying out of ZZZ1 on the ZZZZZ departure, Runway XX. With the right pack deferred already, we received a left pack hi temp on the right, climbing turn. Upon receiving the caution message, we established a benign flight regime at 200kts, 9,000 feet in a right-hand orbit atop ZZZ1. The Captain then assigned duties amongst the crew per [company guidelines], specifically I flew the aircraft and the captain ran the appropriate checklists and assumed pilot monitoring duties. Concurrently, we notified ZZZ Center, ZZZ1 OPS and Dispatch of our situation and intentions. While completing checklists we received a traffic advisory from ZZZ Center and TCAS advisory. We were able to visually acquire the other aircraft quickly and adjust our flight path to continue our response to the situation. After completing all required checklists, we notified the FA and passengers about the situation and reengaged with ZZZ Center about our intentions to return into ZZZ1. We conducted a standard descent/approach briefing, set up a left-hand intercept onto the final approach course and established a slow, deliberate descent profile on the approach [Runway] XX into ZZZ1 and landed/taxied to the terminal without incident. The left pack hi temp caution message caused the crew to conduct the actions as described in the narrative.Issues with aircraft cannot be completely avoided, the crew acted and responded to the situation in compliance with our directives and in a safe manner.
1817660: I took off Runway XX at ZZZ in a Cessna 172S NAVIII GFC700 airplane and veered off to the left of the runway onto the grassy non-movement area due to a loss of rudder control during the initial acceleration portion of the takeoff. The loss of rudder control was pilot error. The airplane parking brakes were left on. When I realized the loss of rudder authority, the throttle control was brought to idle, and the airplane was subsequently shutdown. Shortly afterwards, ZZZ Tower Control arranged Airport 1 (ARFF) to tow the airplane to maintenance hangar. Maintenance personnel inspected the airplane and did not identify any damages to the airframe or propeller. There were also no damages on the runway or the non-movement area.
1817672: I was on a midfield downwind left for Runway XX when the Tower called out traffic for me to follow as a Jetprop on a 3 mile final and asked me to report when the traffic was in sight.I could see the traffic on ADS-B, but did not acquire visually until I was just past a point parallel with the end of the runway. I called traffic in sight and the tower replied with '#2, cleared to land Runway XX'. I waited a few moments until the Jetprop was off my left wing, then commenced my base turn.I was aware of two other aircraft in the pattern, both military trainers (later determined to be T6 Texan II's). I was also aware that at least one of the aircraft was on a right downwind for Runway XX.Shortly after we were cleared to land, the tower called to one of the Texans that his traffic to follow was an experimental aircraft and asked him to report traffic in sight. The Texan replied that he had the Experimental in sight and the tower instructed the Texan as #3 to follow the Experimental.On final, at approximately 350 feet AGL and 80 knots airspeed, I was concentrating on the Jetprop in front, as I was following somewhat closely and wanted to ensure my touchdown point was beyond his (for wake turbulence avoidance). At about this point, my passenger said 'Airplane, Airplane!' I looked right and saw the Texan at my 5:00 position, approximately 10 feet higher and approximately 150 feet lateral distance, on a collision course and overtaking us. At the same moment, the Texan pulled up and turned left, as I pushed the stick forward and dove down. The tower then transmitted: '[Texan], I believe you were looking at the wrong traffic. Traffic to follow is an experimental on final'. The Texan replied that they agreed with the Tower.In retrospect, I should have made an attempt to visually acquire the Texan while he was on the downwind right. However, in my defense, I was concentrating on landing and separation from the Jetprop I was following and did not have much time or feel it was a high priority to be acquiring traffic which had declared me to be in sight and which the tower was monitoring. I did not make allowance for the potential that the Texan in fact did not have me in sight or that the Tower may not have visually confirmed that the Texan was following the correct traffic.In my opinion, this was an oversight between the three of us (myself, Tower and Texan) that had a happy ending, but which could have been a much different outcome if our evasive actions had been delayed by just a couple of seconds.
1817674: Landed Runway XX at ZZZ and taxied on H. Was cleared to cross [Runway] XY with no delay. After entering the runway I noticed a Cessna on the taxiway on the other side in the middle. I pulled to the left side and to clear the runway. While pulling by my wingtip may have gone under his wing tip.
1817701: On roll out after landing I hit the brakes and the aircraft tipped over on its nose and came to rest upside down. Wind was calm and no contributing factors other than human error in judging the speed of the aircraft. I was only going 5 MPH and thought I could hit the brakes without incident. I am assessing the damage to the aircraft at this time. I was by myself at the time of the incident.
1817720: Over two hours on position. Total of 25 'over two' this evening. I was [named position] CIC. 3 different times was I pressured to close a sector on my line for staffing. All three times I explained why I felt we needed to keep Sector X and Sector A split. Sector A Controller was fairly busy working ZZZ1 arrivals, with added complexity of the weather, there was a wind change associated with the weather in the area and the final was compressing more than what it was when the Sector A Controller sat down. In turn, he ended up having some go arounds just before I sat down on position. During the time where I was questioned about keeping Sectors X & A de-combined, Sector A had a VFR aircraft that found themselves in clouds and needed assistance getting down. This all caused 3 destination changes, '7'(as the pilot said) frequency changes and ultimately a local IFR pick up and approach to ZZZ2, after they first tried to get in with ZZZ1 and ZZZ. This caused the workload and frankly (visually) the stress level of the sector to increase significantly. He had no business taking on more airspace and aircraft during this time. The supervisor who was pressuring me to close it, told me he wouldn't normally ask but the OM was forcing him to try to get Sector A closed down. Closing the position would've caused an unsafe situation.At the end of the day its very clear the management team (top to bottom) at ZZZ do not care about the overall safety of the operation. This is going to be the summer from hell and I pray no one dies due to controller fatigue combined with a sector that should've been split but not having the bodies to truly run a safe and efficient operation.Accountability for ZZZ Management.We need 40 more controllers.
1817740: Pushing off gate/listening to Ground. There was a lot going on with weather approaching the field, certain departure gates shut off and others open. Push crew cleared off/weren't using headsets due to [weather hazards]. We were clearly distracted with what was going on with Ground as it was a question of starting one or both engines and whether we were delayed or departing immediately. We thought we were ready for taxi and with the frequency very busy, I called when there was a break. As the Captain powered up #2, it became immediately apparent that there was no nose wheel steering. Captain stopped the aircraft immediately and set parking brake. We were both at a loss that we had skipped the whole Before Taxi Flow/Checklist. We took a minute to discuss how we got there and knowing we had been distracted, 'reset' ourselves and continued with the Before Taxi Flow and Checklist.[Suggest] Self awareness during high workload that things can unknowingly be skipped. Pushed back and disconnected from tug. Only started one engine for departure delays due to weather at the field. As I cleared off the tug, we heard over the Ground frequency that all departure gates were closed for weather. The FO (First Officer) and I discussed our plan to taxi off ramp and wait for weather to pass. After that, I must have believed that he did the after-start flow and we did the Before Taxi Checklist. However, I was wrong. We cleared left and right and I started to move the aircraft, but immediately I knew the aircraft was not configured properly for taxi. I stopped the aircraft and started the after-push procedures again. The distraction of the weather delays got me out of my normal routine, as well as the FO's. Neither one of us trapped the errors until too late. We ended up with a return-to-gate event.While we start engines routinely and do Before Taxi Checklists several times a day, we can get distracted by outside factors. I should have delayed the discussion about weather or anything else until after the start flow and Before Taxi Checklist was complete.
1817741: We were making a visual approach to Runway XXR in ZZZ. The airport was is sight, while the downwind leg and convective activity was present south and west of the airport. After receiving landing clearance from Tower, a wind check was issued and landing speeds adjusted accordingly. The First Officer (FO) was flying and called for landing Flaps 30. The Before Landing Checklist was accomplished and I did a second wind check. We discussed the new speeds and continued the approach. Shortly thereafter, we received a Too Low Flaps Warning. Upon inspection I discovered that the flaps were in the 25 detention. The flaps were moved to position 30. I considered a go-around, but elected to continue the approach as we were on speed and path and a go-around would have been into the convective activity.Obviously, this was a failure to read and verify the checklist items. While debriefing the event with the FO, we both agreed that the monitoring of the wind/ weather was a factor as we considered our performance on final. Also being in a MAX 8 was a factor as the location of the flap gauge is different than the NG, possibly affecting the visual flow of the checklist items. Other factors were the weather deviations on arrival and non-standard arrival into a visual from the north side of the airport and terrain monitoring. Passenger issues requiring Dispatch coordination and the aircraft being met by Law Enforcement at the gate. It was a very busy flight at the end of a long day.
1817754: I was the Line Captain in the First Officer's seat. After numerous delaying vectors which cut into our planned landing fuel, we were finally cleared for the ILS Runway 35L. Passing through 9,000 feet we noticed an aircraft approaching our aircraft from the east at 8,000 feet. As we descended on the glideslope, passing 8400 feet, the TCAS generated an RA on the aircraft, which was still at 8,000 feet. We came within 400 feet. of merging with this aircraft! We circled back for another approach, cleaned up to conserve fuel, and advised Approach that we were now at a minimum fuel state. We circled back for another ILS to Runway 35L, which we completed normally. I called the TRACON Supervisor on my cell phone after parking. He said the other aircraft was supposed to intercept the final for Runway 35R but neglected to do so, which resulted in a rather severe loss of separation. According to the TRACON Supervisor, the other pilot blamed his automation for not capturing the 35R localizer. Working Final Radar. Because of weather, it was necessary for me to use the ILS approach for my runway, 35L. The parallel final for Runway 35R was able to use visual approaches. I had cleared Aircraft X for the ILS to Runway 35L at Denver International. I switched communications to Tower. A few seconds later, the pilot of Aircraft X called on my frequency that he was responding to a TCAS RA and climbing. Aircraft Y was cleared for a visual approach to Runway 35R at 8000 ft. but was crossing his localizer. Aircraft Y ended up turning virtually underneath Aircraft X before heading back northeast to Runway 35R. Aircraft Y was at 8000 ft., Aircraft X was indicating 8400 ft. and climbing. I cancelled the approach clearance for Aircraft X, turned west, and climbed to 9000 ft. Aircraft X was re-sequenced and landed safely on Runway 35L.North landing configuration is the preferred operation. This morning, the wind was out of the south at 8 to 12 kt. Although pilots were complaining about tailwinds, we maintained the north operation. In addition, convective weather was south of the airport, sitting on the final approaches. This affected [the] pilots' ability to see the airport. The only other weather in the airspace was a small area east of the airport that had no impact. In a north configuration, the runways, 35L/35R, are direct parallel runways. If we had landed south, as the wind and weather favored, we would have used a widely spaced configuration and landed on runways 16R and 17R. We also could have easily used visual approaches and the aircraft would have been in clear weather all the way to the airport and had a headwind. Landing north unnecessarily was a major contributing factor in this event. Also, the parallel final for Runway 35R was training and the Developmental forgot to turn Aircraft Y in a timely manner resulting in the overshoot. This could have also been avoided in a south operation because of much more spacing between the runways.
1817756: Aircraft X was holding short for Runway 7 at MBJ while [other airline flights] were on the approach. As Aircraft Y approached the runway (approximately 1 mile final), I heard a voice on the Tower frequency say cleared for takeoff" No callsign was given, and the voice did not match the Tower controller who had cleared us to hold short. We held our position. If we had taxied onto the runway, we would have created a collision threat with the aircraft on short final. We did not respond to the call or mention it to the controller because to do so in that moment would have created confusion on the busy frequency. Operations continued as normal with no additional threats. It is my belief that one of two things happened. Either a person with a transmitter outside the airport attempted to get us (Aircraft X) to taxi onto the runway in front of a landing aircraft, or someone in the Tower spoke too close to an open microphone while discussing a takeoff clearance. I do not think the second scenario is as likely, since the tone was not conversational, the voice sounded young, and no other words were spoken other than "cleared for takeoff"."
1817775: While flying in Murmansk airspace, approximately at waypoint 'TURUK' on airway P995 we experienced a loss of GPS signal. Initially it was one receiver and shortly after that both receivers were not providing position information. This lasted until our oceanic entry point, 'BARUX.' Both receivers were back to normal within seconds of each other. GPS signal interference lasted for almost 300 NM. ATC was notified.
1817781: Very interesting set of circumstances led our flight today to take the clearance to 'Line Up and Wait' that was meant for another aircraft in ZZZ [airport]. After we pushed off our gate, we were cleared to taxi to Runway XXR at [taxiway] 1 from our ramp via taxiways 2, 3 and 4.We were all done with our taxi out procedures and checklist by the time we were number 1 aircraft at the hold short line of taxiway 1 for XXR. Traffic was moving steadily, so the Captain taxied right up to just prior to the 'Hold Short' line. This is where the weird circumstances happened for this event:The first thing that happened is the 737 MAX RAAS (Runway Awareness and Advisory System) EGPWS Aural Callout announced our approach to Runway XXR as it is intended to do so. Also, at the exact same time, the Tower Controller gave a clearance for an aircraft to, 'At XX Right, 1, line up and wait.' What happened is that the two voices, of the RAAS, and the Controller, most likely blocked each other out to us, the crew.Since I was working the radio, I made the assumption that the Controller was calling us since we heard tail end of, 'XX Right, at 1.' I repeated back exactly, 'Line up and wait Runway XX Right, at 1, [call sign].' After that we did not hear anything from the Controller as the Captain taxied into position for the hold. As we were taxiing onto the runway, I noticed from the opposite side of the runway at Taxiway 5, Aircraft Y taxiing what looked like across the runway to me. As the Captain rounded out the turn to line us up with the runway, we hear the Controller say, 'Well, that's interesting.' He then proceeded to tell us that we had taken the clearance for Aircraft Y to line up and wait. I then proceeded to apologize, but that I had also read back to him the clearance.Since Aircraft Y was behind us on the runway, the Controller just told us to hold position, and he proceeded to re-shuffle the order, and was able to let us go first in front of Aircraft Y. We got a clearance for takeoff and had a non-eventful departure. As the Controller handed us over to Departure Frequency, he stated, 'Upon further review, I think I screwed that up, no worries, contact Departure.'At that point we started formulating a theory on what may have happened and the Captain and I started to debrief it in late climb out, and cruise flight.What I believe happened, is that when the RAAS created the aural warning that we were approaching runway XXR at intersection 4X, was the exact time where the Controller called Aircraft Y to line up and wait. BUT, upon further review of the audio of ATC, the Controller gave out the wrong taxi way intersection to Aircraft Y. What we both heard right after the RAAS had completed its aural callout, is the tail end of the clearance. Even though Aircraft Y was on taxiway 5, Tower gave out the incorrect clearance of 'Aircraft Y, Runway XXR at 4X, line up and wait.'At this point, I believe either both the Aircraft Y pilot and I probably keyed the mic at the same time, and repeated back the same clearance since we assumed we heard the tail end of the clearance as 'XXR, at 4X, line up and wait.' Or, maybe I read back the clearance first and the Aircraft Y pilot also assumed since he heard me take the clearance that it may have been for us only? That I don't really know. I was taxiing to Runway XXR at [taxiway] 4X. I was approaching the runway hold short line as Aircraft Y in front of us received their takeoff clearance. I kept the aircraft rolling and was applying the brakes to stop just short of the hold short line when the MAX aircraft that we were in gave us the [aural alert] 'Approaching Runway XXR'...at the same time Tower gave the clearance to line up and wait. The [aural alert] 'Approaching Runway 28R' occurred simultaneously with the call sign when Tower said '[Call sign], XXR at 4X, line up and wait.' The First Officer read back the instructions. Tower did not correct the read back. We were the only aircraft in position to take the runway at XXR at 4X. I continued taxiing onto XXR at 4X and as I was turning onto the center line, Tower said 'Oh isn't that interesting', and then '[Call sign], you took Aircraft Y's clearance.' I had seen Aircraft Y on the other side of the runway, farther east, at [taxiway] 5. And he was actively stopping short of XXR at 5.The Controller basically said 'that is ok, Aircraft X will go first.' He advised us to hold in position, he then cleared us for takeoff. After takeoff he said that 'upon further review, it looks like I messed up.'
1817792: While unloading the aircraft, we removed the city bags first at the direction of the supervisor, which meant we emptied the front of the airplane. There was about 2900 lbs of bags and mail in the rear of the plane. As the passengers were getting off the plane and we started to down load the bags, I notice the first nose strut was starting to move, we were unable to reach the GPU panel to plug the ground power in. A few minutes later the plane nose gear strut appeared to be a full extension BUT THE tire never came off the ground. We were told that tail stands were not needed on the 737 MAX.... I believe we should revisit that decision, or maybe look for another solution.
1817806: Departed VFR on Runway 6 and entered right pattern at 3500 [ft.] for Runway 34. Received a terrain warning from the EGPWS on downwind and established a climb. The warning promptly extinguished after a 200 feet climb. We departed Runway 06, and entered a right downwind for Runway 34. At 3,500 [ft.] we leveled off and maintained visual separation with the mountains. However, we got the terrain warning and complied with it. Within 2 seconds the message extinguished as we were climbing. We leveled off at 3,800 and continued our downwind to [Runway] 34.
1817811: We departed ZZZ for ZZZ1. The climb mode was set to E-CLB. At approx 12,000 feet, I decided to engage max con thrust to climb over weather. Soon after, a pop or bang was felt / heard and the aircraft yawed to the left. The EICAS indicated ENG 1 OUT. Both me and the First Officer (FO) acknowledged the message and I called for the QRH. I received priority from ATC and requested to level off. I maintained the current heading and slowed so that me and the FO could assess the situation. Soon after, we requested a turn back to ZZZ with ATC. As we descended toward ZZZ, we ran the ENG OUT QRH and, after making sure all indications were green, we attempted an APU assisted restart. N2 did not rise above zero. Restart was abandoned and we secured the inop engine and prepared for a one engine inop landing. I spoke to the Flight Attendant (FA), explaining that we had suffered an engine failure and that we would be landing in approx 7 to 10 minutes back in ZZZ and to prepare for a normal landing. I also made an announcement to the pax with the same information. At 5,000 feet, a few miles south west and visual with the airport, we entered a visual hold, maintaining separation from a few weather cells in the vicinity, to finalize setup, checklists and briefs for a visual approach backed up by an RNAV to RWY XX. When ready, we asked for direct-to the final approach fix and executed the visual app. Once on the runway, emergency vehicles followed us to check for smoke or flames. I spoke to the FA to make sure everyone was OK. Both me and the FO made announcements letting the pax know what was happening. After it was ascertained that there was no fire threat, we organized a gate with ops and taxied to it.
1817822: Taxied onto a closed portion of a new runway extension. No indication on runway of the end of the runway. Runway markings wrong for current use. Runway markings are for full length of new extension. No lights visible for daylight operations indicating the runway end. A NOTAM indicating the location of the runway end. Runway markings indicating the runway end.
1817841: Upon arrival at the cockpit, I noticed a bottle that seemed out of place. Upon examination, the bottle was glass cleaner that was labeled as HAZMAT. I removed the item from the cockpit and noticed a spill in the compartment. I read the label and noticed that the label stated 'WARNING: Flammable liquid and vapor...' I notified the Captain and he called Maintenance Control and made a logbook entry. Maintenance Control assigned a Technician who cleaned the spill and made a corrective entry in the logbook. Given the size of the spill, I can assume that the previous crew unknowingly flew the aircraft with a HAZMAT spill in the cockpit.An unknown person must have left the bottle behind after using it in the cockpit. The hazardous item and spill went undetected by the previous crew(s).It's important to use the correct cleaning agents on the aircraft. It's even more important to ensure (and have a procedure) to make sure hazardous items are removed from the aircraft. I self-rated the risk rating as HIGH since the aircraft had presumably flown with a HAZMAT spill that was undetected by a previous crew.
1817878: During climbout from ZZZ passing through approximately FL190 #2 HYD ISO VLV, #2 ENG HYD PUMP, and #2 RUD HYD Master Cautions illuminated in sequence with approx. 10 seconds between each annunciation. I (Captain, CKP, Pilot Flying) identified, verbalized and canceled the Master Cautions after First Officer (Pilot Monitoring) acknowledged each Master Caution. Crew acknowledged that the #2 HYD QTY was approx. 10%, and #2 HYD PRESS was 0 psi. With all 3 Master Cautions illuminated I called for the #2 HYD PUMP caution checklist first. First Officer (FO) began E&A checklist and I took radios. I informed ATC of hydraulic system malfunction, return to field with vectors requested, informed number of souls and fuel onboard, [received priority handling] and advised we would be running checklists and would inform ATC when completed. After we completed the #2 HYD PUMP, and during the hydraulic systems failure checklist, when it states to complete descent and approach checklists, I informed FO to pause there so I could communicate to Dispatch and inform of situation, and have operational control congruency in plan to return to ZZZ. Amendment to Release to return to ZZZ was recorded at XA12Z via phone with Dispatcher Name. I then requested patch through to Maintenance (MX) Control and informed of situation, malfunction, and hydraulics system indications. Aircraft was flying with normal controllability.Flight Attendant (FA) brief was made to include normal landing in ZZZ at approximately XB50lcl. PAX were informed of system indication that required us to return to ZZZ, and to please pay close attention to FAs instructions as they prepare cabin for arrival, and as a standard precautionary measure Fire Department would be standing by with lights flashing. I informed FO of landing weight, FO derived landing bugs from E&A checklist. We completed the descent and approach procedures and checklist, planning RNAV Y RWY XXR, and proceeded with completion of hydraulic system failure landing checklist, followed by alternate gear extension checklist with no operational airspeed exceedance. FAs reported back cabin secure for landing, FO and Captain in agreement informed ATC aircraft was ready for return to land, and that it would be a slower than normal RWY exit and taxi due to inoperative nosewheel steering requiring taxiing with differential power and braking. After normal landing, ATC was informed that Airport Rescue and Fire Fighting (ARFF) [were] no longer needed. FO informed ZZZ OPS to chock main gear also due to emergency/park brake accumulator pressure only available. Taxi to spot was performed with shutdown. AML entry was made with communication with MX CONTROL.
1817898: During boarding, all of a sudden Flight Attendant 1 (FA-1) and Flight Attendant 3 (FA-3), in the front galley, [and] I smelled like a scorched cloth smell when you turn on an oxygen bottle, or a burnt crayon smell. The smell spread in the first-class cabin. I experienced this smell before and knew right away that it was a fumes/cabin odor event. Most likely, the aircraft has an oil leak in or close to the engine. I informed the Captain immediately, and he smelled it, too. After a few minutes, my throat became scratchy, and I started getting lightheaded. When I turned my head, I felt as if my eyes caught up with my head with a slight delay. (said she smelled it, but that she was OK. I went on the jetway as the smell was really getting to me. My heartbeat became faster, and my speech even became slurred: my words were not coming out as fast as they were usually. I started losing the ability to function, almost. Name FA-3 kind of took over and made some announcements or was listening to the Captain, when he was calling me. The Captain reported the fumes/odor, and a mechanic came onboard. The boarding was complete, but the Captain notified the agents of the problem. I needed some fresh air, so I went to the jet way door, opened it, and took a few breaths, but a customer service supervisor, I think, told me to close the door immediately, as in a few minutes some machine was going to be turned on, 2 gates away from ours, and the smell would have come to the jet way from the open door. I did not smell anything outside, but I closed the door immediately, as I was instructed, well before the machine 2 gates away, was turned on, so there was no way that any smell/fumes could have come in through the door. The Captain made an announcement that the passengers needed to deplane, and everybody deplaned. We deplaned as well. I immediately went to sit down, as I felt dizzy. I took a bottle of water with me, to keep me hydrated. After the flight kept being delayed further and further, it was finally delayed until the next morning, to allow the mechanics to work on the plane. The Captains were given the name of the hotel where they were going to layover, but it took over an hour for the Hotels and Limo department to work on our hotel stay. We waited and waited and finally decided to go with the Captains, hoping that Company would put us in the same hotel. When we went outside, still not knowing where we were staying, a van driver flagged us and told us we were going to stay at the hotel with the Captains. As we were driving, I received a phone call from ZZZ Flight Service, Name, confirming that we were staying at the hotel. After a good night sleep, the next morning, I felt much better, however, both of my hands were shaking, and, when I put my contacts back on, I realized that they were foggy. The driver who took us to the airport told us that the plane was fixed by the mechanics. The plane we boarded was, in fact, the same plane we had the day before. When I looked in the logbook, I read that the mechanics could not reproduce the problem, and that, therefore, nothing was done to the plane. They wrote that it could have been a smell/fumes coming from outside and reaching the plane from a door left open. As I described above, the fumes/odor started on the plane long before anybody operated any machine or equipment outside. There were no fumes/smoke/smells outside. In the morning, though, I did not smell the smell from the day prior. However, I felt the presence of the fumes, as by the time we were taking off my throat became scratchy again. Name FA-3 didn't look that good, either. As soon as she came onboard, she did not have the energy she displayed the day prior and sat down immediately in a first class seat. I asked her if she was feeling OK, and she said she felt tired. She did not feel like herself. She said she could not sleep well, as she felt heaviness on her chest. She thought that maybe she ate too much food during the flight, but that now she realized that it was not what she ate. I told her that it could definitely be an increase in blood pressure or other symptom related to the fumes. As the flight progressed, she went to the back. I continued to serve in first class, and, twice, I couldn't even speak, as my throat became really scratchy. I went to the galley to drink some water and felt better. When we arrived in ZZZ, I felt better, but, at night, I had headache, so I had to call sick for the trip I had the next day. After a good night sleep, I felt much better. I thank the Captain for reporting the problem, however, I don't think that the plane is fixed. The problem was not fumes or smell coming from outside but something wrong with the plane, probably an oil leak causing toxic fumes and odor to come in the cabin. It would be nice if they could check and try to find the leak. I do not feel safe flying on this airplane. As far as the operations went, there was a lot of confusion with our hotel accommodations and with communication from the Company to us. The next day, there was also a lot of confusion regarding the new departure time, as the flight info on our tablet, Company, and the information the Captain's had showed all different departure times. Communication between the Company and the crews really needs to improve. Scheduling should contact us directly, instead of relying on automated methods of communication.
1817937: I was returning from ZZZ1 to ZZZ on a training cross country flight with a pre private student. We used flight following for the duration of the flight. While under the 3000 shelve of the Bravo at 2500 MSL and assigned a heading, Approach pointed out traffic to our 9 o'clock and 500 below. The student made visual contact, reported contact with ATC, and pointed out the traffic to myself and I quickly made visual contact also. I was surprised at how close the aircraft was to us, so I had the student continue flying while I maintained continuous visual contact. Initially I thought they weren't in contact with Approach, as it would be highly unusual to return to ZZZ at 2,000 MSL. We continued inbound to ZZZ with the Student flying and myself maintaining contact with the traffic. The traffic began to drift towards both laterally and vertically with only 300 feet. vertical separation at one point. I began to think the traffic was not in contact with Approach, again unusual, and wondered its intentions while constantly preparing for evasive maneuvers. The student was flying excellently so I opted to let him continue to fly while maintaining SA and visual contact. The traffic then began rocking his wings which the student also noticed, I instructed the student to also rock wings. The traffic then began a sudden and sharp turn to cross underneath us in our blind spot. I was rapidly monitoring below us on both sides of the aircraft, the traffic display on the MFD (G1000) and the student's performance. I opted not to make any evasive actions as I felt our forward speed outpaced the traffic's forward speed and continuing flight straight ahead gave us the safest separation at the moment. Once the aircraft appeared on our 3 o'clock side they made another sharp turn to once again parallel our flight path. Approach instructed us to contact ZZZ Tower as we were rapidly approaching the Class D airspace, normally we are switched much further back. We contacted Tower and the traffic began a turn away from us. I maintained visual contact on my side until the aircraft was far enough away to no longer present a danger. I observed them on the MFD skirting the edge of the Class D airspace likely within 1/4 mile. I asked Tower if they were in contact with the aircraft and they said they were not.
1817984: The flight was approximately 5 hours. Had fuel for 6.5 hours.Approximately 2/3rds of the way through the flight the engine began to get rough and vibrate. I started to troubleshoot with the checklist after verifying temperatures and fuel pressure. I used the 'engine discrepancy check rough running engine'. After doing this I determined the problem to be a spark plug on the third cylinder While on L mag.This process distracted me and I most likely did not keep up with changing tanks for the next bit of time as I was thinking about it. After about 15 minutes it went smooth again and so I re checked the magnetos and they were both back to normal. Again I was thinking about it for maybe 15 more minutes. Because of this I believe the fuel on the left tank was left on too long and the fuel gauge did not show an accurate amount.As I got closer to the airport and started descending I used the descent checklist and changed to the right tank. The left at the time was indicating about 13 gallons and the right about 19 gallons. I knew this was probably not correct because I had been flying already for 5 hours and that would mean I have 2 more hours of fuel. I reduced power when I started my descent slowly retarding throttle back to 18 in.As I descended to 4,000 feet and reached 18 in. the engine began to run rough again. I checked the instruments and saw that the cylinder 4 EGT was too low on the annunciator. And also the fuel flow was fluctuating. The engine started surging from lack of fuel. I quickly did the Engine Failure After Liftoff and noticed I was already on the tank with higher indicated fuel so tried the left tank. Without helping I tried to go back to right tank. Notified ATC that I was requesting priority handling and turning to the airport for [Runway] XXL. I knew there was a Learjet approaching for [Runway] XXR and this influenced my decision. Performed the maximum glide checklist. Shut down engine when I had the field made. Landed safely on Runway XXL with no damage to airplane requested for a tow and called my Dispatcher. The fuel gauges were indicating top of yellow arc still on left and half on right tank. After parking it settled down to 1/8th left tank half right tank. Confirming my suspicion, they were not accurate. After fueling the aircraft to bottom of tabs after Maintenance checked it out they found 3-4 gallons useable in the left tank and the remaining fuel in the right tank of approximately 20 gallons. Maintenance did not find anything wrong with the airplane.It is clear to me that I got distracted dealing with the problemMidway in the flight and missed changing the tank for an extended period of time. In the future I will write down the time I change fuel tanks and the estimated remaining fuel in each tank and compare it against the fuel gauge. I will also change tanks more frequently to prevent such a big imbalance. Every 30 minutes. I am unsure of why the airplane struggled to produce power other than the potential low fuel on the left tank. I would think switching to the tank that was fuller in the descent checklist would have solved this issue.Fuel was checked prior to the flight to confirm it was correctly filled.
1817997: While level at altitude we experienced wind shear the aircraft dropped 2,300 ft.We tried to communicate the radio did not work. We got a back up radio. Received a call and made the launch recovery zone back hot.Recovered altitude and continued the mission. We also record a link hit at the same time. Due to what we believe to be strong wind shear we were unable to maintain our altitude above 10, 000 feet. We began troubleshooting and attempted to communicate, but were unable to get through on our radios due to malfunction and had to grab a backup handheld. By this point we had descended roughly 2,500 feet when we established communication, at which point we made the mission hot again. We were then able to establish a climb and continue our mission.
1818026: Aircraft X was looking for a visual approach into ZZZ. The aircraft started descending on his own without a clearance. I issued a terrain alert and instructed the Pilot to climb back to a safe altitude. I notified the CIC (Controller in Charge) but they did not instruct me to issue a brasher. A low altitude alert warning should have to be manually disabled. I don't think it alerted because the aircraft was nearing his destination airport.
1818033: Working arrival wall combined. Aircraft X inbound to ZZZ was vectored around weather to get the Visual Approach for ZZZ. I failed to make a point out to Departure Controller for the inbound aircraft as required and he was cleared for a Visual Approach and shipped to ZZZ Tower. I issued traffic for a VFR aircraft off the field before shipping to Tower. Departure Controller approved automated release for Aircraft Y off ZZZ. Aircraft departed ZZZ but was not on an IFR Beacon but instead on a 1200 code. Aircraft remained on 1200 code and was shipped to Departure Controller. This was in fact the VFR aircraft that I issued traffic for to Aircraft X prior to switching to Tower. Departure Controller assigned new beacon code and then saw the IFR inbound I had already switched to the Tower. Departure Controller immediately issued an Eastbound turn away from the other aircraft. I completely forgot to make the point out or hand off to the Departure Controller. For the last 15 months [the] schedule we worked combined so often I just didn't remember at that moment that ZZZ was not in my sector at the time. I needed to make the point out or hand off and be more aware of the room configuration and this event could have been avoided. This was just an accidental mental lapse in realizing the configuration of the radar room at the time.
1818078: This aircraft just came out of long term storage. It needed a full thrust takeoff, ETOPS verification for hi-altitude APU start and an Autoland update. Two separate Maintenance write-ups occurred after door close but prior to push back. This resulted in delays and multiple MRD updates. Both pilots reviewed and verified FMC load was normal after each anomaly corrected. On takeoff the FO (Flying Pilot) called for 'Autothrottles.' EPR mode engaged normally but throttles were slow to advance and left throttle lagged approximately 1 knob width. At 'check thrust' call FO commented to check left engine throttle. I had noticed the slow movement and manually moved both throttles to the commanded full thrust EPR setting. When passing 3,000 ft. the aircraft speed bug would not accelerate above CMS (approximately). We set 250 manually and each time we tried to engage VNAV or FLCH the command bug retreated to approximately CMS. We also noticed the command EPR was indicating CON thrust. I tried to engage CLB on TMSP panel but had no effect. At this point I said we'll wait until above 10,000 ft. to troubleshoot further. Above 10,000 ft I noticed that the VNAV CLB page appeared normal, but there was an 'ALL ENG' prompt at 5L which I'd never seen. After selecting the ALL ENG prompt the airplane returned to normal CLB mode. At no point during ground operations did either pilot ever select the CLB EO prompt or the subsequent Execute key. After landing and debriefing with Maintenance and the next leg's Captain, this Pilot stated she had also previously seen a 'split throttles on takeoff result in the aircraft believing it was in a single-engine situation and engaging the EO CLB mode. A Maintenance write up for Autothrottles was written up and Maintenance debriefed. (Autothrottles worked normal for remainder of our flight).
1818110: Environmental hazardous spill occurred today at ZZZ. One piece out of a total of 18 located on a skid was punctured releasing product inside while being transported by forklift to the export dock for customer delivery. The trail of the product was identified by the label as CO-FLAKE HZ with the aquatic toxicity label and UN3077 identifier. The spill was immediately contained and Dangerous Goods Specialist was notified to confirm level of hazard. Environmental Coordinator was then notified and instructions were given on cleanup procedures. Product located on floor was then placed in Dangerous Goods container until proper disposal as instructed. Instructions were then given on proper repackage procedure and the customer was notified.
1818115: BHM ATIS advised runways 6 and 36 were active, with visual and RNAV approaches in use to both. Conditions were VMC with good visibility. Upon initial contact with BHM Approach, we were advised to expect Runway 6. The First Officer briefed a visual approach to be backed up with the RNAV Runway 6. As we approached the terminal area, we observed a single heavy rain shower cell located directly on the final approach course for Runway 6, very near the final approach fix. This cell was approximately 5 NM wide and ATC had advised two other aircraft that this weather contained 'light to heavy' precipitation. It seemed to us that if we were to continue to pursue the approach for Runway 6, we would most likely fly through this weather.After brief discussion, the First Officer and I determined that an approach and landing to Runway 36 would keep us clear of that weather. BHM Approach agreed and vectored us for an RNAV approach to Runway 36.
