The First Officer briefed the RNAV 36 approach and I entered the landing data for Runway 36, including current ATIS reported winds - 110 at 6 kt. The approach proceeded normally with the aircraft configured normally for landing and in a stable condition. The First Officer had switched off the autopilot at just below 1,000 ft. and maintained the proper glide path with the 'snowflake' showing on glide path. At some point just below DDA, 1,530 ft., and MDA, 1,480 ft., very near the ridge just south of the airport, we received a terrain caution with [a] 'too low terrain' audible message. The First Officer adjusted pitch and we went very slightly above glide path momentarily. We received no additional warnings or cautions and the First Officer readjusted pitch to resume normal glide path. Touchdown on Runway 36 was normal and within the touchdown zone. At no time did we receive any 'pull up' or 'obstacle pull up' alerts, only the one 'too low terrain' alert. At the time of alert, the FO (First Officer) responded in accordance with the note in [the] POH Bulletin XX-XX, X.X.X. Conditions during the event were day VMC with good visibility, 10 SM.I believe this terrain caution could have been avoided by not performing an approach to Runway 36 in the first place and by maintaining a profile slightly above glide path. I did not observe us ever being below glide path. In thinking about the event afterwards, I realize that while the charted procedure guarantees obstacle clearance down to the MDA, it is the pilot's responsibility to maintain visual clearance from terrain and obstacles once below MDA. In the case of this particular approach, doing that requires one to fly a profile above a normal glide path. I had always known about the ridge and antennas south of the airport, but had never flown an approach to Runway 36 in BHM. Despite it being a charted procedure which is permissible in day VFR conditions, I'm not convinced that it is an approach that I would use in the future - due to the need to maintain a higher than normal glide path in order to avoid the terrain alert. In my opinion, flying a steeper approach could potentially lead to other issues such as landing long or past the touchdown zone if not managed very carefully. In the future, I would likely only use Runway 36 if in an emergency if Runway 6/24 was not available.
1818136: On departure out of ZZZ, we were in level flight at 10,000 feet waiting for ZZZ1 Center to continue or climb. We received an RA and the aircraft got within 200 feet. We then received a second RA and came within 1400 feet of another aircraft. We advised ATC and continued to ZZZ2.ZZZ1 Center kept getting us confused with another aircraft with a similar call sign. We notified them twice that we were not the other aircraft. The Controller was incredibly task saturated and noticeably in over their head.
1818160: We arrived at ZZZ Gate at approximately XA:30. Upon arriving at the gate there were no ramp personnel in the area. We parked as directed by the DGS system, shut down the engines, and performed the Shutdown Checklist (including 'Brakes Set'). After a few minutes, (indicated by the cargo doors opening on the ECAM) ground personnel approached the aircraft to perform their duties. I left my seat to use the lavatory and to assure the #1 Flight Attendant (FA) and our First Class passengers that we were diligently trying to find someone to open the door. Approximately 10-15 minutes later, the agent opened the door. I returned to the flight deck to gather my belongings before saying goodbye to the passengers at the door. We never received the 'chocks in' hand signal and had no ground power connected despite our efforts to get it done. In the mean time, shortly after main cabin door opening, a maintenance tech came up to the flight deck and gathered some pins from the gear pin stowage compartment, for what he indicated was some sort of inspection. I was called the next morning and informed by the ZZZ1 Director of Flight that while we were on the flight deck we had an aircraft rollback causing damage to the jet bridge. Not one person on or near the aircraft indicated that we had any aircraft movement and First Officer (FO) and I were totally unaware of the rollback. Often we arrive at the gate and there are no ramp personnel to chock the airplane. In addition, very shortly after door opening, there is a maintenance technician present to perform required operational inspections. As the flight deck crew, we performed our required post flight duties. We cannot account for the other several departments involved in the safe securing of the aircraft. As the Pilot-in-Command (PIC) of the aircraft, I sincerely believe that the parking brake was set. Given the intense scheduling practices and understaffing of the airline on the Aircraft Maintenance Department and Customer Service, along with the obvious poor training of Ground Support, I have no idea what happened.
1818245: We had begun a descent from our cruising altitude of FL280. Passing FL270 the aircraft violently rolled to the left and then to the right. The pilot flying used TCS (Touch Control Steering) to override the autopilot and maintain control of the aircraft. We where thrown around in our seats from the turbulence. AUTOPILOT FAIL" message was displayed on the EICAS. The forces of the turbulence had disengaged the autopilot. We ran the QRH checklist for "AUTOPILOT FAIL" -which did not mention to re-engage the autopilot so we took the conservative approach and the rest of the flight was hand flown. We reported the severe turbulence to ATC and asked if there was any traffic nearby that may have caused the turbulence -they advised that there was a heavy Airbus 15 miles ahead. We could not be sure as to whether the turbulence was caused by clear air turbulence or wake turbulence. There was no SIGMETS for the area and the weather was clear. I checked in with the Flight Attendant and he said that both he and the passengers where okay. I advised that he remain seated for the rest of the flight. The fasten seat belt sign was on prior to the event and was turned on at top of descent. I sent an ACARS message to Maintenance about the "AUTOPILOT FAIL" message and they responded with that it would require a maintenance write up. The rest of the flight continued uneventful. Upon arrival I wrote up 'Encountered Severe' turbulence and also a second write up for 'AUTOPILOT FAIL'. As we where waiting for the flight data recorder download to be completed by Maintenance a message populated on the EICAS. This was an additional write up 'SPOILER FAIL'. The spoilers where indicating "OPEN" on the EICAS. Speed brakes where set to "CLOSED". We inspected the spoilers outside and they where both in the deployed position. The right hand side spoiler seemed to be deployed a little less than he left hand spoiler. Even though we did not see any indications suggesting this in flight. It's a possibility that the spoilers briefly deployed in flight and possibly caused the turbulence however I feel that this is unlikely to cause the severe turbulence that we encountered. We swapped into a new tail after this 3rd write up. Check the flight data recorder to see if there was a momentary uncommanded spoiler deployment." We started our descent from FL280 at ATC's direction. We were descending at 290 KIAS as per ATC instruction. Passing FL270, the aircraft uncontrollably rolled left and then right. I used the TCS (Touch Control Steering) button to override the autopilot. At that time, autopilot also kicked off and gave an 'Autopilot Fail' master warning message on the EICAS. The PIC, pilot not flying, ran the QRH. We did not consider the hardover protection to be an issue. We flew the remainder of the flight without use of autopilot out of caution, conservative considerations. We reported the severe turbulence to ATC. We checked EICAS and MFD system indications. All appeared normal. We checked with the Flight Attendant, who stated that the turbulence was unexpected, but all was normal after the turbulence. ATC advised that there was a heavy Airbus 15 miles ahead. Weather conditions were very clear at the time with no visible moisture and winds were relatively calm for that altitude. We sent an ACARs message to the company to relay the situation. Upon landing, the First Officer did a walk around and did not notice any significant details to report. After landing and while sitting in the aircraft while waiting for it to be released for the follow-on leg, the aircraft gave a 'SPOILER FAIL' advisory on the EICAS. Upon exterior inspection after the message, the spoilers were raised/partially extended. The right side was lower than the left side. Pictures were taken of the spoilers, spoiler control handle in the cockpit, and EICAS. Suggest checking aircraft system data after download to verify severe turbulence or other system anomalies.
1818252: After takeoff, during gear retraction, we heard and felt 2-3 loud bangs and thuds with associated yaw and shutter of the aircraft. Initially, we considered a landing gear tire might have blown or it was retraction problem due to gear in transit timed with [another] problem. Once gear was fully retracted, a series of bangs and shutters occurred again and during our global assessment (Nothing displayed on ECAM), we noted a spike in temperature on engine 1 EGT as corresponding to the problem. [We suspected] compressor stalls. Reducing the power on engine 1 to idle eliminated the problem and the engine ran normally. We immediately [requested priority handling] with ATC requesting the ARFF equipment, as well as a box pattern back to XXR (longest runway), leveled at 4000 feet MSL, maintained configuration at 180 knots. We ran all appropriate checklists including: Engine 1 Stall in flight with Engine Parameters Normal at Idle, Non-Routine Landing, and Overweight Landing. We made an initial and landing imminent announcement to the flight attendants and passengers. During the initial series of compressor stalls and after the engine was stabilized at idle neither the flight attendants nor any passengers reported any other engine problems such as fire, smoke, vibrations, etc. Once everything was complete we flew the ILS XXC approach to a normal touchdown and landed to a full stop on the runway so that ARFF could look over the aircraft before we taxied uneventfully to the gate. Weight at touchdown was 3,000 to 4,000 pounds over the max with a 200 FPM touchdown. After shutdown, we made 2 logbook entries (Compressor stall after TO and Overweight Landing). We debriefed the Chief Pilot, Maintenance, ARFF Chief, Gate Agent, and Passengers. We saved all paper work, photos, and contact information.An Airbus Pilot jump-seater was very helpful with event CRM. Possible failure factors included heavy weight, TOGA takeoff, and a warm day stressing the engine. In addition, APU had been on MEL for 8 days adding to engine fatigue and stress with ground air and cross-bleed starts, and it was the aircraft's first flight of the day (even with ample warm-up time). Following policies, procedures, flows, and checklists all while maintaining positive aircraft control in an un-rushed manner using all available resources and thorough CRM led to a safe resolution to the engine failure on takeoff. [I recommend] better and more prompt APU maintenance, and the use of non-TOGA flex takeoffs on longer runways in hot and heavy takeoffs situations. Shortly after takeoff, during gear retraction, we noticed a loud thud or two. Initially, I thought it was a problem with landing gear retraction, since it started while the gear was still in transit. Shortly thereafter, the noise occurred again. A spike in engine temp was noted during the sounds, and the spike immediately disappeared. The EGT over-temp readings were happening too fast (and clearing so fast) that no ECAM message was triggered long enough to stay up. Once power on the #1 engine was reduced, the engine ran normally at idle. We requested priority handling and leveled off at 4,000 feet. ATC began vectoring us back for a visual approach to the longest runway, XXC. We requested ARFF to inspect the plane on landing. Flight attendants, passengers and Dispatch were advised of the situation and our intentions. All appropriate QRH procedures were complied with. Non-normal landing procedures were complied with. Overweight landing procedures and landing distance assessment were completed. A straight-out heading was requested and approved in the event of a missed. An uneventful approach and landing was conducted. After stopping on the runway, we requested ARFF to inspect the #1 engine for damage. No damage was noted and we continued to the gate. I'm not sure that this event was preventable. The only unusual thing about this aircraft was the deferral period for the APU. I think it had been deferred 8 days ago, which is quite a lot of external air start cycles and cross bleeds. Just speculation, but if this malfunction was associated in some way with a bleed air valve, the fact that the APU was deferred so long-and all the associated unusual starting procedures (perhaps external air starts) could have been a factor. It might be something to consider from a maintenance tracking perspective. I hear that we are seeing more inflight engine problems lately. I think APU deferrals should be as short as possible for a variety of reasons.I have a feeling that this event may have been associated with the APU deferral. I think emphasis should be put on deferring them for a shorter time and routing planes in need of APU work to a Maintenance facility sooner. In no case is a week deferral reasonable or necessary. (I don't think any troubleshooting had even been attempted to get the APU operating again.) TOGA Takeoff could have been another contributing factor, as we are asking a lot of the engines in hot weather.
1818270: This was a routine flight from ZZZ to ZZZ1, in a B757. We had a normal push back, cross bleed start and taxi. On the takeoff roll, we rotated on speed and pitched to approximately 15 degrees. Noted the airspeed appeared to accelerate in the climb more than normal so I pitched through the flight director to stop at 20 degrees but that did not arrest the abnormal airspeed acceleration. Around 1,000 to 1,500 feet in normal configuration (flaps 5, standard takeoff power and pitched just below twenty degrees) the airspeed entered the red over-speed tape. At the same time we received multiple master warning lights and bells, master caution, clacker, and multiple failure notifications of electrical and avionics in nature (such as red OVSPD, Rudder ratio, Mach Speed Trim, ATC fault, GEN DRIVE, Left EEC, Right EEC etc.). The Captain's instruments indicated over 400 knots and over 40,000 feet of altitude. The Captain and I agreed the standby instrument appeared normal around 185 knots in a climb. I disconnected auto throttles, switched off flight director and recovered the airplane at 180 knots leveling off at 4,000 feet using standby instruments and flaps 5. The Captain noted it appeared my instruments began returning to normal to match the standby instruments. The Captain's complete instrument suite remained failed through the rest of the event. The Captain requested priority handling] and an air turn back with vectors for Runway XX. One attempt was made to re-engage the flight director and autopilot to no avail. Uneventfully, we hand flew a VFR approach to landing. We then had a normal taxi to our remote gate and released Fire Rescue vehicles from assistance.
1818304: We arrived into the alley inbound to gate XXB to find [another] aircraft (737) stopped whilst approaching XXA. Ramp attempted to contact crew to direct a tow-in. The aircraft did not reply, and taxied in. I realized later that it was a MAX aircraft, with new Leap engines that allow for taxi at idle power in all but extremely heavy gross weights. I stopped to allow for the gaining of momentum as XXB gate is poorly designed with significant uphill slope. A swarm of service vehicles approaching XXA did not pay attention to marshaling crew at XXB trying to clear our path. So we lost momentum approaching gate and had to stop almost abeam gate. When it appeared that the gate area was clear, we had no lead Marshaller guiding us in. [I then] realized that the parking guidance system was on, but due to the positioning of the gate it was obscured. While still parallel to the gate, we goosed the power for momentum, went to idle, and just made it up the hill. It really should not be that hard to get into a gate.There were many issues. The SOP speaks to aircraft stopping and needing a tow-in, but what if it is a MAX that is at idle and can move at idle thrust? Additionally, training ramp personnel should include a lesson on situational awareness. [There have been] countless approaches to a gate blocked by vehicles which, in a hurry to service an aircraft, block gate access for other aircraft whilst paying no attention to marshallers. And finally, gate XXB has added a parking guidance system you cannot see until you are almost abeam the gate and committed. How does one know to approach?
1818330: While climbing northeast bound toward GREKI and passing through approx 13,000 feet the FO (First Officer, Pilot Flying) looked out his side window and said we had just passed over a drone by approximately 200 feet. We reported this to ATC who queried us on its color (green), size (approx 3FT by 3FT), altitude (approx 12,800 feet), and direction of flight (apparently south).
1818334: I flew a night operation into PTKK. While I was aware of the NOTAM'd PAPI being out of service, and the flight was flown in accordance with SOP, I would like to make the [company] aware of the potential risk associated when conducting a night RNAV(GPS) 4 PTKK approach under these conditions. I believe this reduction in safety at night is due to several factors:1) Lack of visual reference on short final (black hole effect).2) RNAV(GPS) 4 approach lacks vertical guidance to the runway, resulting in the FD's initiating a missed approach at HAMAX.3) Reaching the MAP 300 ft. higher than published DDA. If not briefed and aware, the FD will command a left turn and level flight prior to the 'expected' minimums.4) Lack of outside and inside references to determine if you meet the stabilized approach criteria once you are in visual conditions.5) PTKK is one of shortest runways in our system.6) Numerous threats associated with preloading an electronic glide path while still on the published approach, especially in IMC conditions (a technique many use to increase the level of safety) 7) Junior and less experienced pilots typically fly this trip.
1818349: Aircraft X was scheduled for flight ZZZ to ZZZ1. First Officer (FO) and I reviewed the aircraft maintenance issues prior to arriving at the airport noting MEL 27-11 and associated MELs. At the aircraft during preflight, I reviewed the MEL procedures for 27-11 and worked with FO Name to perform the test procedures listed. The test stated: To verify both control columns are connected, proceed as follows: 1. Hold LH control column in neutral position. 2. Try and move RH control column forward and backward. 3. If there is no relative movement between the control columns, they are connected. While performing this test, we could see that if the LH column was moved the RH column didn't move at all, and same with the RH column. We immediately called Maintenance Control who said that didn't sound right, and said he would call Maintenance back to the aircraft. Note: the disconnect handle was still in place. Once Maintenance arrived, we performed a flight control check with the hydraulics on. At this point, it was noted the LH column only controlled the left elevator and the RH column only controlled the right elevator. No EICAS messages populated. The only EICAS message was 'Pitch trim Disconnect' which was associated with the original MEL. Maintenance was confused and said they had done all the control checks and that everything checked ok. We sincerely believe that had a flight been attempted, it could have resulted in a catastrophe. Poor maintenance flight control checks. Aircraft released to line with defective controls. I believe if maintenance had read the MEL and done the control check that was listed, they may have caught the system malfunction.
1818393: After block out but before takeoff I was notified that Aircraft X had DG/ lithium ion batteries [onboard]. The crew was not aware so I notified them. I was able to send the paperwork to the ACARS printer and send a picture of the paperwork to the pilots cell phone. After that the crew and I determined the flight was good to depart. I also called the DO and he told me to have the crew fill out [a report]. As we were getting cleared for takeoff, ACARS message to not take off due to messed up DG paperwork. Takeoff clearance cancelled by Tower. Cleared for takeoff. As we were moving to runway, ACARS message to not takeoff as DG paperwork incorrect. Our signed DG paperwork said 'no DG'. We indeed had ADG lithium batteries. ACARS message to call Dispatcher. I called Name and he said he could text me a picture of the correct DG paperwork. I also asked him to send me correct data via ACARS. He did both. I asked if we were legal to takeoff and he said yes. In flight we got another ACARS message from Name quoting FOM verbiage and he said he consulted with the DO and the recommendation was to also fill out a [report]. Bottom line is we were handed incorrect DG paperwork.
1818405: While operating Aircraft X, which was scheduled service from ZZZ to ZZZ1, we received a Master Warning for L ENG OIL PRESS. This prompted me to run the affiliated QRH procedure. After doing so we notified ATC and returned to ZZZ. It appears that the left engine lost oil during climbout. While climbing through FL330 for FL360, we received an aural warning and triple chime for L ENG OIL PRESS. This prompted us to run the L ENG OIL PRESS QRH. As we ran the QRH I gave control of the aircraft and radios to First Officer. The QRH asked if we met any 2 of the listed 3 indications for which we did. The conditions that we met were L ENG OIL PRESS warning message and affected engine oil pressure below limits. The QRH then directed us to complete the Engine Failure/ In-Flight Engine Shutdown checklist. After this occurred we communicated with ATC, Dispatch, the flight attendants, and the customers to return to ZZZ.
1818421: Chaotic flight, distractions occurred during disarming announcement, multiple passengers pushing forward to make impossible connections. Gave thumbs up to open door while it was still armed. It was an airbus, door self-disarmed. You guys are killing us with these days, I believe I've only had one work day under eleven hours in length this month. I am physically and mentally fatigued, we need trips built that are workable. This is why everyone is calling in sick. This fatigue and strain almost cost me my job with this event and compromised the safety of the Gate Agent.
1818480: Aircraft X had a dual engine wash on the night of Date. Maintenance Technician 1 and I performed the run up after engine wash, followed Job Card XXX-XX-XX. Taxi aircraft onto taxiway for run up to 60%, 60% run was not done at the blast fence as paperwork doesn't specify location. At 60% run up and operation of packs system no smell/odor was detected in the flight deck or in the cabin. So we proceeded with the Job Card and finished the aircraft. Following day Aircraft X was taken out of service after a flight to ZZZ1 with crew report smell/odor in cabin. This was the first of 2 aircraft we had engine washes on that evening (both 800s), other aircraft Job Card complied with same was as we did Aircraft X- on taxiway same parameters met. The 'smell/odor' seems to be a common problem with the 800 as the Job Card does not state how long to actually run at 60% just to 'packs operate until the air that goes into the control cabin...no smell of the oil contamination'. The 700 has a different Job Card time requirement and seems to have less issues with 'smell/odor'. Cause of flight crew 'smell/odor' discovery may be out of Maintenance Technician's control as engines and packs have been run longer and at different altitudes/temperatures/parameters. Have the Job Card for the 700/800/MAX mirror each other so all aircraft and all technicians are performing job the same way to avoid gate return/air returns/out of service aircraft. Aircraft X was taken out of service in ZZZ1 for oil smell after it landed there from ZZZ after having performed an engine compressor wash. Flight crew reported it. My co-worker and I believe we followed the Job Card and hit the times and parameters that it asks for. Maintenance Technician 2 and myself did not smell anything, this could be due to becoming acclimated. The company pointed out that we needed to be at the blast fence for the 60% N1. I was unaware of this. The task card does not specify to do so. As it only requires a very short time at 60% we set brakes during taxi to run the engine up. We also did an engine compressor wash on another 800 aircraft the same shift the exact same way. Only Aircraft X was taken out of service. This leads me to think that maybe something else may have caused the oil smell. Also after talking to other employees about this, I hear there have been multiple similar situation of 700 series aircraft going out of service following engine compressor washes. So much so that the company has changed the Job Card for the 700 series engine compressor washes. They run the engine at 60% N1 much longer. Why the 800 does not mirror the 700 Job Card is unknown.
1818497: I was sent out to [the] gate to remove panels for customs on Aircraft X, an A321 Airbus. I requested from lead mechanic for documentation on which panels and was told that there was none. When I arrived at the gate, a mechanic that was assigned to an aircraft in the gate next to [our] gate informed me that a Customs Agent had put a stand underneath the aircraft nose when it was extended during cargo unloading and the aircraft had settled onto the stand and was pulled out. When I asked the customs agents about the stand to question the agent about how hard it was to remove the stand to give me an idea of possible damage they said they didn't know. I believe they lied. I was asked by a Customs Agent to remove a panel in the forward cargo bay. When I went to get assistance and the log book to document the maintenance, the Customs Agent removed the panel himself. Non compliance with company section XX.XX and associated 14 CFRs. No coordination between corporate security and aircraft maintenance management. Corporate security notifies maintenance management of the need for mechanics to assist Customs. Maintenance management documents needed maintenance (panels removed ect.) Mechanics are assigned to monitor customs agents and accomplish required assist.
1818502: I pulled plane out of hangar and conducted a thorough inspection. I checked the fuel level and decided not to add fuel since this would be only a taxi check of the plane. I decided to go through the engine start procedure, warm up the engine and do a high speed taxi to the end of the Runway and taxi back to the fuel pump. Runway XX was recently in use by another cub doing pattern work. After completing the run up check list, I announced on the CTAF frequency my intentions to do a high speed taxi to the end of Runway XX and exit the Runway.I proceeded to taxi onto the active Runway. I reduced power as I approached the far end of the Runway. I applied brakes. At this point the plane nosed over and came to rest on its back. I pulled the mixture to cut off fuel flow, turned off Master switch and exited the plane. The airport manager and some other people who work at the field came to assist. We pulled plane back over onto its wheels and stored it back in its hangar. Airplane suffers some damage. There were no injuries or other damaged property as a result of this occurrence.
1818506: Right after I made my departure radio call and taxied onto Runway XX (the preferred departure runway) for a short field takeoff. as I released the brakes to start my roll forward I saw an airplane taxiing at high speed past me on the right and then in front of me onto the runway. I immediately re-engaged the brakes and aborted the takeoff. The other aircraft (a Cessna 210) made a radio call saying 'Cessna 210 is back taxing for Runway XY'. We advised him that he had cut in front of us during our takeoff roll. The pilot replied 'I had bad info. I will expedite my taxi out of your way.' The other CFI who was in the left seat of our plane asked for a radio check, and another aircraft in the pattern confirmed that he had heard our radio calls taxiing to the runup area, to the runway, and our departure call. All radio calls I made were loud and clear. There were no calls from the Cessna 210 pilot that cut in front of me until his call that he was back taxing after he had cut in front of my takeoff roll. There is no way he could have not seen me. He had to taxi forward of my position and around me in a very tight area to avoid striking my wingtip or going off of the narrow 40 feet wide runway. Unfortunately the pilot of the 210 was taxiing so fast I could not get his N number, and he never appeared on my ADSB-IN traffic system. He never identified himself as anything other than a Cessna 210.
1818516: Returning from a camping trip, while descending over mountains east of ZZZ near ZZZ1 the fuel low level light came on, I checked the fuel and the sight gauge on the right tank showed half full indicating at least 6.5 gallons of fuel. The left tank sight gauge showed empty. Shortly after that the fuel pressure began to fluctuate and the engine began surging. I turned on the second boost pump and moved the stick around to try and keep the engine running. The engine continued to surge but did not quit. However the engine power was not enough to maintain altitude. I continued to descend and decided I would not make the airport. At that time I picked an open, grass field and landed. There was no damage to the aircraft nor any injuries. I called a friend to bring me some fuel. When he arrived I added 8 gallons to the left tank. I had help in pushing the aircraft up onto the county road at which time I started the engine and ran it up to full power. The engine ran with no adverse indications. I took off from the county road and flew to ZZZ. I rechecked the engine operation after topping off both tanks. On my continued trip to my home field, at altitude I turned the left tank valve off. Within 8 to 10 minutes the fuel low level light would illuminate. Turning the left tank back on would extinguish the light. I will be examining the right tank fuel feed system as there could be some kind of blockage.
